papers.title: TeamLearn: A Multimodal, AI-enhanced Dashboard for Reflection During Collaborative Problem-Solving
papers.authors: Rogers Kaliisa, Crina Damşa, Jan Arild Dolonen, Malcolm Langford, Runar Hilleren Lie, Terje Kristian Lian Thoresen, Richard Nesnass, Krishna Siddharth Rajasekaran
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This demo presents TeamLearn, a multimodal collaboration analytics dashboard designed to facilitate reflection and provide feedback on developing group artifacts during long- term collaborative problem-solving projects. By integrating meetings, documents, and collaboration experience analytics, the dashboard offers visualisations that help groups monitor participation, task progress, and collaboration dynamics. Developed through a design-based research process, the TeamLearn dashboard provides structured opportunities for reflective dialogue. The demo will showcase the dashboard’s core features and illustrate how it can be integrated into collaborative project activities.

papers.title: Frame Alignment and Feedback in CT-ified Science Classrooms
papers.authors: Connor Bain, Uri Wilensky
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: While computational thinking (CT) is an integral part of modern scientific inquiry, STEM teachers struggle to incorporate these ideas in classrooms. We report on the efforts of a design-based implementation research project in which teachers participate in a constructionist co-design process to design and then implement CT -ified STEM units in their classrooms. Using feedback teachers left on student responses from these unit implementations, we utilize a basic bag-of-words model to show that teachers did specifically attend to student learning at the intersection of CT and STEM. We then further explicate this evidence through a qualitative think-aloud interview with one of the teachers who designed and implemented a curriculum based around computational models in biology. What we find is evidence that STEM teachers in CT -ified classrooms can assess both CT and S TEM skills at the same time though this intersection still needs additional attention in terms of tools and PD for teachers.

papers.abstract: To support preschool educators’ integration of science in their classrooms, our project is co-designing the Early Science Hub (Hub), a professional learning resource based on promising components identified in prior work, with partner educators and curriculum/media designers. The Hub and its components are being designed to leverage technology and include educative features to make the resource widely accessible across early learning contexts. This paper details the design and iteration of one specific Hub component, the interactive simulations of science core ideas and cross cutting concepts designed to support preschool educators’ understanding of these. The session will invite participants to explore the interactive simulations and engage in a discussion to gather their insights and feedback, which can inform potential future iterations.

papers.authors: Allison Hall, Cynthia Ellis, Susan R. Goldman
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This paper presents a case study of a teacher and researcher who worked together as part of a larger research -practice partnership. Collaborative reflection on the development and success of their work together over time highlighted several critical events in their learning process. The case describes these events as well as common themes that emerged across them and how they supported changes in the teacher’s practice. Implications for teacher learning and effective professional development are discussed.

papers.title: Semi-Formal Learning Groups as Design Interventions in Doctoral Education
papers.authors: Somi Lee, Rachel Gu, Ava Maken Ali
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: A semi-formal learning group of four doctoral students and one faculty member in art education met biweekly over two years (2023- 2025) to share artworks, written reflections, and personal narratives. The group formed organically and later adopted design-based research to identify the design choices that shaped emotional safety and creative risk- taking. Data included written reflections, meeting transcripts, photographs of artworks, and reflexive journals. Qualitative analysis produced three initial design conjectures: lightweight routines that stabilize participation without pressure, emotion -centered feedback that foregrounds empath y over correction, and shared documentation that links private reflection to public pedagogy.

papers.title: What Children’s Books Do and Do Not Teach About AI: An Analysis Using the AI4K12 Framework
papers.authors: Feiwen Xiao, Shiyan Jiang
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Although many storybooks introducing artificial intelligence (AI) to young children are now available, their quality and educational value have not been systematically or empirically examined. This study addresses this gap by analyzing how AI- themed storybooks conceptualize and communicate foundational AI ideas, practices, and values to young learners. Guided by the AI4K12 framework, this study shows that while most books make AI approachable through friendly robots and playful visuals, they rarely explain how AI actually works. Concepts such as representation, reasoning, and learning were largely introduced as vocabulary rather than as processes, and ethical or responsible AI use was largely absent. These portrayals risk reinforcing AI as magical or infallible. The study offers implications for designing AI literacy materials for young children that balance engagement with conceptual transparency and critical awareness.

papers.title: Learning through Partnerships: How Co-Design and Embodied Play Can Shape a Playful Learning Ecology
papers.authors: Melinda Renteria, Elsa Baumgartner, Haydee Renteria, Heidi Baumgartner, Akshay Nagarajan
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: What happens when teachers and researchers partner to co- design a tangible, embodied game to foster computational thinking? Byte Beads is a game in which children compose and perform sequences of beads associated with actions to represent computational patterns. Initially conceived within computing education, the game evolved as teachers helped shape a design supporting pattern- based reasoning, collaborative embodied sequencing, and executive functioning skills, including attention and cognitive flexibility . Drawing on constructionist and embodied learning traditions, we examine how researcher -practitioner partnerships shaped the evolution of the game and the pedagogical practices surrounding it. Tracing these interactions across relational collaborations, p rofessional development, and classroom enactment, the paper illustrates how partnership itself becomes a site of learning where design, pedagogy and play co-develop. This work contributes to the ISLS 2026 theme of Partnerships with Purpose by conceptualizing partnership as an ongoing process of co-designing and sustaining environments supporting playful embodied learning.

papers.title: Multi-Layered Brokering for Family Engagement in Out-of-School STEM: A Case Study of a Statewide Learning Network
papers.authors: Maggie Dahn, Kylie Peppler, Kari Denissen, Keem Anderson
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Out-of-school time (OST) programs play a critical role in broadening participation in STEM by offering young people opportunities to explore interests and develop skills beyond formal schooling. Yet, the potential of these programs is constrained by limited and uneven strategies for engaging families —key partners in sustaining youth interest and identity in STEM. This study applies a multi- layered brokering framework to examine how Ignite Afterschool, Minnesota’s statewide OST intermediary, advanced family engagement in STEM programming. Using a qualitative case study approach, we analyze how Ignite brokered resources, knowledge, and opportunities that positioned families as active participants rather than peripheral supporters in their children’s OST STEM learning. Findings show how coordinated brokering across interpersonal and organizational levels can foster more inclusive, culturally responsive, and sustainable forms of family engagement. This work contributes a theoretically grounded model for understanding how network- level intermediaries can strengthen family learning and build connected, equitable OST ecosystems.

papers.title: The Power of Scaling Slowly: Negotiation of Science Teaching in a Long Term Research- Practice Partnership
papers.authors: Scott McDonald, Jonathan McCausland
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Moving innovations in education from small initial efforts to broader impacts has been a central challenge of supporting change in schools. This study is a part of a larger design- based research project where we worked in partnership to redesign the secondary science program at The Pennsylvania State University. We used the context as a test-bed for innovations and design-based research to develop “humble” theory and contest theory in teacher education. This study views teacher learning as the sociocultural practice of negotiation of professional vision within a community in broad temporal and physical scales . Professional vision is theorized not as a small scale, local negotiat ion of individual acts of practice , but as the on- going and dynamic collaborative negotiation of a learning community in response to the overlapping political economies of social organizations that occurs across different sites, places, or contexts, spanning decades. Subject/Problem Changing educational systems , and particularly the embedded cultural practices of teaching, requires in -depth, rich, extended engagement focused on building and sustaining trusting relationships. Characterizing this kind of change lies at the intersection of systems of community and individual learning, which are naturally intertwined. To address this complexity and support system change requires the cultivations of a learning environment for multiple role actors (e.g, preservice and in -service teachers, students, university faculty) and as a result involves bridging multiple cultural communities. While teacher learning occurs both in (and outside of) institutions of higher education and K -12 schools, the relationships between these two institutional contexts are often complicated. The culture and practices of K -12 institutional contexts often operate in tension with those of institutions of higher education, described as the two- worlds problem (Braaten, 2018). This tension complicates efforts at systemic change as do the multiple layers of practice involved in the culture of schools (Windschitl & Stroupe, 2017) - students engaged in science practices (as articulated by documents like the National Research Council’s Framework for K-12 Science Education or the Next Generation Science Standards); teachers engaged in designing and enacting learning environments to support students science practices (as articulated by documents/frameworks like Ambitious Science Teaching); and teacher educators engaged in designing and enacting learning environments for teachers (both in- service and preservice) to develop teachers’ practices (by extension, Ambitious Science Teacher Education). This multi -layer complex of interwoven practices contributes to the massive challenge facing attempts to change the culture of schooling, and of particular concern to us, science teaching as a cultural practice. Approaches to supporting these complex cultural shifts frequently involve attempts to “scale -up” changes, most often via curricular interventions in combination with distributed professional learning (e.g., Edelson, et al., 2021). While there has been success with change at scale, at least at the level of school districts attempts at large- scale change are mixed (e.g. Spillane, et al., 2018), generally have been shown to impact only smaller groups of “maverick” teachers more directly engaged with funded projects, or produce superficial changes in practice leaving the instructional core relatively stable (Cuban, 2013). Repeated efforts to change practice over time can also lead to a kind of change exhaustion, where teachers see all change efforts as transitory and choose to wait them out (Del Schalock, 2006). This manuscript describes an approach to school change that conceptualizes scaling in a long- term and organic way. The context is a 15+ year research-practice partnership built around a core community of secondary in-service science teachers, science teacher educators, preservice secondary science teachers, and middle school students. P articipants are in multiple overlapping professional learning experiences, but given our roles our narrative focuses on one activity of the community - an embedded, practice -based science teacher preparation program. The beginning of the partnership is retroactively marked by the meeting of members in 2006 and more officially and externally recognized with a more intentional and structured community of teacher learning that began to form five years later. Regardless, the consistent focus of the community has been on the negotiation and transformation of the cultural practices of science teaching and the intimately related transformation of the identities of the individuals of the community and their institutional contexts – their university, their schools, and more distal impacts on other schools, the state, and the field of science education. 774 Organizational structures are fundamentally dynamic, cultural, and porous. They are constantly being created and recreated by the interactions of the participants that make them up. As participants move between contexts they carry with them and create anew their identities as members of their multiple communities. They are constantly negotiating the work of those communities and how the present set of participants are constructing the meaning of that work. There is historicity to this process, which constrains and affords the possible work of participants and frames their on -going negotiation of meaning. To understand the nature of the organizational interactions (and change) that occur via more localized negotiations of meaning, there is a need to attend to interactions across scales. To see how small moments of interaction and negotiation construct patterns over time and (re)create the constituent communities. Much of the research on organizational change attends to macro scale, change is typically addressed via policies (including curricula and assessments) or other formalized components of organizations (e.g. Spillane, et al., 2018). Other approaches attempt to study change by focusing on micro-scale negotiation of meaning occurring between participants in classrooms or in professional learning contexts (e.g. Gomoll, Hmelo-Silver, & Šabanović, 2022). There is also a meso-scale, the stories and negotiated meanings that are created at the micro -scale and bridge to the creation and reification of macro -scale formalisms. As participants move through various contexts their pathways intertwine and separate creating a temporal fabric as imagined by Kurt Vonnegut’s Tralfamadorians, who see human lives as a kind of temporal skein of yarn. This fabric is woven of stories told between participants about themselves and each other across the contexts that make up their lives and their community participation. To successfully cultivate change in these tapestries of human interaction, we need to attend not just to the individual interactions, or the structure of the entire fabric; we need to think about the creation of learning environments as the creation of space to allow others to become new people, to create new selves that reflect new meanings they have negotiated with each other. To conceptualize this process we draw upon professional vision (Goodwin, 1994) to help us understand these social negotiations and how they continually recreate professional communities and their practices. Professional vision is not the particular lens an individual uses to view social interactions, it is a description of the stabilities and instabilities created by participants through the negotiation of meaning in a communities’ social practices over time. Conceptual/Theoretical framework “Knowing is inherent in the growth and transformation of identities and it is located in relations among practitioners, their practice, the artifacts of that practice, and the social organization and political economy of communities of practice” (Lave & Wenger, 1989, p. 122). Theoretical understandings of and research on teacher learning is often limited by its contextual focus (e.g., universities, schools, professional learning activities) or the conceptualization of teacher learning as individual/cognitive (e.g., knowledge framed as Pedagogical Content Knowledge, beliefs, or dispositions), which often carries with it a deficit framing ( Gray, McDonald, & Stroupe, 2022). In contrast, this study views teacher learning as a sociocultural practice of negotiation of professional vision (Goodwin, 1994) within a teacher community of practice at broad temporal and physical scales. We focus not only on a group of teachers in a single context negotiating a current set of dilemmas regarding changing practice (e.g., McCausland et al., 2023), but as a defining characteristic of an on-going, historical, and dynamic learning community that occurs across different sites, places, or contexts, as well as spanning years of collaborative negotiation, all of which is in response to the overlapping political economies of relevant social organizations. Communities of Practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991) is a well-established framing of how people learn focused on social practice as not just the mechanism of learning, but the definition of the outcome of learning. Learning is viewed as a change in practice, both of the individuals in the community, but also, in interaction with the changes in the norms and practices of the community. Similarly, individuals’ learning can be thought of as changes in identity within the community that are negotiated and manifest through practice with other participants in the community. One of the core pieces of this process identified by Wenger, is the negotiation of meaning. The term negotiation tends to evoke a discourse or even an argument, in the argumentation sense of that concept, between members of a community about the meaning of their practice; however, negotiation is more subtle and implicit in communities of practice. It entails subtle shifts in what is acceptable practice and talk that happen as groups of individuals determine what it is that defines the collective work of their profession. In short, it is a negotiation of professional vision. Over the past ten or more years, Goodwin’s (1994) original notion has often been taken up as a more individually cognitive focused notion (e.g., vanEs & Sherin, 2021), characterizing professional vision as a sort of 775 individual lens for viewing teaching and guiding individual’s decision making. We take a broader and more practice focused conception directly grounded in Goodwin’s original notion: “Discursive practices are used by members of a profession to shape events in the domains subject to their professional scrutiny. The shaping process creates the objects of knowledge that become the insignia of a profession's craft: the theories, artifacts, and bodies of expertise that distinguish it from other professions. Analysis of the methods used by members of a community to build and contest the events that structure their lifeworld contributes to the development of a practice-based theory of knowledge and action." (italics added, 1994, p. 606) It is this building and contesting that we consider to be a characterization of the negotiation of meaning that occurs in communities of practice. This kind of social negotiation is not only seen in the minute -to-minute discourse between members of a professional community ( McCausland et al., 2023), but also in how those members draw on other external communities they participate in, for example, to play with policies cutting across organizational levels of a system (Bateman & McDonald , 2023). Professional vision’s social negotiation focuses on how community norms and understandings shift over longer periods of time and are reflected in the reified and tacit activities of those communities. This can be seen in how teachers change the focus of their own profe ssional learning, the problems of practice they identify, and ideally how those problems without ceilings (Thompson, 2015) are continually renegotiated as the community deepens their understanding of their own goals and practices. Our work uses this more community negotiation focused framing of professional vision as a key construct of analysis to determine the dynamically negotiated objects of knowledge that form the core of a learning community. For the research community to move beyond less productive and deficit framings of professional learning that proliferate in the field such as short term (e.g. one week) sessions or narrowly focused session (e.g. targeting particular curriculum or content topics), we need to have ways of investigating teacher learning at different grain-sizes and scales which conceptualize teacher learning as the complex and embedded social practice that it is. This manuscript is an attempt to tell a richer story of the organic origin, development, and eventu al design-based evolution of a community of teacher learning thorough the negotiation of meaning done to establish the objects of knowledge that make up professional vision. Specifically, we address the research questions: 1) What are the patterns of growt h and development of the objects of knowledge for a teacher learning community that intentionally interweaves university and school contexts? 2) What attributes seem to support the long- term engagement, growth, and learning of such a teacher learning community? Design/Procedure The research-practice partnership in this study developed over the course of 15+ years. In that time, numerous funded and unfunded research projects took place, hundreds of pre -service science teachers were educated, thousands of K-12 science students were impacted, and generations of science education researchers were a part of participating in and investigating teacher learning within the partnership. We say this to indicate the context we are describing is complex both temporally and socially. To attempt to capture this complexity, to describe how the partnership negotiated science teaching and learning over time (Goodwin, 1994), we recognized that traditional qualitative coding of interactions would not suffice, so we turned to narrative methods. By using narrative methods, we can navigate temporal, social, and contextual boundaries to communicate and transmit complex knowledge (Huber et al., 2016) about a dynamic social system of learning. Narrative methods allow us to show how educational contexts might be transformed and render visible “things heretofore unnoticed” (Lewis, 2011, p 504) by telling “real stories” (Gallagher, 2011) that can help shift practices and pedagogies. In fact, narrative methods make it possible to capture the people, places, and events that occur over time in relation to learning. By telling stories it is possible to weave together learning and the context in which learning happens because as Clandinin and Connelly (2000) state, “People are individuals and need to be understood as such, but they cannot be understood only as individuals. They are always in relation, always in a social context” (p. 2). So, while narrative methods are used to delve into an individual’s experience, they can also be used as “an exploration of the social, cultural and institutional narratives within which individual’s experiences are constituted, shaped, expressed and enacted - but in a way that begins and ends that inquiry in the storied lives of the people involved” (Clandinin & Rosiek, 2007, p 42). To gather the narratives, we generated stories based on our memory and we contacted preservice teachers, mentor teachers, and others involved in the community over time to describe “your experience and what you feel are key takeaways about how students learn science and how teachers learn to teach.” Part of this process included revisiting data, that included video, audio, and documents, from previous funded and unfunded projects 776 and articles written that focused on actors in the partnership to help create a timeline of events, confirm particular stories, and support our narration of how the partnership grew over time. Once we gathered the data, we constructed narratives through a process of mutual storytelling to explain the learning in context rather than produce a cause -and-effect relationship (Connelly & Clandinin, 1990). Our process took the form of writing and rewriting narratives based on moments in the larger data corpus that stood out as important (Maclure, 2013). The stories demonstrated the tensions, successes, and serendipitous moments involved in the development of the partnership to help demonstrate the negotiations (i.e. learning) that occurred within it (Rodriguez & Morrison, 2019). Finally, we took the narrative(s) and embedded theory to help us make “connections” between learning and the “individual lives” of the participants and discern the “order and pattern” (Maclure, 2013, p. 229) necessary to produce “humble” theory (Cobb et al., 2003) that goes beyond a report of “what happened.” Below is an abridged narrative intended to provide insight into the data, findings, and analysis. papers.title: Teachers’ Co-Evolving Insights on E-Learning Design and Design-Aware Learning Analytics
papers.authors: Pakon Ko, Linyuan Wang, Nancy Law
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Learning analytics (LA) can provide teachers with timely insights into student learning, helping them adjust learning design (LD) and optimizing educational outcomes. However, the concept of LA is relatively new, and the use of LA integrated with e- learning platforms remains uncommon, particularly among K –12 teachers. This paper reports on a Research Practice Partnership ( RPP) project involving primary and secondary schools to develop a system and workflow that supports the integration of LA into teachers’ everyday professional practice, beginning at the LD stage. A qualitative case study of a teacher team over two years reveals how their professional learning evolved, from identifying meaningful learning analytics questions (LAQs) relevant to their LD context to recognizing the importance of selecting appropriate e- learning tools as a prerequisite for meaningful LA, and finally to incorporating targeted LAQs into their LD decision making process , thereby consciously closing the LD-LA loop in their professional practice.

papers.title: Designing AI Partner-Embedded Learning Environments to Support AI Literacies
papers.authors: Mon-Lin Monica Ko, Marcelo Worsley, Michael Alan Chang, Chelsea Chandler, Sierra Rose
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into schools, questions arise about what students should learn about AI and how AI-powered tools can support collaborative learning. This symposium reports on the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), which designs AI partners and curricular activity systems to promote AI literacy and collaboration. Unlike most classroom AI tools designed for 1:1 interactions, iSAT develops AI partners as social collaborators that both facilitate group learning and serve as objects of inquiry —helping students “look under the hood” of AI systems. Our multi -year co-design process across three U.S. states engages teachers, students, and parents to build integrated systems of curriculum, technology, and professional learning. The symposium’s six posters span AI design, infrastructure, curriculum, and teacher learning, illustrating how AI can be productively embedded within classroom collaboration. Together, they advance understanding of how AI systems can meaningfully support and transform collaborative learning. Objective of the session As AI technologies become increasingly embedded in education (Reich & Dukes, 2024), so do questions about what students should learn about AI systems (AI literacy) and how AI -powered tools may support (or hinder) student learning. While there is growing excitement about AI’s potential to transform education, decades of research highlight repeated failures of earlier innovations to do so. Scholars argue these failures often stem from underappreciating the infrastructural nature of technology and overestimating its power to drive change in classroom practice (Roschelle et al., 2010). First, technology is infrastructural in that its value lies not in its particular content but in its ability to generate new representations of disciplinary ideas and create opportunities for students to engage more deeply in those ideas (Hegedus & Kaput, 2003). Second, like previous technologies, today’s AI tools will not transform education on their own. Their success depends on how curriculum activity systems—teacher professional learning (PL), instructional materials, and technology —work together to reshape learning environments (Vahey et al., 2013). Their success also depends on how teachers and students work together within the system to support learning. This symposium reports on work from the Institute of Student-AI Teaming (iSAT), an institute that aims to design AI -powered tools and curricular activity systems that promote collaborative knowledge building and student learning around AI -literacy specifically (D’Mello et al., 2024, OECD, 2025). Our project intentionally combines both AI -literacy and AI as a tool for collaborative learning in ways that will enable the AI -partner to serve simultaneously as a collaboration support and an object of inquiry as students think critically about how the AI works. That is, our AI partners play a dual role of supporting student collaboration and as a tool for “looking under the hood” at how AI systems work. Supporting collaborative learning is a longstanding goal of both the ISLS and CSCL community, and is crucial because we know that learning is inherently a social process. Yet, the dominant approach to incorporating AI inside K-12 classrooms focuses on 1:1 interactions between students and AI systems. iSAT’s approach is radically different: we aim to develop AI as a social, collaborative partner that works alongside students and teachers to deepen their engagement with one another. This goal has required that our team engage in multi -year co-design processes to better understand the needs and desires of multiple users 556 and stakeholders (e.g. teachers, students, parents) as we work to develop and refine AI partners, curriculum materials, and professional development to support the development of AI literacies. Over the past five years, our work has involved working with stakeholders in districts across three U.S. states to conceptualize, develop, enact, and refine our curricular activity system. This session will focus on the design of iSAT’s curricular activity system to deepen the field’s conversation about the role of AI -systems in supporting collaborative learning. Across the posters, we will describe how our co- design practices, back -end models, classroom pilot studies, professional learning, and curricular routines and designs worked toward our emerging understanding of the utility of these tools for supporting collaborative learning. Overview of the symposium The 6 posters that constitute the symposium represent our collective efforts to take seriously what it means for AI systems to partner within the curricular activity systems of secondary schools. Poster 1 will detail the trajectory of co-design for our first AI partner, the Community Builder (CoBi) and how the ongoing design, implementation and analysis of the co- design space informed the values of our institute. Poster 2 will present on the design, development, and pilot studies of our second Jigsaw Interactive Agent (JIA) in secondary classrooms and how productive uncertainty was leveraged to design the AI partner interventions to suppo rt small group jigsaws. In Poster 3, we will report on the architecture and analytic pipeline that underlies our two existing AI partners, documenting how the pipeline infrastructure, state detection and dialogue policies inform the AI- partner outputs and interventions. Posters 4-6 address how we built both curriculum materials and teachers’ capacities to leverage them so that the AI partners could be meaningfully integrated into everyday classroom activities. In Poster 4, we examine how curricular routines can support students' sensemaking of their own collaborative practices. In Poster 5, we show how our PL design supported teachers’ learning about AI, our AI literacy curriculum and pedagogical approaches that center student sensemaking. Finally, Poster 6 describes the design and refinement of our curriculum materials that focus on AI literacy, a process guided by co- design, adaptation and refinement with teachers in their classrooms. Scholarly significance This session is both timely and essential. First, AI tools are becoming increasingly embedded in schools and in our world. At the same time, few teachers are currently prepared to teach about AI, use AI -enabled tools, and adopt student-centered, collaborative pedagogies—what we call a triple innovation challenge . We also know that external forces (e.g. social and news media) shape students’ understanding of AI, and that schools/educators play a less significant role (OECD, 2025) This session highlights a new approach to supporting AI literacy through the design of curricular activity systems where AI Partners are meaningfully embedded to support AI literacies through collaborative learning. Structure of the session The symposium will be organized as a structured poster session. The chair of the session will first provide a brief overview of the session (4 mins). Each presenter will give a one -minute elevator pitch to introduce their project (6 mins). Presenters will then move to their respective posters; participants can view posters, demos (if applicable) and engage in discussion. We will invite participants to engage in two “rounds” of poster-viewing (30 mins each), so that co-presenters have a chance to view other s’ posters . Our discussant will synthesize the posters and pose questions for the audience to discuss, focusing on the challenges and affordances of AI -powered systems in supporting collaborative learning in schools (20 minutes). CoBi Origins: Co-design narratives as boundary objects to translate Co-design findings into interdisciplinary implementation Michael Alan Chang Objectives Collaborative and participatory design is increasingly used to inform the design and implementation of AI -Ed tools that are responsive to the needs and lived experiences of interest holders (Ravi et al., 2025). An AI -Ed research team hosts a co -design context, completes an analysis of it, and then responds to the co- design efforts through implementation. While this sequential and linear process simplifies the already complex and interdisciplinary process of building AI-Ed tools, it can constrain both the types of analysis that can be conducted within the co-design context and the ways in which stakeholders can engage in the ongoing design of AI-Ed tools 557 (Chang, under review). Here, I share our efforts in iSAT, where there were parallel, longitudinal efforts to (a) develop and analyze a three- year co-design study with high school youth to surface their hopes and concerns around the use of AI in schools and (b) respond to the findings of those co- design studies to develop AI partners and curricular activity systems that surround the use of the technology. Here, I ask: how does the ongoing design, implementation, and analysis of co- design spaces shape the des ign activities of an interdisciplinary research institute? Perspectives Here, I view stories about co-design activities as an evolving boundary object that guides how large-scale AI-Ed implementation teams take on co-design findings (Star & Griesemer, 1989). Boundary objects are conceptualized as “how artifacts can fulfill a specific function in bridging intersecting practices” (pg. 134, Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). As Star (2010) clarifies, a boundary object is characterized by interpretive flexibility across different contexts, allowing each context to tailor the object to its own needs locally. Finally, boundary objects follow particular trajectories within organizational contexts; once created, boundary objects evolve through local tailoring, standardize over time, and, finally, fade away as the standardization practices begin to constrain possible local adaptations. In turn, new boundary objects are then created.

papers.title: Science at Work: Science and Learning among Coffee Roasters
papers.authors: Bradley Davey
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: For more than a century science education has been guided by a promise that schools will prepare students to use science in everyday life. Yet little research has examined how science is actually used in everyday life. My dissertation takes this gap seriously by studying science and learning as they occur outside of school. Drawing from extended ethnographic fieldwork, I analyze how professionals in the coffee industry use, teach, and learn science in their daily work. Goals of the research My dissertation has three goals: First, to document how science is used outside of laboratories, which have long defined what counts as science. Second, to analyze how learning unfolds through the embodied, material, and social practices that constitute such work. Lastly, to translate those findings into principles for designing science learning environments. Taken together, these goals address a long-standing gap in science education and learning sciences research: the disconnect between the things learned in schools and those used in everyday life. My dissertation argues that reimagining science education-and education more generally-requires renewed attention to the diverse settings in which science and learning occur.

papers.abstract: This paper reports on findings from a research-practice partnership that co-designed, piloted, and iterated on discussion -based world history lessons. Drawing on survey responses from design teachers (n=11) across two years, we identify that participation shaped three interconnected areas of teacher learning: (1) sustained shifts in instructional practices towards integrating clas sroom discussion, (2) growth in expertise and confidence as discussion facilitators, and (3) expanded professional identity and agency as mentors and leaders. In addition, the importance of collaboration and relationships w as strongly emphasized by all participants across both years, and analysis suggests that this was the key factor anchoring the co-design process.

papers.authors: Ananda Marin
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this talk, Dr. Ananda Marin traces her own history with the methodologies of community-based design research and co-design, linking what she has learned to key organizing constructs in this domain — matters of purpose, place, scale, impact, power, and equity. She shares axioms that were surfaced and re-membered while partnering alongside Indigenous families and most recently with improvisational jazz artists to design generative contexts that move toward collective thriving. From here, Dr. Marin reflects on how partnering can extend the field’s conceptualizations of learning in consequential ways. Sociocultural theories in the learning sciences have conceptualized learning as both the acquisition of practices as well as shifts in the use of cultural and cognitive resources for the purposes of meaning making. She suggests that these theories, which have played a pivotal role in her scholarly trajectory, can be expanded when we theorize alongside scholarship in Indigenous Studies and the work of Black and Indigenous learning scientists who have foregrounded the importance of kinship, relationality, respect, responsibility, reciprocity, and reverence. Turning to questions of human maturation, the talk will invite the learning sciences community to consider the field-wide consequences of theorizing from human centrism. Building with the work of scholars who have reminded us that sociality is organized through the interconnectedness of talk and interaction, as well as four years of conversations and art making with creative musicians, Dr. Marin proposes that wondering about and with sound making can expand our understandings of human learning in ways that are necessary for meeting the challenges we face as a society. Bio: Ananda Marin is associate professor in the Department of Education and faculty in American Indian Studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (Tongva territory). papers.title: Extending CSCL Affordances for Multilingual Classrooms: Teacher Perspectives on AI -Supported Collaboration
papers.authors: Pragati Maheshwary, Alina Guha, Shamya Karumbaiah
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Multilingual classrooms add layers of complexity to collaboration: teachers rarely share every student’s home language, peers struggle to build common ground, and AI translation can miss linguistics nuance. We report findings from focus groups conducted with teachers of multilingual students to gauge their view on AI-supported collaboration across three collaboration pathways: student -student, teacher-student, and student-AI. Teachers welcomed real-time subtitling/translation to support comprehension and questioning, and lightweight tools that surface peers’ ideas via transcripts and highlights for clarifications. They were skeptical of in-class 1:1 student-AI partnering, citing risks to social connection, teacher workload, and scope creep. Using Jeong & Hmelo -Silver’s seven affordances as our lens, we identify where affordances blend within pathways, and where they need rethinking for multilingual equity. We translate teacher concerns into CSCL -aligned design adaptations and contribute extended versions of affordances to guide AI-integrated CSCL that is equitable for linguistically diverse classrooms.

papers.abstract: Teachers have the potential to be transformational agents of change. And yet, fewer accounts from practice illuminate the process of teachers becoming transformational agents. In this paper, we present a composite counterstory developed with six high school teachers to demonstrate how they and their colleagues evolved as transformational intellectuals through their participation in professional activities over the years, including inquiry -based teacher professional development (PD) sessions, co- designing a justice -oriented computing program, and reflecting on their experiences . Drawing from thematic qualitative analysis of video recordings of five reflective sessions with teachers at the end of a three -year-long codesign work, we answer: How did teachers develop as transformational intellectuals through co- designing a justice -oriented computing curriculum alongside inquiry- based professional development and reflective practice? The counterstory highlights themes that emerged from the analysis, showing that teachers developed trusted relationships , agency, and solidarity through critical historical analysis and reflectivity.

papers.title: How Transnational Youth Make Sense of Multiscalar Citizenship Towards Climate Justice
papers.authors: Batoul Y. Abdallah, Wisam Sedawi, Rachel Sherwin
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigates how transnational youth make sense of climate change across personal, local, and global contexts. Drawing upon critical participatory design-based methods, we bear witness to how youths’ embodied experiences, including transnationa l identity and cultural, ecological, and geopolitical positioning, become onto- epistemological resources for climate sense-making. Through a case study, we illustrate how one youth connected scientific climate knowledge to war experiences, framing war as climate catastrophe encompassing increased carbon footprints and ecological devastation, displacement, cultural erosion, and trauma. Youth draw on their vulnerability to deepen understanding of climate causes and consequences, while fostering empathy-driven solidarity and advocacy. They amplify silenced voices and call for collective responsibility in confronting intertwined climate and geopolitical injustices. Youth’s multiscalar experiences constitute legitimate knowledge that expands and critiques dominant climate narratives, offering onto -epistemological testimony that reframes climate justice scholarship and pedagogy.

papers.title: Codesign and Translanguaging as Tools to Challenge Monoglossic Spaces in Teacher Preparation
papers.authors: Kira LeeKeenan, Gavin Tierney, Ferran/Fernando Rodriguez-Valls
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In an era where knowledge and identities have been dismantled by reductionist views and voices, this paper examines how co-design, a process of shared power and equitable voices, and translanguaging, a framework for identity development and social and linguistic justice, draw from each other to reimagine a teacher credential program. Within the context of redesigning a teacher credential program, we study how co-design processes leverage past ‘pre- service teachers’ expertise as plurilingual individuals and examine hierarchical relationships to disrupt traditional instructor roles. We examine the reproduction of power, privilege, and inequity in educational domains, employing frameworks to affirm diverse identities and challenge monolingual epistemologies. Methods include constructivist grounded theory and critical discourse analysis to understand participants' language use. Co- design sessions with faculty and alumni aim to foster equitable classroom discourse, enhancing pedagogical repertoires and challenging traditional roles to support English Learner/ Emergent Plurilingual (EL/EP) students effectively. Purpose Research highlights the importance of creating spaces for pre- service teachers to evaluate their language and languaging practices and the subsequent impact on lesson design, implementation, and assessment for English Learner/Emergent Plurilingual (EL/EP) students (e.g., Yoon, 2008; España, Herrera & Garcia, 2019; Yilmaz, 2019; Cárdenas et al., 2024). Fostering linguistically inclusive and just classroom discourses ensures students: a) participate in experiences celebrating, embracing, and amplifying bilingualism (Dover & Rodriguez-Valls, 2018); b) achieve academically and socio -emotionally (López et al., 2015); and c) develop critical consciousness (Cannizzo, 2021). This proposal focuses on how two faculty members engage in a co- design process focused on linguistic inclusion and justice with students and alumni from our teacher preparation. The following research question guides this paper: What language and languaging practices guide, persist, and emerge from co -designing and redesigning university courses that focus on linguistic inclusion? This research is part of a larger grant -funded project that examines how pre -service teachers, clinical coaches, and in -service teachers redesign learning experiences to support EL/EP students by reaffirming their identities and including their language and languaging in the core of learning and teaching praxis. Spanning from October 2025 to September 2030, the larger project seeks to leverage past teachers’ expertise in a co -design and redesign course process. We aim to examine hierarchical relationships in learning sites, disrupt typical instructor/pre -service teacher roles, and amplify students’ perspectives through a co-design process. Theoretical perspectives Theories of critical literacy and translanguaging and linguistic justice provide the analytic lenses we use to understand the co- design space discourses and how they intersect with structural, cultural, disciplinary, and interpersonal domains (Collins & Bilge, 2016). Theories of critical literacy (e.g., Freire & Macedo, 1987; Janks, 2010) argue that language forms and shapes experience (Anderson & Irvine, p. 98); furthermore, languaging is always situated and contextualized (Zuñiga, 2019). Aligning with other critical literacy researchers, our research continues to work toward the goal of action, which challenges social inequality and is informed by the interrelationships between theories of domination and power, identity and social difference, equity and access, and multimodal design and redesign. Translanguaging as a concept/construct captures how many named language scholars conceptualize and operationalize and how language users create meaning with their linguistic and semiotic resources (García, 2011). García (2011) argues that when people translanguage, they are using knowledge of multiple named languages and varieties (their linguistic resources) in “a single language system that creates meaning and accomplishes goals” (p. 45). Translanguaging informs and frames our research to examine how language and languaging practices could contribute to or deny identity development, equity-centered practices, and social justice (Dover, Rodríguez- Valls, Ott & Bryant, 2025). Finally, the concept “linguistic justice” (Baker -Bell, 2020) is a useful analytic to ol 1642 because it helps us conceptualize when participants act in ways that disrupt monocultural and monoglossic spaces. Recognizing how systems oppress plurilingualism requires reconciling how society silences or enables language. Collectively, translanguaging emphasizes affirming the identities of culturally diverse students and disrupting processes that privilege White, monolingual epistemologies. Our goal is to identify how, why, when, and where white-gaze ideologies enacted by teachers interrupt and deny emergent plurilingual students’ opportunities to fully contribute to the learning and teaching occurring in their classrooms, in their schools, and in their communities (García-Mateus, Strong, Palmer, & Heiman, D., 2020)

papers.title: Creating Artifacts for Expansive Science Teaching through Art-Based Collaboration
papers.authors: Deborah Dutta, Miwa A. Takeuchi
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The need for newer ways to enact human- nature relationships calls for educational practices to expand their boundaries of learning. Several educational initiatives have engaged in integrating arts -based practices with science learning to broaden the scope and aims of learning. However, the creation of artifacts that mediate the processes by which science educators can expand their pedagogical repertoire to engage with the emergent possibilities of arts-based practices has received less attention. This study describes collaborative processes between an artist and a pre-service teacher, Becca, which inspired her attempts to reimagine her teaching aims and practices, as part of a summer camp research –design partnership on a community urban farm. The study highlights how the evolution of pedagogical artifacts through collaborations made space for emergent learning anchored in embodied experiences.

papers.title: Community Convergence Among Science Education Practitioners, Structural Biologists, and Biology Teacherspractitioners
papers.authors: Amber M. Cesare, Amy Voss Farris, Kathleen M. Hill
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: We present the design of a partnership among science education practitioners, molecular biologists , and high school biology teachers. Using Lave and Wenger’s (1991) construct of legitimate peripheral participation, we demonstrate how the partnership created conditions for meaningful engagement in the specialized epistemic and cultural practices of structural molecular biology. The SHAPE MATTERS project facilitated an iterative professional learning program in which 24 teachers and their students engaged in increasingly sophisticated approximations of modeling practices ––from using physical and computational molecular models to presenting molecular stories. The team also developed a continuum of molecular modeling for high school biology. The structural biologists ensured disciplinary authenticity; science educators provided pedagogical knowledge. Our case presents a proof-of- concept for a practical approach that moves beyond generalized enactments of scientific practice by grounding teaching and learning in specific research contexts, supporting teachers and their students to develop experience in nuanced enactments of scientific modeling.

papers.title: Revisiting Wise and Schwarz’s Provocations for CSCL: Partnerships for Transformation and Educational Change
papers.authors: Breneil Malcolm, Marcela Borge, Alyssa Wise, Marcelo Worsley, Sebastian Simon, Tanner Vea
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In 2017, Wise and Schwarz proposed eight provocations for the field of CSCL following their interactions and analyses with scholars within the field. We broaden the call to the entire LS community to once again pause, reflect, and discuss a vision for the next 10 years of opportunities, challenges, and impacts we seek to make. This collective ambition is not simply to be responsive to technological changes but also to inform their design and use. Towards this end, we invited researchers from the ICLS and CSCL communities to propose new provocations for us to consider and discuss that focus both on the changing technological landscape and the need to ensure that diverse perspectives and viewpoints are brought into the forefront of technology-enhanced collaboration in meaningful ways.

papers.title: Insights from International Partnerships on Infrastructuring for Maker Education
papers.authors: Yuval Segev, Yotam Hod, Shiri Kashi, Akshay Nagarajan, Alekh Velayudhan, Ann Berger Valente, Anna Santo
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Maker education is a disruptive innovation spreading globally, fundamentally challenging schooling by shifting focus from abstract ideas to creating and sharing tangible artifacts. Often driven by grassroots enthusiasm rather than top- down mandates, this diffusion lacks corresponding supportive infrastructure from established systems, posing a timely question: What can be learned about the infrastructures and infrastructuring processes required to support the integration of maker learning? Maker education offers an opportunity to employ infrastructuring as a conceptual lens and strategy to analyze the inherent tensions between this movement and formal schooling. This structured poster symposia embodies the Annual Meeting's theme, Partnering with Purpose . It convenes international research groups who actively collaborate with local stakeholders to share diverse insights from their efforts to integrate maker learning into school systems. By illuminating these infrastructuring processes, we aim to inform a more robust theory of sustainable, systemic change within the Learning Sciences.

Network analysis of 136 coded ICLS papers (2004–2025) revealed three modular configurations of practice linked by bridging nodes such as museums. papers.title: Towards Dignity for Multilingual Learners in Science: A Framework to Examine Dignity- Conferring Classroom Interactions
papers.authors: Caitlin G. McC. Fine, Samuel Lee, Melissa Braaten

papers.abstract: Resisting dignity-denying practices in education is urgent. This paper is guided by Poza’s (2021) call to center racialized multilingual students as rights- bearing individuals through a dignity frame grounded in meaningful participation, social agency, and social equality. Using secondary qualitative analysis of our own prior studies in science classrooms, we reexamine classroom moments to identify how dignity is conferred. Two cases illustrate this frame: bilingual students’ poetic talk during formative assessment, and a teacher’s curriculum design that leveraged multimodality as poetic “talk” and inclusive sensemaking. Findings highlight how discourse moves, translanguaging, and multimodality can confer dignity by affirming students’ humanity and agency. The dignity frame provides educators and researchers with an analytic and pedagogical tool to identify, enact, and design dignity-conferring classroom interactions.

papers.title: Exploring Epistemic Affect in Middle School Students’ Peer Critique
papers.authors: Qiuyu Lin, Ravit Golan Duncan, Clark A. Chinn, Ava Lubin, Jinzhi Zhou, Joshua Danish
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Peer critique is a social epistemic practice. Productive engagement in critique requires attention to its affective dynamics. We conducted discourse analysis of two focus groups across two rounds of peer critique. The groups showed different understandings and enactments of epistemic ideals for critique. The negative epistemic affect that emerged signaled differences in students’ epistemic ideals . Yet students strategically managed affect and negotiated epistemic ideals, thereby transforming affective tensions into opportunities for shared understanding.

papers.title: Improving Co-Designed Asynchronous Graduate Learning Through Network Analysis
papers.authors: Dina Samson, Jonan Phillip Donaldson
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This design-based research study investigated student experiences in a co- designed, asynchronous online graduate course. We applied learning experience network analysis to examine 43 student reflection papers. The analysis identified seven distinct learning ecologies, each characterized by different configurations of learner agency, theoretical principles, and challenges. While two ecologies represented successful engagement, five others revealed specific struggles. These struggles included translating individual work into group collaboration and managing anxiety during transformative learning. This study shows that co-design resulted in varied learning ecologies of experiences. We proposed specific design moves for each challenging configuration. Network analysis offered a valuable method for systematically improving co-designed learning environments through responsive, theory-based support.

In this piece, we reflect on our enactments of solidarity and care by sharing about moments of calling-in, which we refer to as moments of curiously challenging. We use examples from our co-design sessions to showcase how call -ins function as transformative disruptions of harmful knowledges and how these moments are situated within other relationship building practices. We call on other scholars within the Learning Sciences community to consider the complexities surrounding systemized mindsets and how to attend to harmful productions and reproductions of knowledge within community-based partnerships.

papers.title: From Tool to Encounter: Generative AI as a Catalyst for Ethical and Epistemic Transformation in STEM Teacher Learning
papers.authors: Sophia Jeong, Sevil Akaygun, Mutlu Şen Akbulut, Ulku Seher Budak
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reconfigures teacher learning within STEM education through a posthumanist and diffractive lens. Drawing on an empirical study involving preservice and inservice teachers engaged in AI -integrated science and mathematics classrooms, the paper reconceptualizes GenAI not as an instructional tool but as a pedagogical encounter and an active participant shaping teachers’ epistemological and ethical becomings. Using data from microteaching sessions, collaborative lesson design, and reflective narratives, the study maps how teachers negotiate distributed learning and ethical response-ability as they design and critique AI -mediated learning activities. Findings reveal three entangled processes : emergent agency in classroom dialogues, distributed learning between teachers and AI tools, and ethical reconfigurations of teacher becoming. The paper proposes an onto- epistemological framework for GenAI integration that emphasizes relationality, reflexivity, and culturally responsive practice, contributing to lea rning sciences scholarship on technology-mediated teacher education.

papers.title: Supporting K-12 Science Teachers in Equitable Science Teaching through Co-design
papers.authors: Yang Zhang
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research explores how to support K-12 science teachers’ professional development toward equitable and justice-centered teaching. Positioning teachers and students as those who decide what matters to them in their local contexts, I leverage design-based research to co-design, test, and co-refine pedagogical tools with practitioners. Through this process, I study teacher learning by drawing upon a professional identity development lens. In my most recent work, I study how to support middle school science teachers in customizing high-quality instructional materials and investigate how curriculum customization catalyzes teacher teaching. Looking forward, I hope to explore how community-based curriculum design and customization help science teachers create equitable learning experiences for their students.

papers.title: “I Didn’t Drink Any Water That Day”: Marginalized Children’s Understanding of Climate Change–Induced Water Issues in NOLA
papers.authors: Ayça K. Fackler, Gülçin Kaplan
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Climate change education in the early years of schooling is often overlooked, even though children already experience its effects in their daily lives. In New Orleans, where histories of marginalization are tied to place, the impacts of climate change– related water pollution are both immediate and lived. This qualitative case study draws on a justice-oriented, critical pedagogy of place to examine how kindergarten, second- grade, and fourth- grade students made sense of water quality issues through an interdisciplinary unit focused on Lake Pontchartrain. Children’s responses ranged from personal accounts to affective reflections and critical commentaries on the challenges facing their communit ies. Findings highlight how justice-oriented, place -based climate education can help marginalized children connect disciplinary understanding with lived experience, fostering early awareness, care, and agency. Major issue addressed For children in and around New Orleans, Louisiana (NOLA), daily life is shaped by close ties to the lakes, estuaries, and wetlands that define the region’s livelihood, culture, and recreation (Colten, 2002). Yet these same connections make them and their families especially vulnerable to climate change impacts such as sea level rise, stronger hurricanes, water contamination, and flooding (Environmental Protection Agency, 2016). C limate change education in the early years has often been overlooked, even though children already encounter its effects in their everyday lives. This study responds to this gap by examining how marginalized children made sense of water quality issues in disciplinary, affective, and ethical terms through Our Water, Our Future—a project that engaged kindergarten, second-grade, and fourth-grade students in an interdisciplinary, placemaking unit centered on Lake Pontchartrain in NOLA, a city where histories of marginalization are inscribed in place and community (Fackler et al., 2026) . W e ask: What types of understanding emerge for marginalized children in an interdisciplinary placemaking unit on water quality? Theoretical approach Justice-centered, critical pedagogy of place Justice-centered science pedagogy, grounded in culturally sustaining pedagogy, positions learners as transformative intellectuals by weaving together equitable learning expectations, antiracist teaching, and agency (Morales-Doyle, 2017). Central to this vision is treating marginalized children as producers of knowledge and culture who develop complexity in their thinking, commitment to their communities, and credibility as scientifically capable individuals, reimagining science education as a catalyst for both academic achievement and social transformation (Adah Miller & Fackler, 2024). This vision aligns with the critical pedagogy of place, which situates learning within local communities and issues (Gruenewald, 2003). Placemaking pedagogies emphasize experiential, multidisciplinary learning that connects disciplinary knowledge to the attributes of a place, fostering ecological literacy and care for the environment (Visintainer, 2023). Meaning making in science as stance We conceptualize meaning making as a layered process through which children interpret events, discourse, feelings, and artifacts in relation to place, knowledge, and experience. Drawing on Goodwin’s (2007) framework, we understand participation in meaning- making as stance, whereby children continually shape their roles as intellectual, moral, and social actors. These multidimensional forms of meaning -making, encompassing instrumental, epistemic, affective, moral, and cooperative stances, reflect how children embody, explore, and negotiate their understandings in interaction with others, places, and experiences.

papers.title: “Both Are Useful”: Student Epistemic Navigation in a Co-Designed Science Unit about Traditional Chinese Medicine
papers.authors: Weiying Li
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Science education in rural China often privileges Western epistemology, creating disconnects with students ’ community knowledge systems like Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). This design-based research study addresses this gap through a co-designed three-lesson unit in a rural middle school in central China. The unit on Shanghuo ( 上火, internal heat) positioned TCM and Western science as complementary systems with distinct goals, reasoning processes, and evidence criteria. Using a Knowledge Integration framework, analysis of 40 eighth-graders' responses reveals how students navigated between correspondence -based and reductionist causal reasoning without devaluing community knowledge. Students shifted from binary epistemological stances ( “TCM is superstitious” ) to purposeful differentiation, recognizing when each system serves specific purposes. Three instructional routines supported this work: organizing family knowledge as analyzable data, using parallel comparison structures, and scaffolding dual justification. Findings demonstrate that rural students possess rich epistemological resources that Western -dominant curricula render invisible, offering design guidelines for culturally relevant science pedagogy.
