papers.title: More Than Meets the Eye: Transforming Black Boys’ STEM Identities through Liberatory Co-Design and Computational Making
papers.authors: Kareem Edouard
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines how liberatory co- design within computational making fosters agency and technical skill development among Black boys. Drawing on a pilot program in the Black Male Animation Lab, we show how connecting students’ cultural interests like Transformers and anime to stop- motion animation created co -designed learning. Findings highlight three themes: storytelling functioned as identity work through community narratives; collaboration and co-design shaped the lab as students negotiated problem-solving, positioning themselves as leaders; and students bridged cultural and technical literacies by connecting fabrication to culturally relevant themes. These findings demonstrate how liberatory co- design transformed the lab into a space where Black boys resisted deficit framings, affirmed identities, and pursued STEM on their own terms, offering a methodological contribution to equity- centered learning.

papers.title: Co-design as Transformative Pedagogical Spaces: what zooming out teaches us about learning to co-design together
papers.authors: Michael Chang, Areej Mawasi, Angel Osorio Pizarro, Thomas M. Philip, Amani Rohana, Jool Farra
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together Learning Scientists and practitioners engaged in co- design practices embedded in diverse traditions (participatory design, human- centered design, youth participatory action research, design- based implementation research, and research practice partnerships) across diverse geographies. In different ways, these collections of papers challenge two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) designed, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. By zooming out temporally and analytically, we make visible co- design processes that are deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practices, ones that researchers and participants construct a nd hone together over longer units of time. Through our collective discussions, we show how co- design spaces are unique spaces of being, doing, and becoming, for researchers and participants alike. Objective of the session In recent years, collaborative design has emerged in the learning sciences as a key method supporting the development of learning artifacts (Yoon et al., 2016; Gomez et al., 2018). Like other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences seeks to surface participants’ lived experiences and needs to directly inform the design of some learning artifact. Unlike other design-oriented disciplines, co-design in the learning sciences has focused on the relational, social, and dynamic learning processes that occur within co-design spaces (Mawasi et al., 2023; Penuel, 2019; Philip et al., 2022). This burgeoning line of research from the learning sciences complicates how we design, analyze, and assess co -design spaces, particularly when time constraints often necessitate that these co -design sessions occur over short or infrequent periods. Extrapolating concrete design decisions from co- design spaces can be exceptionally difficult given the fluidity, tensions, and outright contradictions that emerge ( Chang & Philip, 2025). Here, rather than narrowly conceptualizing the telos of co- design spaces as surfacing fixed designs, we build on Rogoff’s conceptualization of “learning as a process of transformation of participation” (1994) and argue that co- design spaces must be understood as sites where participants and researchers dynamically learn to co -design together. In this way, we understand co- design as a deeply context-dependent, relational, political, and ethical practice that researchers and participants construct and hone together; design decisions thus emerge as an ever-evolving byproduct of these practices (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Vossoughi et al., 2021). Past work in the learning sciences offers several starting points for exploring co-design spaces as sites of mutual learning about co-design itself. McKercher (2020) argues that building conditions for co-design workshops 2274 require intentional power sharing, relationship and trust building, and creating safe spaces for participants. The relational nature of co -design spaces presents a key challenge, as co -design engagements (in practice) typically occur over a short, condensed time period (10s of hours). Such tensions, even when unintended, raise important questions for the Learning Sciences community regarding what co-design entails and how to educate participants and researchers in co-design. Prior work has begun to conceptualize co-design as co-researching with participants and youth (e.g., Clark et al., 2022), while educating learners about the research process. While past work gestures towards the deep relational work that happens in co- design processes, our understanding of how those relational processes unfold is often constrained by two artificially imposed constraints on how many co- design spaces are (a) desi gned, as short, condensed, irregular, or infrequent activities, and (b) studied, as analysis primarily focused on the interactions happening within the formal co -design activities themselves. This symposium brings together five projects that seek to zoom out from these constraints in different ways and conceptualize co -design as a pedagogical space that generates educational possibilities (Freire, 1976) for transformation and shifts in interactions, dynamics, relations, roles, and knowledge, while positioning both researchers and participants as learners of co-design. The projects offered here are hardly the only projects in the learning sciences that thoughtfully challenge those constraints; we seek to make a humble contribution by bringing together a highly diverse group of co-design projects that engage with those constraints and possibilities in creative ways. By exploring these constraints and possibilities, we collectively explore different approaches we have taken in exploring this argument, by focusing on five examples of what we consider a form of co-design research work. Across these projects, we take care to highlight the conditions for co- design, describing the process of mutual becoming and what is transformed in the process, emerging issues in the co-design process (e.g., relational trust, context, power, shifts, ideologies, axiologies), and the tensions or possibilities between desired outcomes and what was eventually achieved. This focus enables us to make the following contributions: (1) We bridge between various co-design projects in the field to recognize the multiplicity of approaches to co-design, and to refine our conceptualization of co-design. (2) We outline key challenges for conceptualizing co -design spaces in the learning sciences for both technology-mediated environments and work with educators, practitioners, and learners using participatory methods. (3) We examine the kind of learning co-design environments afford to participants and, researchers in their collaborative learning process. (4) We examine the ways co -design can be a potential space for creative and constructive exploration and deconstruction and construction of ideas, among participants and researchers with no necessarily defined outcomes needing to emerge - enabling possibilities for critical thinking, liberatory education, and fluid outcomes that create new possibilities for groups and that could be similar to group work in psychology treatments. Overall, the symposium provides guidance on addressing co- design not only as a methodological approach, but also as a learning environment design that enables diverse possibilities for learning for both participants and researchers. Each of the five projects here identifies different ways to zoom out from the typical frames used to study co-design spaces, thereby illustrating different ways that researchers and/or participants learn from each other in ways that enrich the co -design process: (1) Chang et al. zoom out from one -off co-design intensives to show how researchers and youth participants negotiate the aims of co- designing AI-for-education tools over a three -year period. (2) Mawasi et al. zoom out from the formal co- design activities and show how a team of researchers/designers, themselves operating from the margins, learn from each other in order to create co- design spaces around ethical AI that respond to the political contexts of Arab/Palestinian youth. (3) Romero & Lee zoom out from simplified descriptions of participant needs to demonstrate how decision junctures during long-term co -design processes, both big and small, shape how researchers and participants participate in co- designing math and computer science curriculum. (4) Takeuchi et al. zoom out from recent history to demonstrate how researchers and participants learn to attune themselves to the agency and teachings of the Land through mutual learning and imagining, spanning approximately 12,000 years of land stewardship by indigenous communities. (5) Ehrenfeld et al. zoom out from the seemingly convenient touchpoints between researcher and academic during co-design and demonstrate how mismatched rhythms of co-design create pedagogical and ethical tensions when researchers partner with math educators. Collectively, these projects illustrate heterogeneity in co -design research enactment across geographies, topics, and methodological choices of design- based research, and demonstrate how co -design can serve as a productive framework across disciplines, including AI in Education, Mathematics Education, and STEM Education. Together, these contributions assert the need for teams t o co-design for co- design—to continually 2275 examine and refine the very processes and relationships that make co-design possible. As a final point, to illustrate our conceptualization of co-design across these five papers, we share Figure 1, an example of tatreez, Palestinian embroidery art. The art of tatreez , as described by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2021), particularly among women, is an intergenerational and sociocultural practice whose symbols and motifs (e.g., birds, trees, flowers, and places ) carry knowledge, stories, memories, and epistemologies. It has been, and continues to be, widely practiced within Palestinian communities. By “zooming out,” the front and reverse offer two vantage points on a single, entangled practice in which the product carries the process: some makers keep the reverse deliberately neat; others show thread paths and revisions. As Palestinian women engage in tatreez , they enact several choices while being intentional about what they are creating; they often do so in community and in circles, talking with one another. Like co -design, tatreez interweaves structure and improvisation, and ties knowledge to land, relations, and stories. Made collectively—in circles and conversation—the practice is both what is created -and-process itself, a space for care and knowledge-building. Figure 1 Tatreez Tatreez (noun and verb) as co -design: form-and-process as one entangled practice. The patterned front and the reverse—whether kept deliberately neat or showing thread paths —are complementary views of the same iterative making. As in co -design, meaning emerges through interwoven structure and improvisation, situated relations, ties to land, and storytelling. Handmade by Areej Mawasi. Overview of the symposium A key theme of this year’s International Society of the Learning Sciences (ISLS) conference centers on creating learning experiences that “partner with purpose” with the communities we design with and for. However, such intentions for purposeful partnership require a nuanced understanding of the educational ecologies that shape research–practice partnerships and collaborative design efforts. These intentions also call for an acknowledgment of the resources, capacities, and constraints at play for both communities and researchers across the various cycles of design and partnership—such as temporality, sociocultural and political contexts, histories, relational dynamics, and the lived experiences of participants (e.g., Bang & Vossoughi, 2016; Ehrenfeld & Stengel, 2025; Mawasi et al., 2023). While we expect this symposium to be held entirely in person at the conference venue, we will intentionally build in the option for remote participation by presenters to accommodate emergent circumstances that affect presenters’ ability to travel. This symposium will begin with an introduction by the session co -chairs, addressing the need for dialogue across various approaches to co- design within the Learning Sciences. The

papers.title: Toward a Socio-Cognitive Framework for AI Literacy in K–8: Integrating Cognitive Science and Learning Sciences Perspectives
papers.authors: Jessica Vandenberg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the civic, social, and educational landscapes that children inhabit. While calls for K –8 AI literacy are expanding globally, the field lacks coherent theoretical grounding for how children learn to understand and r eason about AI systems. This paper proposes a socio-cognitive framework that integrates cognitive science and Learning Sciences perspectives to conceptualize AI literacy as a process that is both individually constructed and socially situated. The framework highlights how cognitive mechanisms (such as analogy, metacognition, and reasoning about uncertainty) emerge through collaborative, participatory learning contexts. By positioning cognition within designed social ecologies, this framework provides a foundation for designing equitable, developmentally appropriate AI literacy experiences. We argue that understanding how children make sense of AI requires integrating cognitive and sociocultural theories to advance design, research, and practice in AI education.

papers.title: Collaboration and Competition in Educational Gameplay: Strategic Student Decision -Making
papers.authors: Tianyu Ma, Jennifer Kahn
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how middle school students engaged in strategic decision- making when collaboration and competition were tightly intertwined in an educational gameplay setting. Drawing from a design-based research study of an afterschool program, six students played Isles of Ilkmaar, a multiplayer game designed to support data science learning. Using Activity Theory as an analytic lens, we traced how students mobilized tools, interpreted rules, and negotiated roles in the game’s diner competition. Analysis of three gameplay episodes showed students adapting in real time, moving from tool learning to contested claims and finally to rule negotiation. Findings highlight that collaboration and competition were not separate modes of activity but operated together, with conflicts often catalyzing adaptation and role change. This work contributes to CSCL by showing how collaborative learning can be sustained under competitive pressures, offering implications for the design of educational environments that integrate both cooperative and adversarial elements.

papers.title: From Implementation to Innovation: Re-imagining the role of Practice in Research
papers.authors: Linette Victor
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Reverse Translation (RT) is a conceptual framework repositioning educational practice as a generative source of knowledge. Drawing from Design-Based Research (DBIR), Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs), and Improvement Science (IS), RT challenges the conventional theory-to-practice pipeline by beginning with practitioner-identified tensions and insights. It offers a structured process for elevating practitioner insights into theoretical discourse, fostering reciprocal learning, and context-specific innovation. This model is especially relevant for knowledge mobilizers, such as instructional coaches and teacher leaders, who often support others ’growth without sustained opportunities to develop their own practice. RT contributes to the learning sciences by expanding methodologies for practice-initiated inquiry, deepening commitments to equity, and strengthening the relevance and adaptability of contextually grounded interventions. Using vignettes and applied examples, this paper identifies how RT can inform professional development and research design, bridging the research- practice divide in more effective ways.

papers.title: Teaching and Learning Mathematics with Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Victoria Delaney
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Novel technologies influence the curriculum, pedagogy, and learning in schools. My research explores the impacts of AI-based tools in mathematics education, attending to how these tools influence teaching practice and how students learn to think mathematically. My scholarly goal is to support mathematics and stochastics teachers in developing innovative and robust pedagogies that uphold cognitive demand in learning even as tools that automate humanistic thinking become endemic to schooling. Overview My research centers curriculum, pedagogy, cognition, and AI/LLM automation in mathematics. I am interested in how AI-based tools mediate students’ mathematical thinking and teachers’ development of expert teaching practices to support student thinking. My interests stem from my experience as a high school math teacher of seven years, where I learned that mathematics tools and curricular resources played a major role in lesson orchestration and what my students ultimately learned (Brown, 2011). I conceptualize teachers and learners as agentic, creative, and curious drivers of learning rather than recipients of societal changes influenced by developments in AI automation. I further envision teachers as lesson designers and orchestrators who, when faced with the latest technological disruptions, can design effective instruction based in part on multi-faceted forms of teacher knowledge, including knowledge of how students’ interactions with tools impact their learning. To support teacher learning with insights about AI-tools’ impacts on students’ mathematical thinking, I have recently begun to research students’ AI-mediated problem solving processes (Delaney et al., 2025b). This work is in its second year and involves both well-defined and ill-defined mathematics tasks. I conduct video- recorded task-based interviews and observe the problem solving processes that surround students’ decisions, evaluations, AI trust, and epistemic judgments of mathematics output produced by chatbots. I have initiated this work in both clinical and classroom settings with algebra, calculus, statistics, data science, and numerical reasoning tasks. The findings from these studies inform my own teaching practice and AI adaptations, and with this knowledge, I continuously work to help other teachers develop design skills for an AI-integrated future. Establishing this program requires proficiency with the latest technologies. Under some conditions, technologies can create dynamic, inquiry-driven learning experiences that raise the cognitive demand required to solve nonroutine tasks, such as appraising the quality of a dataset or designing a facial recognition classifier (Delaney & Lee, 2024; Delaney & Selbach-Allen, 2025). In other circumstances, technology can derail students (or teachers) from their learning goals. My research program explores how teachers and students use novel technologies, the affordances and challenges that arise from their technology use, transformations on student and teacher thinking that are mediated by technology, and implications for learning. Theoretical frameworks I draw from theoretical frameworks that foreground the complexity of teaching and learning. I have several lines of research that build from different lineages of theory. When I conceptualize relationships between math curriculum and teaching, I draw from Brown’s illustration of teaching as adaptative, improvisational design work, akin to orchestrating a jazz concert (Brown, 2011). His pedagogical design capacity framework formed the basis of my dissertation, where I studied how statistics teachers adapted and enacted a machine learning curriculum (Delaney, 2025). When I conceptualize teachers’ mathematical professional learning with AI, I draw from teacher knowledge (Shulman, 1986) and teacher noticing (van Es & Sherin, 2008). What teachers attend to, interpret, and how they respond to students is directly related to their knowledge. Yet while teachers are still in the early stages of developing their knowledge, they may not yet have the multimodal forms of expertise to evaluate LLMs’ output and/or claims about students’ mathematical thinking. I am therefore developing theories about when and how mathematics teachers may prompt LLMs as cognitive supports, and what additional (human) supports they need to grow their pedagogical content knowledge and noticing abilities. From the student perspective, I have recently explored knowledge building with AI-based tools (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2020) and building expertise in mathematics with LLMs (Chi & Glaser 1985; Hiebert & Carpenter, 1992). Today’s LLMs can imitate humanistic mathematical reasoning, and can complete most of K- 12 mathematics tasks with minimal prompting specifications. It is therefore necessary for students and teachers to discern how to use LLMs to build knowledge and foster their own expertise rather than bypass the cognitive work involved in mathematics problem solving altogether. Recent work has begun to explore what human learning a nd epistemic agency may look like when LLMs are involved in mathematics tasks, proposing that students’ uses of LLMs are indicative of how much problem solving agency they retain versus offload to intelligent agents (Wu et al., 2025). I intend to extend this work and study how students’ LLM uses mediate their moment-by-moment thinking and what agency they preserve as they develop problem solving skills.

papers.title: Bodies, Participation, and Power: Learning as a Site of Inclusion, Exclusion, and Resistance
papers.authors: Morgan Vickery
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Youth bring diverse ways of knowing, communicating, and creating meaning to school, yet classrooms often privilege a narrow slice of these practices—treating difference as deficit and leaving many disabled, neurodivergent, queer, or trauma-impacted youth at the margins of participation. These exclusions affect belonging and access to civic, community, and disciplinary life. My research investigates how to design asset-oriented, participatory, and body- inclusive learning environments for young adolescents, where questions of identity and belonging are especially acute. Drawing on sociocultural and critical learning theories, participatory design-based research, and social models of ability and the body, I examine how multimodal repertoires can be recognized and leveraged as learning resources. This agenda advances three strands focused on designing multimodal learning environments that prioritize learner and educator dignity: (1) expanding conceptions of adolescent participation and literacy, (2) designing inclusive multimodal technologies, and (3) positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning. Strand 1: Expanding conceptions of youth participation This strand is grounded in my experiences and those of current adolescents regarding secondary schools’ narrow conceptions of participation. Secondary schooling has privileged print and verbal literacies while devaluing embodied, affective, and multimodal avenues for meaning-making. These framings disproportionately exclude multiply-marginalized adolescents and reinforce deficit orientations and hegemonic norms. In my previous work, I employ a social model of disability to explore how schools ‘disable’ and ‘enable’ certain bodies, calling for researchers to shift responsibility for student performance away from the individual and onto the design of the system in which they operate (Vickery, 2023). In my dissertation, I introduce a five- dimensional inter-theoretical framework that conceptualizes the body as simultaneously thinking, feeling, observed, politicized, and autonomous. I also provide methodological guidance for conducting humanizing, dignity-affirming research with youth living in non-normative bodies (Vickery, 2025a) and employ critical resistance narrative analysis to examine how adolescents navigate and resist normative embodied expectations in schools (Vickery, 2025b). Moving forward, I expand normative notions of participation in youth civic education. I extend this work into civic and technical domains—motivated by the current sociopolitical climate. Such work demands multidisciplinary and multimodal competencies that cannot be siloed within individual subject areas. To these ends, I hope to support adolescents’ learning of media, data, digital, and scientific literacies through engagement with culturally relevant issues. Building from epistemic practices in science and engineering education (e.g., evidence evaluation, systems reasoning, modeling), I see opportunities to extend these into literacy/language education (rhetorical device usage, media & data literacy, interpretation of misinformation), social studies/history (complex sociopolitical systems, causal mechanisms), and computing education (engineering ethics, data privacy, transparency, ethical AI adoption). As political systems increasingly disenfranchise multiply-marginalized youth, these literacies become not abstract skills but conceptual and tangible tools for civic and social change. A society of care must acknowledge and design against these barriers. Strand 2: Designing inclusive multimodal technologies This strand is rooted in my experience as a UX designer and researcher, where access and inclusion were often addressed retroactively rather than prioritized from the start. In educational technologies, this reinforces deficit- oriented assumptions about learners whose practices do not align with normative expectations. This work centers on learners’ histories, needs, and desires in the edtech design process, ensuring technologies are proactive, responsive, and adaptive to learners’ needs. In my recent work (Vickery & Danish, 2025), I share my rapid design and iterative refinement of a mixed-reality embodied learning environment for a reverse-inclusion summer camp for youth with moderate-to- severe disabilities, aimed at identifying and addressing barriers to expression and participation. In my 2024 work o n the GEM-STEP project (Vickery et al., 2024; NSF Grants #1908632 & #1908791), I led my team in integrating trauma-informed pedagogies into the facilitation and evaluation of mixed-reality embodied activities (where students use motion-tracking technologies to collaboratively model complex scientific phenomena), demonstrating how centering comfort, choice, and agency can amplify students’ capacities for participation. In Zhou et al. (2025), we investigate how elementary learners' group-divergent embodied practices afford opportunities to learn about complex scientific phenomena. As a Visiting Research Scientist funded by the Engage AI Institute, I design and develop narrative-based, AI-scaffolded, gamified experiences for middle school students that are context-relevant and engage learners in critical thinking about food and environmental justice (Humburg et al., 2025). I build on my dual background in software engineering and UX design to critically engage with how ‘cutting-edge’ technologies such as AI, XR, and asynchronous learning tools are implemented at scale. My prior work has often relied on retrofitting inclusion into technologies – moving forward, I hope to (1) establish trusting partnerships with schools and communities, (2) conduct on-the-ground needs assessments, (3) co-design contextually grounded solutions with these needs prioritized at the onset, and (4) iteratively evaluate implementation. Access and inclusion are not endpoints but baselines; innovation must be defined by—and accountable to—those most impacted. Strand 3: Positioning youth as co-designers and co-theorists of their learning This strand addresses a tension across education and research alike – that too often, youth are positioned as passive users of and participants in designs they had no role in shaping. Thus, these designs (which here include pedagogies, activities, tools, communities, and theories) fail to provide the necessary scaffolding for youth to thrive and learn within them. My work takes an asset-oriented stance, treating adolescents’ perspectives and repertoires of practice as valuable resources for designing more sensitive, equitable, and emancipatory experiences for youth who would otherwise be forced to (at best) change themselves for the sake of compliance. In prior work, I’ve offered autoethnographic accounts of how my traditional notions of research-practice partnerships were challenged and remade in a collaboration with local paraprofessionals, special educators, and youth with disabilities (Vickery & Peabody, Under Review). In my dissertation Article 2 (Vickery, 2025c), I drew on Vygotskian notions of mediation and affect to understand what affective, sensory, and lived experiences are activated for youth with non-normative embodied experiences in the presence of various instructional design elements (i.e. various activity/task framings, technologies, proximity of embodiment, sensory demands, forms of movement, & participation structures). Further, Article 3 positions youth as co-theorists of a framework for dignity-affirming, body-inclusive embodied learning environments (Vickery, 2025d). This strand responds to a recurring theme across my projects—that “grown-ups just don’t get it.” This perceived ignorance strains opportunities for authentic educator–youth relationships and deepens youth distrust of educational systems. To address this, I aim to develop organized, protected “designer spaces”—digital and physical—for youth to co-design community-facing projects and professional development for educators and youth-service providers. Theoretically, this strand validates youth knowledge as legitimate civic and pedagogical insight; methodologically, it redefines youth’s role in research beyond that of participants to that of educators and researchers with the means to help adults “do better.” References Humburg, M., Danish, J., Kim, Y., Hmelo-Silver, C., Dragnić-Cindrić, D., Ryan, Z., Glazewski, K., & Lester, J. papers.title: Examining AI as Design Partner in Creative Computing: Digital Dialogue to Embodied Expression
papers.authors: Joey Huang, Christiana Varda, Dongkuan Xu
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study investigates how AI-supported creative computing fosters computational thinking (CT) and creativity among rural middle school students. Thirteen students (ages 12- 14) participated in a six -session Creative Computing Workshop using ArtAlgo, a p5.js -based platform with Aiko, a conversational AI, alongside Makey Makey physical computing kits. Analyses revealed significant learning gains and three themes: (1) Exploring Color as a Computational Medium, progressing from syntax verification ("show me #b3c8ff") to aesthetic expression (generating color palettes); (2) Iterative Remixing and Creative Debugging, where students showed two distinct engagement patterns: extended AI dialogue versus minimal engagement; and (3) Translating Digital Art into Embodied Interaction, bridging computational abstractions with tangible experiences. Aiko functioned as a dialogic partner rather than tutor, maintaining student agency. Findings demonstrate how conversational AI can scaffold technical skills and creative expression when designed as an optional dialogue resource, suggesting possibilities for expanding computational participation in under-resourced contexts.

papers.abstract: This study examined how integrating generative AI (GenAI) and analytics-supported reflective assessment (ASRA) within a Knowledge Building (KB) environment supports preservice teachers’ (PSTs) design thinking (DT). Participants were 110 PSTs in a semester - long instructional design course. We implemented a design that combined collaborative inquiry, delayed GenAI use, and reflective analytics, positioning GenAI as a design partner. Data from a DT scale and instructional design artifacts were analyzed. Results showed gains in problem discovery and definition and a shift toward more iterative design practices. The study offers a learning sciences account of integrating GenAI and ASRA to support DT in teacher education.

papers.authors: Shivani Davé, Lindsay Lindberg, Ananda Marin

papers.abstract: This paper brings together three cases to examine the question, what happens when we approach the design of research contexts to explore professional noticing with care? Through video-based interaction analysis, a pattern emerged within the researcher -participant interactions. When researchers engaged with care, research contexts became sites of collaborative sense- making that supported participants to come to new insights about their practices. Essential to the development of these research contexts was the emic nature of the researchers’ connections to the partnerships–each researcher had a personal connection to the professional practice. Together, these insights point to possibilities for the study of a researchers’ noticing practices, which we argue is integral to the analysis and design of future research partnerships and contribute to meaningful and care-full learning and research.

papers.title: Connecting Teacher Sensemaking to Instructional Practice
papers.authors: Christina Kimmerling, Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Rossella Santagata
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: A large body of research has identified core features of effective professional development (PD). Recently, scholars called for moving beyond core features to understand the mechanisms that support teacher learning. This study contributes to this aim by tracing teachers’ sensemaking of PD to their classroom implementation. In the context of a two-year PD initiative in mathematics, this study investigates the relationship between seven teachers’ perceptions of the PD and their instructional practice. Emergin g findings suggest three profiles of teachers’ conceptualizations of the PD approach to teaching and learning. How teachers conceptualized the PD was tightly aligned with what was observed in their practice. These findings have implications for theories of action to support teacher learning during PD. Objectives A substantial body of research has identified core features of effective professional development (PD) (e.g., Desimone, 2009; Darling- Hammond et al., 2017), recognizing the need for high -quality teacher learning experiences that change teachers’ practices and, in turn, improve student outcomes. Recently, this scholarship has been critiqued for overlooking the theories of action and mechanisms that support teacher learning and the highly contextualized nature of PD programs (Asterhan & Lefstein, 2024). Yet, h ow teachers take up PD learning is informed by their individual and collective sensemaking processes, and situational factors they face (Warner et al., 2022). Moreover, impactful professional learning often requires building teachers’ situation-specific decision- making skills, which is more complex than asking teachers to implement a set of procedures with fidelity (Kennedy, 2019). This suggests that the field needs more fine -grained analyses of how teachers make sense of PD focused on developing their decision-making skills and how that sensemaking is reflected in their instructional practices. This paper aims to serve that purpose. In our context, elementary school teachers participated in PD around Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI; Carpenter et al., 2015), which aims to increase teacher knowledge of research on children’s mathematical thinking to inform their instructional decision- making. In this study, we ask: How do teachers conceptualize the PD’s approach to teaching and learning? How are teachers’ conceptualizations connected to their instructional practice? Implications from our findings can contribute to refining theorizations of how teachers learn and inform future PD designs that move beyond core features . Theoretical framework We draw on sensemaking theory (Weick et al., 2005), which recognizes sensemaking as an individual cognitive process and as socially situated. Teachers make sense of PD through an iterative, interpretive process of both talk and action; they begin to conceptualize PD learning within their existing understandings and practice, enact these new understandings in their teaching, which then leads to new conceptualizations of PD learning. At the same time, their sensemaking is influenced by the broader context in which they work, including their interactions with colleagues (Spillane et al., 2018) and the guidance they receive from school leaders (Coburn, 2005). Recent research on teacher sensemaking has highlighted its culturally situated (Liang et al., 2025) and socially constructed (Daniel et al., 2023) nature, suggesting that teachers make sense of PD through mental frameworks shaped by not only their district infrastructure but also broader cultural narratives surrounding mathematics teaching and learning. In this paper, participating teachers engaged in PD aimed at improving their knowledge-based reasoning and situation -specific decision -making skills. This type of PD recognizes that teachers must learn to enact particular practices contingent upon what their students understand and aims to develop teachers’ strategies and insights (Kennedy, 2019). In this study, we extend limited research that has investigated the link between teachers’ sensemaking of PD and their classroom decisions (Knapp & Peterson, 1995; Rimbey & Kucan, 2018; Warner et al., 2022), particularly around responsive mathematics teaching that builds on students’ emerging understandings.

papers.title: Teachers Bridging Technical and Reflective Stances in K–9 AI Education
papers.authors: Ane Vielandt Jensen, Inger Malene Surrow, Ekta Shokeen, Line Have Musaeus, Yu- Yu Liu
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students
papers.abstract: As AI tools enter K -9 classrooms, teachers face the challenge of supporting both technical understanding and critical reflection. This study examines how lower secondary teachers integrate technical and reflective stances of AI through participatory lesson design with simplified Large Language Model activities. Analysis of classroom enactments, lesson plans, and interviews shows that : First, technical and reflective stances can be bridged in discrete, well-structured activities. Second, teachers stress technical insights before critical reflection. Third, abstract reflection concepts can cause classroom detachment, and fourth, bridging technical and reflective stances requires more than explanation. Additionally, these findings lead us to suggest implications highlighting awareness of teachers’ assumptions, deliberate activity scaffolding, and pedagogical strategies to support teachers in balancing technical and reflective stances of AI literacy.

papers.title: “He probably did something really, really badder than anything”: Leveraging Black Children’s Sociopolitical Sensemaking as Resources in Co-Learning with Educators
papers.authors: Natalie R. Davis
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigated how educators interpreted and responded to a case of a Black child’s sociopolitical sensemaking. As part of a larger social design experiment and interviews conducted with 12 justice-oriented teachers, I presented participants with an extended example of a child (“Chase”) describing circumstances surrounding the highly- publicized murder of Freddie Gray. The purpose of this paper is to (1) report on select findings related to educators’ analysis of the Chase example and (2) discuss the relationship between their sensemaking and subsequent pedagogical design thinking. Findings show how many defaulted to developmental lenses that emphasized naivete, empathizing while overlooking the complex reasoning embedded in Chase’s ideas. This shaped the pedagogical possibilities they imagined in response. This work highlights the need for conceptual and methodological tools that attune educators to the sociopolitical and intellectual lives of Black children and, that position children as epistemic contributors and partners in justice-oriented educational design.

papers.title: From Making Sense to Taking Ownership: Teachers’ Evolving Participation in AI Education Across Disciplines
papers.authors: Qiuqing Li, Daria Smyslova, Amanda Williams, Shiyan Jiang, Carolyn P. Rosé, Jie Chao
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how teachers’ participation evolves as they engage in learning about and implementing AI -integrated lessons. Grounded in the Community of Practice framework, this study traces teachers’ movement from peripheral understanding to central contribution within an emerging AI educator community. Findings reveal four forms of participation: disciplinary entry, reframing for disciplinary fit, recognizing the scope and fit of AI practices, and envisioning coherent student learning across courses. These findings show that sustainable AI integration begins with disciplinary anchoring and develops toward ownership and systemic coherence.

papers.title: How Teachers Learn by Designing AI-Ethics Scenarios Using an LLM-Supported Authoring Tool
papers.authors: Jeanhee Lee, Sieun Park, Yue Wang, Kyuwon Kim, Yeji Ko, Hyo-Jeong So
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study investigates how teachers learn by designing AI ethics scenarios using a customized LLM-supported authoring tool. Seventeen pre - and in-service teachers engaged in dilemma-based scenario design within the Learning by Design framework through int eractive dialogue with the LLM. Data from prompt logs, think- aloud sessions, surveys, interviews, and reflections revealed diverse prompting patterns. Teachers alternated between seeking guidance and generating, evaluating, and refining ideas. Through this process, they developed a deeper understanding of AI ethics, greater confidence, and more student -centered perspectives, viewing AI as a collaborative design partner. The findings suggest that iterative prompting and scenario design provide an effective pathway for teacher learning and highlight the potential of LLM-supported environments for professional growth in AI-integrated education.

papers.title: Modelling Complex Learning Interactions—A Hands-on Workshop on Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis (HINA)
papers.authors: Shihui Feng, Kester Yew Chong Wong, Tongguang Li, Dragan Gasevic
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Learning is inherently a complex, multi-faceted process situated across learners, tools, and environments. This workshop introduces HINA (Heterogeneous Interaction Network Analysis), a methodological framework for modeling and analyzing complex learning interactions through networked relationships across diverse entities such as students, behaviors, and artifacts. By representing learning process data as heterogeneous interaction networks, HINA provides researchers with a means to uncover latent patterns, measure theoretical constructs, and derive actionable insights into learning processes. This half-day workshop features interactive discussions and a hands-on tutorial with the HINA webtool (hina- network.com), enabling participants to analyze their own data, followed by featured case studies and collaborative discussion on future applications in learning sciences. This workshop will contribute to the learning sciences community by disseminating a novel open-source tool for analyzing complex learning interactions, enhancing the methodological capacity for theoretical development.

papers.title: Bridging Theory and Practice: A Design-Based Research Approach to Strengthening Evaluation in Science Museums
papers.authors: Kari Ross Nelson, Lisa Lundgren
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This design -based research study examines the relationship between evaluation theory and practice in science museums. Through interviews with six museum evaluators and a broader survey, researchers found that museum evaluators have minimal engagement with formal evaluation theory, relying instead on on- the-job training, templates, and practical tools. This tenuous practice -theory relationship stems from limited formal evaluation training, with most evaluators entering the field through adjacent roles rather than intentional career planning. While evaluators do reference some pragmatic frameworks, they more commonly draw from concrete resources and theories from adjacent fields such as education and psychology. This work-in-progress outlines the first phase of a multi-phase DBR project aimed at co-designing a professional learning tool that strengthens evaluation theory use among science museum evaluators. This research demonstrates how learning sciences methodologies can advance understanding of learning in informal contexts while simultaneously contributing to practice - based theory development in evaluation.

papers.title: Modeling Discourse Shifts in Critical Machine Learning: How Black Girls Reimagine Surveillance through Design
papers.authors: Atefeh Behboudi, Golnaz Arastoopour Irgens, Omer Zahid
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines how the discourse of surveillance shifted among middle school Black girls through their participation in a Critical Machine Learning (CML) project grounded in sociocultural learning theories and Critical Race Technology Theory. Using a Quantitative Ethnography research design, this study collected data through students' interaction in their groups over two consecutive sessions within a twelve -session program implementation. Ordered network analysis (ONA) reveals that students initially positioned surveillance in a binary category, either for care or control, with a weak connection between the two. Eventually, students began to position care as a primary purpose of surveillance and justified why care was important. These findings underscore the importance of integrating critical STEM education in schools, providing students with opportunities to engage and question the technologies they design.

papers.abstract: This scoping review examines how AI supports collaborative learning as knowledge creation in varied educational contexts. Unlike previous reviews that discuss learning more broadly, this study focuses on the epistemological and methodological foundations of AI - supported collaboration. Using the PRISMA protocol, the authors analyzed 72 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025, employing bibliographic coupling and ENA to identify research communities and their research strands. Six research communities emerged, each representing different strands —ranging from cognitive and sociocultural to design -based and systemic approaches. These communities reveal diverse perspectives on AI’s role. The findings indicate that much of the current research centers on individual learning and distal outcomes, while studies oriented toward knowledge creation, especially within CSCL and the LS, remain limited but are increasing. papers.title: Learning through Partnership: Integrating Disciplinary and Experiential Knowledge in Teacher Education
papers.authors: Richa Sharma, Gomathi Jatin, Subhankar Rana, Rafikh Shaikh
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: This practice -oriented paper presents a Research -Practice Partnership between (organisation 1), a formal pre -service teacher -education institute (TEI), and (organisation 2), an experiential learning organisation. While the core design of the collaboration was informed by Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory, this paper demonstrates how the integration of Gandhi’s principles of 3H (Head, Hand and Heart) facilitates non -linear, transformational reflections within a structured design. By analysing a 5- day-long urban expedition in Mumbai, we gained valuable insights about structuring immersive experiences, balancing guidance with autonomy, supporting diverse learners, and maintaining authentic engagement. Based on which we argue that the ‘Heart’ (affective immersion) acts as a catalyst that integrates the ‘Head’ (disciplinary knowledge - Knowledge that) with the ‘Hand’ (procedural knowledge-knowledge how ). The paper also offers design principles for RPPs enabling transition of a "Legitimate Peripheral Participant " (LPP) from ‘periphery’ to the ‘core’ of the learning processes.

papers.title: Designing for Radical Imagination
papers.authors: Brit Claiborne
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This dissertation examines how learning environments for K–12 teachers can be designed to foster radical imagination through speculative activities. Data were collected across four mathematics teacher education courses at a large U.S. university, and a core group of participants joined a collective inquiry group to explore how to create elements of their imagined futures in their present classrooms. Anticipated findings include design principles that promote radical imagination among teachers, the forms of collectivity that emerged within the inquiry group, and the focal points of teachers’ radical reimaginings of mathematics teaching and schooling. Goals and background The aim of the present study is to design and analyze various learning environments where K-12 mathematics teachers engage with radical imagination and collective futuring. Radical imagination is the act of crafting new possibilities for the future that are not constrained by systemic structures or the status-quo of the “possible.” Neoliberal logics typically locate the source and the solution of (educational) problems in the individual, and thus leave unexamined the structures and collective action needed to challenge systemic forces (Barker & Scheele, 2016). Radical imagination by collectives of teachers, and fostering that imagination through teacher education, intentionally endeavors to rewrite the dominant power structures that maintain the status quo of capitalist, white supremacist, and settler-colonial systems in education. This is of particular importance in mathematics teacher education, as the discipline of mathematics is viewed as politically neutral (Harouni, 2015), which ultimately serves to maintain hierarchies of power and underscores patriarchal ways of knowing (Hesse-Biber et al., 2004). Specifically, this research explores: (1) How can learning environments in mathematics education be designed to contribute to the development of teacher radical imagination, and (2) How can collectives of teachers act on their imagined future in the present? Study design and methods This qualitative dissertation comprises of three studies with data collected in the mathematics teacher education department of a large U.S. university. Across the studies, 40 participants consented to include their data for analysis, and I collected over 170 speculative writing artifacts. In study 1, I incorporated identical speculative writing prompts into four education courses to explore the content of teachers’ imagined futures. papers.title: Reimagining Early AI Literacies: A Care-Centered Co-Design Study with Parents and Young Children
papers.authors: Grace Yaxin Xing
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: While AI literacy has gained increasing attention in education, existing frameworks often privilege technical competencies and workforce preparation, overlooking the developmental, relational, and ethical concerns central to early childhood education. Grounded in socio-constructionist theories and an ethics-of-care lens, my dissertation reimagines AI literacy as a care-centered, co-constructed practice within family ecologies. This three-paper dissertation includes: (1) a care-centered critical review of AI literacy frameworks that advances a new conceptualization of early AI literacies in ECE; (2) a techno-ethnographic study investigating parents’ beliefs, practices, and contexts shaping children’s AI learning at home; and (3) participatory co-design with parent–child dyads to iteratively develop a Family AI Literacy Starter Kit. These studies bridge conceptual, perceptual, and design perspectives by identifying gaps in current frameworks, mapping parental engagement, and co-creating developmentally appropriate resources toward justice-oriented early AI literacies in families.

The Innovation Hub is committed to providing computationally-rich, community-driven, and project-based instruction to every middle school student in the school division. Instead of pulling students out of existing schools to form a separate laboratory school, the Innovation Hub uses a push-in model to provide experiences for all students across grade levels in a school district. Using principles of effective design- based implementation research as guiding principles, this paper describes the history of the RPP, the iterative refinement of the Innovation Hub, as well as current and future directions of the effort.

papers.title: Design as Relational Pedagogy: Culturally Sustaining Computing with Tibetan Girls in Diaspora
papers.authors: Yeshi Paljor, Heather Killen, Shakuntala Devi Gopal, Chris Proctor, Sameer Honwad

papers.abstract: This paper examines how design and pedagogy jointly shaped learning, belonging, and identity in a six-week virtual computing program for Tibetan diaspora youth in the United States. Guided by sociocultural and relational perspectives, we analyze two cases—Lhamo and Tenzin, Tibetan girls who designed games and websites that expressed community stories, language, and values. Using abductive thematic analysis of session recordings, artifacts, and interviews, we identify four mechanisms of design as relational pedagogy: pedagogical mediation of tools, collaborative care, storytelling as reflection, and community -oriented visioning. Design elements such as demo codes and AI chatbot became meaningful only when relationally activated through modeling, dialogue, humor, and recognition. These interactions transformed computing into a practice of cultural care —a medium for remembering , reimagining, and embracing Tibetan identity. The study advances a relational framework for culturally sustaining computing, highlighting how pedagogical and design interactions animate learning as an ethical, affective, and community-rooted practice.

papers.authors: Dalia Hassan, Ravit Golan Duncan, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Na'ama Av-Shalom, Mariam Hassan

papers.abstract: Drawing on frameworks for Justice -Centered Pedagogy and Rightful Presence, we designed a genetics unit that engages students with reasoning about racial health disparities in the context of diabetes. We provide a design story tracing our design conjecture, how we embodied it in learning activities and artifacts, and the ways in which these were taken up b y high school students in terms of their understanding of the structural aspect of racism. Our findings suggest that while students recognized that racialized groups endure harmful environments, they did not fully grasp how historical and ongoing racism created and reproduces these environments.

papers.abstract: From Mapuche palikantun rhythms in Chile to Uruguayan rural futures, from WhatsApp organizing at the Mexico-US border to Brazilian constructionist reinterpretations— this symposium weaves together studies reimagining the Learning Sciences through Latin American epistemologies. We gather not to import theories from distant academies, but to honor knowledge systems flowering in our territories: mathematical wisdom in Mapuche weaving, learning that unfolds at the Tijuana -San Diego border, resistance enacted through digital practices. Our work traces how communities transform constraints into creativity, how intergenerational memory becomes a pedagogical method, how the periphery generates its own centers of gravity. Through empirical studies spanning Colombia, Ecuador, and beyond, we demonstrate the generative potential of putting Learning Sciences theories in dialogue with Latin American frameworks —where constructionism converses with conscientização, ethnomathematics meets epistemic footprints, and speculation becomes decolonial praxis. Together, we offer distinctive interpretative lenses that expand the field by centering community knowledge and lived experiences situated in Latin America.

papers.title: Learning With and About AI: Building Capacity for Equitable Participation in an AI-Shaped Future
papers.authors: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research investigates how learners and educators understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation. Using design-based research, participatory design, and qualitative and computational methods, I study AI education and disciplinary integration of AI in K–12 contexts. My work aims to design equitable learning environments, develop theoretical models of learner engagement with AI, and build cross-disciplinary approaches to teaching with and about AI. Theoretical and methodological foundations that inform my work My research sits at the intersection of the learning sciences, data science and artificial intelligence (AI) education. I am particularly interested in how educators and learners understand, design with, and collaborate with AI systems, and how these sociotechnical interactions shape equity and participation in society. In my work, I frame learning as a socially and materially mediated practice, drawing on sociocultural perspectives that conceptualize knowing as participation in activity systems rather than simply the acquisition of decontextualized concepts (Vygotsky, 1987; Wertsch, 1991). Within this view, AI tools and data infrastructures function as cultural tools (Cole, 1996; Saxe, 1991) that shape what becomes visible, what is considered authoritative, and whose perspectives are deemed valid as knowledge. I also draw on constructionist (Holbert et al., 2020; Kafai & Resnick, 1996; Papert & Harel, 1991) and design-oriented traditions that treat building computational artifacts as a powerful avenue for learning. When students build or critique AI applications and data stories, they are engaging in epistemic work that reveals their assumptions about what counts as evidence, how models relate to the world, and whose experiences are encoded in data (Vakil et al., 2022). I am particularly attentive to how young learners develop both conceptual and sociotechnical understandings of the affordances and limits of AI technologies, and how educators can support these competencies in ways that foster agency, critique, and creativity.

papers.authors: Enruo Guo, Emily Kerzabi, Jessica Andrews-Todd, Jiangang Hao, Patrick Kyllonen, Stephen Elliott

papers.abstract: This study presents the design and implementation of a fifth- grade Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum within a hybrid digital collaborative environment. Using a user -centered design approach, we engaged teachers and a school administrator as co - designers over a four -month period to iteratively refine the features and tools from a collaborative learning and assessment system (EPCAL). Key design decisions, such as tailoring class analytics to SEL and integrating feedback and rewards systems, were informed by teacher input. A semester-long pilot study involving two teachers and 22 students demonstrated the feasibility of delivering SEL through a hybrid model using EPCAL. Findings highlight strong teacher engagement and meaningful student participation. This research contributes a scalable framework for hybrid SEL delivery, demonstrating how a participatory design approach can be effectively applied to curriculum and technology enhancements - an approach that can be generalized to other hybrid learning contexts.

papers.abstract: This symposium presents cutting- edge research that explores how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can be leveraged to enrich human-AI collaboration in CSCL for Knowledge Building (KB). It challenges prevailing educational paradigms of ‘learning from AI’ and instead it foregrounds collaborative creation, emphasizing how GenAI can be harnessed to enrich epistemic agency empowering learners in knowledge building. Building on four decades of KB research, this symposium aims to enrich both the conceptualization and design of human- AI collaboration for knowledge advancement. Seven interrelated contributions demonstrate emergent KB -AI design approaches, including dialogic approaches that engage learners in collaborative dialogue with AI, and integrated approaches that embed AI affordances into knowledge building environments. These designs span diverse contexts from doctoral interdisciplinary research to K -12 classrooms. Grounded in a design-based approach, this symposium positions these contributions as conceptual artifacts for design advancement and envisions new KB-AI synergies that enable emerging forms of CSCL and knowledge creation.

papers.title: Cultivating Relational Trust in Community-Engaged Educational Research Partnerships for Environmental Justice
papers.authors: Chris Jadallah, Emily V. Reigh, Symone Gyles, Devon Azzam, Lauren Daus, Sam Burmester, Minjung Shin, Amanda Gonzaga, Danielle Harlow, Julie A. Bianchini, Hosun Kang
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Community-engaged educational research partnerships have the potential to catalyze new approaches to environmental justice teaching and learning by bringing together multiple actors with different lenses, positionalities, epistemologies, and expertise to unsettle normative approaches to educational practice. Such work, however, requires situating relational trust as central to partnership development. In this paper, we examine how relational trust was built across four different educational partnerships working toward environmental justice. We identify five themes that support developing and sustaining relational trust: (a) collectively working toward socio-ecological change, (b) naming and disrupting hierarchies, (c) purposeful processes, (d) centering relationality, and (e) redistributing resources. Theoretically, this paper advances our understanding of relational trust as central to partnership work; methodologically, it deepens our understanding of using partnership artifacts to understand partnership dynamics; and practically, it provides insights and tools for researchers who aspire to cultivate and sustain relational trust in partnership activities. Major issue(s) addressed In the face of ever -increasing environmental challenges, there is a growing need to innovate novel forms of teaching and learning that support youth and communities in understanding, interrogating, and taking action to address environmental injustice and to work toward socio- ecological well -being. Taking this as a point of departure, this paper examines community -engaged educational research partnerships as having the potential to catalyze novel frameworks, models, and approaches for environmental justice education. These types of partnerships involve collaborations that extend beyond researchers and school districts; they intentionally include researchers, youth, families, teachers, administrators, frontline communities, land workers, and other actors who are collectively working toward educational and environmental improvement. Such partnerships are uniquely positioned to support this work because they bring together people with different perspectives to jointly identify problems of practice, co-design potential solutions, and monitor their effectiveness across iterations (Bang et al., 2010; Coburn & Penuel, 2016; Ishimaru et al., 2016). Within these partnership processes, diverse sets of actors bring together different sets of expertise in order to envision, implement, and evaluate novel curricular, pedagogical, and material interventions in support of environmental justice education - from new infrastructures like green schoolyards and outdoor classrooms, to new curriculum that engages environmental justice as an anchoring phenomenon of inquiry. In examining community -engaged educational research partnerships, we focus on the construct of relational trust. Relational trust is defined here as the willingness to participate in relationships that potentially involve risk, vulnerability, and tension on the basis of interactions premised on benevolence, competence, reliability, and respect (Kolleck, 2023). Specifically, we ask, how is relational trust built in community -engaged educational research partnerships working toward environmental justice? Theoretical and methodological approach(es) pursued Theoretically, we draw on literature on research-practice partnerships (Coburn & Penuel, 2016) and participatory design research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) to frame our study of relational trust. From these perspectives, we understand partnerships and design processes as spaces of learning in and of themselves, where researchers, teachers, and, in the present cases, additional community-based partners collaborate across boundaries to negotiate 388 goals, engage in shared practices, and innovate pedagogical and curricular practices (Goldman et al., 2022; Morales-Doyle et al., 2025). Engaging in boundary crossing necessitates nurturing sustained relational trust. Cultivating relational trust happens over time and is a continuous process, entailing a deliberate, intentional focus on power and privilege given partners’ diverse histories, social positions, and range of prior experiences (Henrick et al., 2023; Vakil et al., 2016). When partners with diverse organizational and personal identities, structures, and routines come together, there is opportunity and risk, both of which may be amplified in work to address environmental justice given different histories of marginalization, contested meanings and values associated with the environment, and intersecting challenges that cut across political, cultural, and ecological lines (Morales - Doyle et al., 2025). This makes relational trust all the more important as an area of inquiry.

papers.title: A Design Space for Dialogic Assessment in CSCL
papers.authors: Rolf Steier, Magnus Hontvedt, Jacob Davidsen, Charlotte Beal, Morten Oddvik, Marit Solem
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Dialogic assessment remains remarkably unexplored as a research and design setting in CSCL. We address this gap by developing a design space to support future partnership-based work in our field. Our design space reflects a 1.5- year investigation of dialogic assessment practices and perspectives conducted through literature review work, focus group interviews with practitioners, formal and informal discussions with colleagues and prototype development work with technology designers. First, we frame the design space concept before arguing for the relevance of dialogic assessment as a potential CSCL activity. Then, we present our design space through a cumulative distillation of four relevant perspectives and seven design dimensions. Finally, we conclude by laying out an agenda reflecting how this design space can inform future work and prompt innovative assessment practices.

papers.authors: Jessica Andrews-Todd, Jeremy Lee, Dante Cisterna, Yi Song, Edith Aurora Graf, Yang Jiang

papers.abstract: Conversation-based assessments (CBAs) incorporate conversational agents into computer-based tasks to elicit evidence about learners’ knowledge and skills in a domain. We describe the design of a science conversation -based assessment incorporating AI agents that engages high school students in a scenario related to storm formation and storm prediction. We further discuss results from a usability study in which students completed the CBA task and subsequently responded to interview questions about their perceptions related to the design and usability of the task. Students generally had positive experiences with the task and its design, though challenges related to information clarity and AI interaction authenticity were noted.

papers.title: DotQuest: Accessible STEM Games to Support Blind and Visually Impaired Learners
papers.authors: Ariel Han, Rajeev Joshi, Daniel Tsivkovski, Dylan Ravel, Maryam Etezadbrojerdi
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Blind and low vision (BLV) students face persistent barriers to full participation in STEM learning, particularly due to the limited availability of accessible tools. This study introduces DotQuest, a technology probe that integrates haptic feedback, and a conversational agent to create narrative- driven, game -based STEM activities. To examine how such tools might support equitable participation, we conducted interviews with seven Teachers of Students with Visual Impairments (TVIs) across U.S. Analysis reve aled that teachers emphasize the importance of simultaneous tactile and auditory access, the need for classroom tools that foster both independence and inclusion, and the value of designing accessibility from the outset rather than as an accommodation. Fin dings show that multimodal game -based environments can enhance STEM engagement while revealing systemic barriers for BLV learners. This work contributes to the learning sciences by deepening understanding of how multimodal and inclusive design can guide the development of equitable STEM learning environments.

papers.title: Dialogues with Objects: Learning through Relational Attunement in Making
papers.authors: Xinxin Feng
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: By engaging participants in an expansive example of open- source sharing practice, this study explores how dialogical encounters with others’ designs can inform more just and contextually grounded pedagogies in making. Building on a long- term design-based research partnership among a museum, schools, and community members, the study invited learners to engage with artifacts that carried the histories, relationships, and aspirations of youth makers. Analysis of dialogical sequences—moments of response and counter -response between people and artifacts—identified three forms of dialogical responsiveness: attending to contextual detail, negotiating conflicting representations, and sustaining dialogue through uncertainty. Findings suggest that engaging with materially and historically rich artifacts cultivates empathy, critical interpretation, and ethical imagination, reframing making as a practice of listening and responding to the social worlds that materials embody.

papers.title: From Idea Consumers to Knowledge Co-Creators: A 3-Year Design Study of Sustained Creative Work Through Cross-Community Partnership
papers.authors: Robert Huang
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This three-year design-based research (DBR) study investigates how to shift students from being passive consumers of information to active co-creators of knowledge. Conducted in three iterative phases, the study progressed from a local Grade 2 classroom to a cross-national partnership between Grade 2 (Canada) and Grade 9 (Spain). Using a mixed-methods approach, including a novel AI-based analytical tool (StAS), results demonstrate a clear progression from students reproducing authoritative information to engaging in authentic knowledge synthesis and co -design. These findings provide a model for cultivating epistemic agency by progressively expanding the "public" for student ideas and utilizing multimodal tools for collaborative theory building.

papers.title: Integrating the Learning Sciences into Technical Infrastructure for the Future of AI in Education
papers.authors: Jeremy Roschelle, John Whitmer, Rene Kizilcec, Xin Wei
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly influential in education, attention must extend beyond AI applications to the technical infrastructure on which those applications depend. Datasets, models, benchmarks, and governance mechanisms are already shaping the future of educational AI, yet these foundational resources are often developed without sufficient engagement with the learning sciences. This workshop explores how learning scientists can contribute to the design of such infrastructural public goods in ways that better reflect what is known about learning, while also addressing concerns related to safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. By bringing together researchers working at the intersection of AI and learning, the workshop seeks to identify promising lines of work, articulate key tensions, and stimulate future collaboration on learning-science-informed AI infrastructure. Overview The learning sciences offer strong conceptual foundations for the design of educational AI, drawing on longstanding research on scaffolding, feedback, self-regulation, and collaboration (Quintana et al., 2004; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Järvelä et al., 2016; Sawyer, 2022). Yet these principles still only lightly shape the datasets, benchmarks, and model documentation on which AI systems depend. Training data rarely reflect what is known about productive learning interactions; benchmarks tend to measure task completion or factual accuracy rather than the quality of scaffolding or the depth of learner understanding; and model documentation seldom describes how a system's design relates to evidence on how people learn. Recent work by major AI developers signals growing interest in grounding educational AI in learning sciences principles (Jurenka et al., 2024; LearnLM Team, Google, 2025), but without more intentional integration into underlying infrastructure, educational AI risks prioritizing efficiency or engagement over meaningful support for learning. As past waves of "personalized learning" have shown, technology that optimizes for engagement without attending to how learning works can reproduce rather than address longstanding inequities in educational opportunity. This challenge is particularly pressing as new efforts seek to build openly shared educational AI resources as public goods. The K–12 AI Infrastructure Initiative, a five-year, $26 million effort led by Digital Promise and a coalition of partners, is funding the development of tutoring interaction corpora, learning-aligned benchmarks, and model documentation frameworks that embed pedagogical principles by design (Digital Promise, 2025; Roschelle et al., 2025). For such resources to genuinely advance learning, learning scientists must be actively involved in their co-design alongside AI engineers, education practitioners, and policymakers — contributing not only domain knowledge but also the critical perspectives needed to navigate questions of safety, privacy, ethics, and equity. This workshop therefore explores how the learning sciences can be systematically integrated into these infrastructural public goods. It brings together learning scientists, AI developers, education practitioners, and funders to examine where and how learning sciences expertise is most needed in the development of technical infrastructure for educational AI. Its goals are to inform participants about emerging infrastructure efforts and the role learning sciences can play in shaping them, create space for participants to share current work and articulate concerns, identify promising directions for future research and investment, and stimulate the formation of cross- sector collaborations. Building on recent ISLS programming on AI and education (International Society of the Learning Sciences, 2022, 2024), the workshop positions the learning sciences not only as a field that evaluates AI applications after they are built, but as one that can help shape the foundations on which educational AI is constructed.
