Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108776462 GoGoData Participatory Sensing: Students, Educators and Researchers Building Collaborative Data Networks Charles Pimentel charlespimentel@ufrj.br Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ) Vithoria Cabreira vithoriacabreira@gmail.com Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR) Walter Akio Goya, Paulo Blikstein, Renato Russo aag2197@tc.columbia.edu, paulob@tc.columbia.edu, renrusso@gmail.com Teachers College, Columbia University Arnan Sipitakiat arnan.s@cmu.ac.th Chiang Mai University Abstract: In this half-day workshop, participants will engage with GoGoData, an open learning plugin that connects the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) communication, and the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) to support participatory sensing and collaborative exploration of real-time data. Beyond experimenting with the plugin’s features for data collection, transmission, and interpretation, participants will analyze GoGoData as a design case that integrates constructionist principles with learning sciences perspectives on data literacy. Participants will, in turn, extend these theoretical and design lenses to examine how collaborative data networks can foster critical engagement with data in their own educational and research contexts. Proposers/Organizers Charles Pimentel Charles Pimentel is a Research Fellow at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, supporting the documentation of the GoGo Board and the development of data-focused learning activities. He holds a Master’s degree in Informatics from UFRJ and works in K-12 education with Programming, Artificial Intelligence, and Educational Robotics. Charles is a doctoral student at the Institute of Computing at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, researching Data Literacy, and a member of the FabLearn Fellows Cohort 3. He also teaches Design & Tech at Graded in São Paulo, developing tech-for-good projects connected to sustainability. Vithoria Cabreira Vithoria Cabreira is an undergraduate student in Computer Engineering at the Federal Technological University of Paraná (UTFPR). She supports the development of digital tools and web technologies for educational and research projects. Her interests include software development, web platforms, and the creation of digital solutions that improve user experience. Vithoria is currently strengthening her technical skills through practical projects and experimentation with new technologies. Akio Goya Akio is an Educational Technology Designer for the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, coordinating the design, implementation, and documentation of GoGo Boards in Brazil, as well as the implementation of makerspaces in public schools. Akio holds a Master’s degree in Instructional Technology and Media from Teachers College, Columbia University (USA) and a Master’s and a Bachelor’s degree in Computer Engineering from University of Sao Paulo (Brazil), and a Teacher Licensure in Mathematics (Middle and High School) from FIAR (Brazil). Paulo Blikstein P aulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Teachers College and an Affiliate Associate Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, where he directs the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab and the Lemann Center for Brazilian Studies. His research focuses on how new technologies can transform the learning of science, engineering and computation. Paulo is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading its research and development since 2001. Paulo has a Ph.D. from Northwestern University, a MSc. from the MIT Media Lab and an M.Eng. and B.Eng. from the University of São Paulo, Brazil. Renato Russo Renato is a doctoral candidate at the Technology, Media, and Learning program at Teachers College, Columbia University and a researcher at Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. In his research, Renato explores how learning technologies can promote critical and emancipatory knowledge construction practices. Renato earned a MA degree in Learning, Design and Technology from Stanford University Graduate School of Education. Arnan (Roger) Sipitakiat Arnan (Roger) directs the Teaching and Learning Innovation Center (TLIC) at Chiang Mai University in Thailand. As a faculty and researcher at the Computer Engineering Department, he also directs the Learning Inventions Laboratory (LIL). Arnan is the co-inventor of the GoGo Board, co-leading research and development on the toolkit since 2001. Arnan focuses on designing technologically-rich learning tools, such as the GoGo Board, that have allowed students to explore areas including robotics, interactive art, games, agriculture, and community development. Arnan earned his MSc. and Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and B.Eng. from Chiang Mai University. Intended audience This workshop is intended for graduate students, educators, and researchers interested in exploring participatory sensing, critical data literacy, and learning technology design through hands-on experimentation. It particularly welcomes those studying or developing tools that connect physical computing, IoT, and real-time data exploration to promote collaborative inquiry and learning. More broadly, the session is open to all participants interested in integrating constructionist and learning sciences perspectives into the design of educational technologies. (Note that GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP are open-source platforms.) Duration of the event Half-day (3-4 hours, flexible depending on conference scheduling demands). Description of the event The GoGo Board was invented in 2001 as a low-cost and learner-friendly robotics and scientific sensing platform. In the years since, the project has undergone several design iterations, each affording new possibilities for students across diverse ages and backgrounds to explore powerful ideas in computing and STEM. In this workshop, participants will also engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that connects the GoGo Board to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data communication and visualization. CODAP, developed by the Concord Consortium, has a long-standing history as an open-source environment for data analysis and modeling that supports inquiry-based learning. Together, GoGoData, the GoGo Board Kit version 7, and CODAP create a participatory sensing ecosystem that enables students to collect, share, and interpret live data while examining the learning sciences principles underlying the design of these tools [1-3]. Workshop Format The workshop will be organized into five main activities. I - Historical framing. Participants will begin with a brief discussion on the evolution of tangible interfaces within the Learning Sciences and basic education contexts. This discussion will be situated alongside the rise of big data practices and participatory or crowd sensing, showing how learner-generated, real-time data from distributed sensors can reshape inquiry, evidence making, and classroom discourse. The framing will surface design lessons on openness, transparency, and agency, linking data practices to issues of provenance, privacy, and ethics, and highlighting how collaborative data networks can support critical engagement and community action. II - Exploring the GoGo Board 7 / GoGoData / CODAP. Participants will explore the core features of the GoGo Board version 7 and the GoGoData plugin, examining how each component emerged from research data and i terative design decisions. Using onboard controls, they will visualize sensor values, directly before connecting to a computer to interact with GoGoData and its integration with the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP). Through this connection, participants will experience how real-time sensor data can be collected, transmitted, analyzed, and explored within CODAP’s interactive environment. Facilitators will highlight how each feature embodies specific design principles that link tangible experimentation with data-driven inquiry. III - Participatory sensing exploration. Participants will collaboratively select a variable to measure, such as temperature, luminosity, pollution, or sound level, using a GoGo Board 7 kit sensor. Working in small groups, they will connect the GoGo Board to CODAP through the GoGoData plugin and deploy sensors in different internet-connected areas across the UCI campus. Each group will collect and share real-time data through the open-source plugin integrated with the data analysis platform, contributing to a collaborative network of distributed measurements. As data accumulate, participants will analyze emerging patterns across locations, drawing inferences about environmental or contextual factors. The activity will conclude with a collective discussion where groups interpret their findings, reflect on methodological decisions, and connect their insights to broader perspectives on participatory sensing, open data collaboration, and critical data literacy in education. IV - Conclusion and gallery walk. Participants will share and discuss the outcomes of their activities, reflecting on the lessons learned and insights gained throughout the workshop. The session will conclude with a collective show-and-tell, allowing groups to present their findings, highlight key observations from the participatory sensing exercise, and connect these experiences to broader questions about learning, design, and data literacy. V - Post-workshop interaction. Optional follow-up opportunities will be provided for participants who wish to continue collaborating after the session. These interactions may include online discussions, exchange of design ideas, and updates on future developments of the GoGoData platform. Participants will be invited to share reflections, resources, and potential research connections that extend the learning and collaboration initiated during the workshop. Throughout the workshop, facilitators will guide discussions connecting the design of GoGoData, the GoGo Board, and CODAP to learning sciences and constructionist frameworks, emphasizing how participatory sensing and data exploration are enhanced by open-source ecosystems. The session will highlight how openness, transparency, and accessibility in these tools empower learners and researchers to collaboratively collect, analyze, and interpret real-time data. Rather than serving as a technical training, the workshop offers a hands-on exploration of how open, theory-informed technologies developed through over twenty years of design-based research can foster agency, collaboration, and critical engagement with data. Participation requirements No requirements. We invite to join all participants interested in tangible interface design, educational robotics, and data science, irrespective of skill or experience levels. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past The author team conducted an NSF-funded project at the New York Hall of Science in collaboration with Teachers College, Columbia University, using the GoGo Board in data science camps for middle school students under the AISL program. We also did a physical computing workshop at ISLS 2024. Facilities and equipment required Facilities: ● Projector / screen for workshop facilitators ● Wifi connectivity Equipment: ● Gogo Boards Kits (board and sensors - we will provide them) ● Participants will be asked to bring their laptops with an available USB-C port. Minimal and maximal number of participants expected 8 - 15 participants Draft call for participation C alling all researchers, designers, and educators interested in exploring the power of participatory sensing to connect learning, data, and design. In this half-day workshop, you will engage with GoGoData (2025), a new open-source plugin that links the GoGo Board microcontroller, sensors, and Internet of Things (IoT) communication to the Common Online Data Analysis Platform (CODAP) for real-time data exploration. Together, these tools create a participatory sensing ecosystem where learners and researchers can collaboratively collect, share, and interpret live data (Figer 1). Beyond experimenting with the platform’s features, you will analyze GoGoData as a design case informed by constructionist and learning sciences perspectives, building on over two decades of iterative design research with the GoGo Board. This workshop offers a unique opportunity to experience how open-source technologies can empower communities to transform local data into meaningful insights and to apply these theoretical and design perspectives to your own educational research and development projects. Figure 1 Participatory Sensing Ecossystem : GoGo Code - GoGo Data on CODAP - GoGo Board GoGo Code and GoGoData CODAP plugin displaying sensor data from a GoGo Board. Workshop format The workshop is planned for in-person delivery, with the option of hybrid participation if necessary. The program will include interactive, hands-on activities supported by remote contributions from members of the international workshop team, ensuring collaboration and engagement across locations. papers.authors: Rachel Sherwin
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. Dr. Wise holds a Ph.D. in Learning Sciences and M.S. in Instructional Systems Technology from Indiana University, as well as a B.S. in Chemistry from Yale University, was previously a Professor of Learning Sciences and Educational Technology and Director of the Learning Analytics Research Network (LEARN) at New York University and has worked in industry, with non-profits, and in classrooms across the Americas. https://tinyurl.com/alyssawisescholar https://peabody.vanderbilt.edu/bio/?pid=alyssa-wise https://lab.vanderbilt.edu/live https://www.linkedin.com/in/alyssawise

papers.abstract: This study contributes to computer -supported collaborative learning research by examining human– artificial intelligence (AI) dialogue patterns across teams with different experience levels with generative AI (GAI) -supported inquiry -based learning. Epistemi c network analysis of dialogues from 26 teams reveals that teams using GAI support for the second time exhibit projective actions toward their goals through active questioning and concept clarification. In contrast, inexperienced teams rely on GA I scaffolding with passive responses. Notably, goal -oriented questions emerge as critical mediators connecting different question types among first-time user teams.

papers.title: Learner Pathway Analysis: An Approach for Evaluating STEM Persistence in Learning Ecosystems
papers.authors: Seth Corrigan, Maggie Dahn, Kylie Peppler
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Learning ecosystems provide children and youth with opportunities to explore STEM and non-STEM topics across in -school and out -of-school (OST) settings. Supporting learners in navigating the opportunities available to them across their local learning ecosystems is critical to ensuring learners can effectively investigate their interests. To do so, we introduce Learner Pathway Analysis (LPA), a Design -Based Research approach that operationalizes a pathways heuristic to evaluate STEM learning ecosystems. Buil ding on patient pathway analysis in healthcare and other fields, LPA assists in longitudinal tracking of individual participation and transitions across programs. We illustrate the approach with TGR Foundation’s afterschool programs, showing how LPA reveals patterns of enrollment, continuity, and transitions. By combining conceptual framing, principled measurement, and practical tracking tools, LPA provides a framework for evidence -informed design and coordination of connected, interest - driven STEM learning opportunities.

papers.title: Conceptualizations and Mechanisms of Teachers’ Learning to Notice
papers.authors: Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem, Thorsten Scheiner, Heather
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together a set of posters that focus on science and mathematics teachers’ learning to notice. Teacher noticing is a core construct of teaching, and refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making amidst the “blooming, buzzing confusion” of classr oom interactions. The goal of the session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” is conceptualized and unpack mechanisms that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Symposium overview: Goal, structure, and highlights Teacher noticing, a core construct of teaching (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023), broadly refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making of classroom interactions (Jacobs et al., 2010; Sherin et al., 2011). With the growing recognition of noticing as a core practice of teaching, there is an expanding line of research that seeks to understand how to support teachers’ learning to notice (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Prior research shows that well -designed professional learning opportunities can foster teachers’ learning to notice students’ thinking and teaching in interaction with student learning (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa et al., 2018; Warshauer et al., 2023). As this knowledge has grown, it has prompted scholars to investigate what constitutes learning of noticing. In this symposium, we pause and ask: How do we think about what constitutes learning to notice? While efforts to support teachers’ learning to notice is evolving, less is understood about the mechanisms of teacher learning to notice (Walkoe & Luna, 2020). Some research investigates how video tagging tools focus teachers’ attention on particular features for further analysis (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2020). Others have considered how different kinds of video clips are selected and situated in professional learning and how collaborative analysis of particular types of clips can shape teachers’ learning (e.g ., Sherin & Dyer, 2017). Recent work has pointed to the role of discourse as a mechanism of teachers’ learning to notice (van Es et al., 2024). However, there is more to be understood about how teachers come to notice complexities of teaching and learning, and designs to better 2318 support that. Going beyond the descriptive account of noticing, in this symposium, our work collectively explores: What drives teachers’ learning to notice? All in all, the goal of our session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” has been conceptualized, and unpack the "mechanisms" that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Using multiple methods such as participatory design research approach and typological analysis of artifacts of teaching , these studies document shifts in teachers’ learning to notice, factors that contribute to teachers’ learning of noticing, and the design choices in facilitating teachers’ learning this complex practice. T he studies identify mechanisms of teachers’ learning to notice such as coding schemes that serve as epistemic mechanisms and collective sensemaking of the complexity of teaching through analysis of classroom videos in professional learning contexts. While some papers zoom in on noticing subprocesses that different video processes afford, others seek to understand teachers’ learning to notice when teachers worked on making links to socio-ecological issues relevant to their lives. Together, these papers advance theory on teachers’ learning to notice, while also considering the situated and relational features of teacher learning. At the same time, they offer methodological tools and frameworks to advance research on learning to notice across math and science. This 90-minute structured poster session will consist of a brief introduction to the session by the session co-chairs (5 min), followed by the interactive discussion of 10 posters (60 min), 10-minutes of commentary from a discussant, Adam Lefstein from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, who brings expertise on teachers’ learning in professional development. We will conclude with 15-minutes of questions and discussion. The discussant will consider commonalities and differences across these studies, surfacing the considerations and tensions for supporting teachers’ learning to notice and mechanisms that drive learning of noticing among math and science teachers across the trajectory of teaching careers. Poster 1: Grounding prospective mathematics teacher noticing in socio- ecological issues: learning to notice in turbulent times Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem This study addresses the gap between current turbulent times and the seeming ‘objectivity’ of mathematics. We explore what constitutes prospective teachers (PTs) of mathematics learning to notice, during a time of war, the links they make to socio- ecological (Coles et al., 2024) issues of relevance to their lives, and the role of the mathematics teacher educator. Following van Es and Sherin (2002), we conceptualize teacher noticing as attending to and interpreting students' mathematical thinking. Following Mason (2002), we emphasize attention to event details for in -depth interpretation. We focus on “critical events” - moments when teachers notice students' mathematical thinking has potential for deepening. We also bring a notion of “authenticity”, which relates to teachers’ task design choices, and the extent to which tasks include social or ecological issues of relevance to their lives and the extent to which the mathematics includes opportunities for generalization. The study was conducted during wartime, heightening turbulence and data significance. We employed a case study methodology, to research a year- long problem-solving course in a B.Ed. mathematics program. The course focused on a reform in mathematics educati on emphasizing "mathematics in everyday life" and incorporated two design-teach-reflect cycles where participants: 1) photographed and discussed socio- ecological concerns (photovoice method); 2) designed mathematical tasks; and 3) taught and reflected on critical events they identified. Among 23 participants, we focus on Nadin (Bedouin community member) as an illustrative case. Our analysis examines shifts in her articulation of event details, interpretations, the social- ecological issue's authenticity and the role of the teacher educator. The analysis revealed three key findings. First, Nadin was able to bring a highly relevant socio-ecological issue to her classroom, surfacing deeply held beliefs and engaging with students about their beliefs. Secondly, Nadin wrote in great detail and we observed subtle and shifting relationships between detail and interpretation in her accounts, which is of significance to how noticing might be supported. Thirdly, in examining the role of the teacher educator, we uncover the significance of the way space w as offered on the course for PTs to discuss and work on socio-ecological issues of relevance to their lives. Through examining the particulars of one case, our findings offer an example of how teacher preparation, during a time of war, can still support the noticing of prospective teachers, in connecting mathematics to relevant socio-ecological issues. We tentati vely point to a role for prospective teachers’ sharing stories from their lives, and to the power of engaging in design-teach-reflect cycles, in supporting their noticing. 2319 Poster 2: Learning to notice students’ strengths: Coding schemes as epistemic mechanisms in design-based teacher education Thorsten Scheiner This investigation addresses a critical challenge in teacher education: developing teachers’ capacity to recognize and build upon students’ strengths rather than defaulting to deficit -based orientations. While research demonstrates that strength -based noticing practices foster more equitable learning environments (Louie et al., 2021), significant gaps remain in understanding the mechanisms through which teachers develop these sophisticated ways of seeing. This study examines how structured coding schemes function as epistemic tools that bridge cognitive and socio- cultural dimensions of professional learning, offering insights into design -based approaches for transforming teacher noticing practices. The study advances an integrated framework synthesizing professional noticing theory, transformative learning mechanisms, and frame analysis. Professional noticing encompasses attending to critical aspects of student reasoning, interpreting student thinking, and deciding how to respond instructionally (Jacobs et al., 2010). Frame analysis illuminates how interpretive schemas shape what teachers notice and value in student work (Sherin & Russ, 2014). Transformative learning theory provides mechanisms for frame shifting through critical reflection and conscious reorientation of perspective (Mezirow, 2000). The framework positions coding schemes as mediating artifacts that operationalize frame orientations while scaffolding transformative professional development through the dynamic interplay of cognitive restructuring and socio-cultural meaning-making. This exploratory study used a participatory design research approach within an intensive professional learning context. Prospective teachers engaged in three iterative cycles of analysis using a structured coding scheme distinguishing deficit-based, strength-based, and uncommitted orientations across noticing practices. Each iteration incorporated fine -grained examination of transformative mechanisms through structured reflective prompts targeting frame awareness, conscious reframing, and progressive integr ation. Data collection utilized standardized noticing tasks, complemented by reflective journals documenting participants’ evolving interpretive frameworks. Analysis combined quantitative tracking of orientation patterns with qualitative mapping of transformative processes. Analysis revealed three primary mechanisms driving teachers’ learning to notice strengths. First, epistemic visibility emerged through the coding scheme’s dual function as analytical tool and pedagogical scaffold, rendering implicit interpretive frames explicit and actionable. Participants demonstrated systematic shifts from deficit- based toward strength- based noticing practices. Second, collaborative meaning -making facilitated frame shifting through structured protocols that created social spaces for negot iating alternative interpretations of student thinking. Third, reflective reframing supported progressive integration of strength-based orientations through systematic comparisons of deficit-based and asset-oriented perspectives. The iterative design revealed how these mechanisms operated synergistically, with cognitive restructuring mediated by socio-cultural practices of professional discourse and collective analysis. The findings illuminate coding schemes as powerful epistemic mechanisms that render interpretive frames both visible and actionable in teacher education. By functioning simultaneously as analytical tools and pedagogical scaffolds, structured coding schemes support the cognitive work of frame identification while creating social spaces for collaborative meaning -making. This dual functionality bridges individual cognitive transformation and collective professional development, revealing how participatory desi gn research can systematically develop teachers’ capacity for strength- based noticing. The study contributes methodological insights for designing equity- oriented professional learning experiences that leverage the sophisticated interplay between cognitive and socio-cultural dimensions of transformative practice. Poster 3: From noticing to navigating: Pre-service teachers' expansive sensemaking in science instruction Heather Johnson, Tara Barnhart Teacher noticing—especially of student thinking—has become central in teacher education research (Weston & Amador, 2023). Noticing can be cultivated during teacher education (van Es, 2011), but connecting it to student - centered instruction requires space to reflect on the interplay between interpretations, decisions, and institutional contexts (Schwartz et al., 2021). In this study, we explore what pre -service teachers apply from their noticing of expansive sensemaking in videos of accomplished teachers to video analysis tasks in which PSTs design and enact student-centered science experiences. We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who 2320 share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We conducted a typological analysis (Miles et al., 2014) of written coursework and fieldwork from PSTs enrolled in a secondary methods course prior to student teaching. Data included their planning documents, video analysis templates, and written reflections for four video tasks: one around an accomplished teacher’s classroom and three around their own teaching. Analysis of what teachers noticed in their own and others’ videos was guided by the Expansive Sensemaking framework (Bautista & Davis, 2024). By applying this framework, the study illuminates how PSTs bridge noticing of student thinking with enacting responsive science teaching. Accomplished teacher video When analyzing videos of accomplished teachers, PSTs attended to how classroom culture shaped student participation. They noticed who was given access to share ideas publicly, how ideas were taken up by the teacher and peers, and how norms and structure supported collaborative learning. PST Videos In their own lesson planning, PSTs designed inclusive tasks that positioned students as epistemic agents and included multimodal participation strategies. They also aimed to expand what "counts" as science and promote diverse ways of knowing. However, enac ting these plans surfaced asset -oriented, equity- oriented, and participation-oriented challenges. Though each PST intended to empower students, their enactments did not always lead to the anticipated engagement. These realizations revealed a gap between in tention and impact, especially in balancing student agency with institutional constraints such as pacing guides and test preparation. Equity-related challenges emerged as PSTs attempted to make lessons culturally relevant. Some PSTs reflected on how their examples did not resonate as expected. PSTs also identified challenges in fostering student-to-student interactions. They reflected on classroom dynamics, noting the need for psychological safety and clearer norms. Importantly, they attributed participation issues to instructional design, not student deficits—demonstrating asset - oriented thinking. Prior work on noticing student thinking has presumed that teachers will apply what they learn to notice in coursework to their own practice. These results support this hypothesis while also highlighting the challenges of responsive instruction and affirming the importance of reflection and collaboration in preparing teachers to sustain asset-based noticing through opportunities to analyze their own artifacts of practice and contribute to the research base for preparing teachers to teach responsively in diverse, authentic contexts. Poster 4: Noticing in college mathematics: Development of noticing discourse in a video-based professional development Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Alessandra Pantano, Roberto Pelayo College mathematics classrooms can be marginalizing spaces, particularly for women and students of color (Riegle-Crumb & King, 2010). Persistent inequalities motivate the call for more responsive and equity- oriented college teaching. Teacher noticing is at the core of responsive teaching, with substantial research primarily conducted in K-12 settings (Santagata et al., 2021). Building on K-12 evidence, we developed and tested a video- based curriculum for instructors and graduate and undergraduate teaching a ssistants that fostered expansive noticing of students' mathematical thinking and participation (Santagata et al., 2025). Recent work has emerged suggesting that evidence of learning to notice includes uptaking a particular form of discourse (van Es et al. , 2024). We seek to unpack the relationship between participants' discourse during PD sessions and observed changes in the groups' noticing. We ask: What are the features of participants’ discourse around video- based noticing tasks? Except for a few characterizations of exemplary cases (e.g., Louie et al., 2021), little is known about how educators can learn to notice for equity. We adopt a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000) and draw on van Es et al.’s (2024) work on learning to notice by engaging in discourse-rich spaces where educators collectively make sense of instruction. Their model characterizes discourse practices that enable participants to learn how to attend to and interpret student thinking. We extend this to student participation. The authors define features of generative noticing for the different purposes that the discourse practices serve. 2321 Participants include three college instructors, five graduate and four undergraduate assistants. They engaged in whole and small group discussions around video clips during four PD sessions. For this study, we selected all segments where small groups discussed noticing prompts after watching a video clip (20 in total) and subsequent whole-group discussions. We portioned the transcribed data into conversational turns and idea units and created analytical memos. Finally, two of us deductively coded the data using van Es et al.'s (2024) features of noticing discourse (Table 1), allowing for emergent codes as well. Table 1 Features of Noticing Discourse Feature of a Noticing Discourse Definition of Feature Negotiating noteworthy phenomena A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending activity, defining what is and is not worthy of attention, and supports learning to decide what to call out and what to ignore. Problematizing and puzzling over objects of teaching and learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support interpreting and sense-making activity, which is adopting an inquiry stance toward objects of focus, such as offering conflicting viewpoints of what is observed or grappling over intent and meaning. Creating moments for further inquiry of objects of attention A collection of discursive practices that intend to support shaping interactions to gather more information for further attending and interpreting. Being accountable to evidence A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending and interpreting activity by supporting one’s claims with concrete observations, using artifacts of teaching and learning to advance an idea, and elaborating one’s ideas with more specific and precise explanations. Positioning students’ ideas and actions as resources in learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending, interpreting, and shaping activity by requiring an openness to seeing what might appear as mundane, or correct/incorrect, as something important and meaningful that can be figured out and used toward understanding. Connecting to their experiences of teaching and learning (emergent A collection of discursive practices that intend to extend the discussion from what was observed in the video to their own past experiences when teaching and/or learning, or with potential future teaching scenarios. Participants discussed aspects related to student thinking and participation, primarily focusing on problematizing objects of teaching observed in the clips, and less frequently engaging in negotiation of noteworthy phenomena. An emergent and predominant feature of their noticing discourse was making connections to their own experiences, which included extending the observed episode to past or potential future teaching scenarios. Additionally, although there is little evidence of positioning students' ideas as resources, participants maintained an asset-based perspective as required by the facilitators. The identified features in our data provide evidence that PD video prompts supported productive noticing discourse among participants and shed light on the processes through which their collective sensemaking contributed to their learning to notice. Our findings reflect the PD emphasis on noticing as multidimensional and are encouraging as they suggest tangible implications for participants' future instruction. This work contributes to the limited literature on how mechanisms for learning to notice take place at the college level. Poster 5: Attending, interpreting, and shaping: How varied ways of working with video connect with subprocesses of teacher noticing Jennifer Richards, Miriam Sherin, Sarah Larison 2322 Research has documented how video- based environments can provide rich opportunities for teachers’ learning, including learning to notice student thinking (e.g., Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Further, advancements in video-related technology have expanded how teachers can engage with video — moving beyond watching and discussing videos to filming and editing their own clips. In this poster, we extend a prior exploration of how teachers noticed student thinking as they engaged in multiple video processes (Richards & Sherin, 2025) by specifying ways in which these video processes map onto posited subprocesses of teacher noticing, contributing to understandings of potential drivers for noticing. The framework we animate specifies several interrelated subprocesses of teacher noticing — attending, interpreting, and shaping (van Es & Sherin, 2021). “Attending” refers to what teachers focus on in classrooms, acknowledging that humans cannot pay attention to everything. “Interpreting” refers to how teachers reason about classroom events. “Shaping” refers to what teachers do in order to support their noticing during or after instruction. While these subprocesses dynamically interact with and influence one another, we think they also reflect important opportunities for learning in their own right. Data come from three iterations of an online, video- based course for early elementary teachers in the United States on mathematical argumentation (Lomax et al., 2017). Twenty -nine in-service teachers participated in the course, in which they engaged in four sequential video processes — recording video in their own classrooms, watching and reflecting on the video, editing clips to share in the course, and interacting with others around their clips. Data sources included interviews and think- alouds with teachers about these video processes and video annotations on clips. Our prior analysis explored the affordances and constraints of each video process for teachers’ noticing of student thinking (Richards & Sherin, 2025). Here, we build on this prior analysis to characterize the noticing subprocesses that different video processes seemed to afford. When teachers recorded video in their classrooms, all three noticing subprocesses seemed to be in play as teachers iteratively focused on student ideas that required attention, sought to make sense of them in real time, and shaped interactions to test working interpretations and gather more information. Watching and reflecting on the video tended to afford continued “interpreting” and “shaping,” as teachers primarily used the video as a tool to make sense of and gain more evidence about student ideas that had intrigued them. Editing clips , in contrast, afforded “attending” with some further “interpreting” as teachers selectively identified moments of student thinking to make visible to colleagues. Finally, when interacting with others around clips , all three subprocesses were again in play as teachers highlighted specific student ideas to consider, discussed varied interpretations, and at times reviewed the video to seek more information. These findings suggest potential implications for targeted video-based designs to facilitate specific noticing subprocesses (e.g., cultivating teachers’ attending by providing multiple opportunities to edit clips). Further research could deepen understandings of how engaging with varied sequences of video processes drives teachers’ learning to notice over time. Poster 6: Developing professional vision through negotiating understanding of videorecorded whole-class talks in mathematics Håvard Johnsrud Evang, Inga Staal Jenset Supporting teacher candidates’ development of ambitious and equitable mathematics teaching is a key challenge in teacher education (Louie, 2018) and requires that teachers adapt their instruction in response to students’ content-specific ideas and ways of participating in the talk (Jacobs & Empson, 2016). Prior research has studied this situation -specific competence through concepts such as ‘noticing of students strengths’ (Jilk, 2016) and ‘equitable noticing’ (Louie, 2018) demonstrating how video- anchored activities may support candidates developing this capacity (Jenset et al., 2024). Building on a recent socio- cultural turn in noticing research (Scheiner et al., 2026), the present study extends this work by investigating how teacher candidates’ professional vision develops as they engage in discussions of video-recorded mathematical classroom talk in Grade 8 settings. This study draws on Goodwin’s (1994) concept of professional vision, defined as the ability to construct relevant knowledge through socio-historically developed practices of highlighting and coding. This framework is used to examine how teacher candidates interpret students’ utterances and actions within recorded episodes of classroom discourse. Adopting a socio- cultural perspective, the study assumes that cultural frames —that is, culturally and historically shaped interpretive lenses regarding school mathe matics, mathematical teaching, and learning (Goffman, 1974; Scheiner, 2021) —function as mediational means that shape these practices. Consequently, the negotiation and adaptation of cultural frames to make sense of students’ mathematical contributions are understood as mechanisms that drive the development of teachers’ professional vision. The study investigates how video- anchored discussions contribute to the development of mathematics teacher candidates’ professional vision. Data consists of approximately 30 hours of video recordings from five 2323 seminars integrated into an existing mathematics-didactics course across one academic year (24 candidates). The seminars were structured to progressively broaden candidates’ highlighting and coding practices, with the goal of fostering increased attention to students’ diverse mathematical reasoning and forms of participation. Candidates’ discussions were scaffolded through an observation rubric and prompts encouraging them to focus on the qualities of students’ contributions, rather than on perceived defici encies or errors. Through reflective thematic and discourse analysis, the study examines how these practices evolved over time and how cultural frames informed candidates’ interpretations of students’ mathematical work. The study yielded three insights into candidates’ professional vision development: (i) a shift from “glossy” to complex understanding of students’ participation, (ii) an expanded understanding of students’ multiple mathematical competencies, and (iii) pers istent privileging of an authoritative view on valuable mathematical outcomes. Video-anchored discussions supported candidates develop richer framing of students as valuable resources in building mathematical knowledge. However, persistent cultural frames constrained candidates’ appreciation of student’s mathematical thinking (Louie, 2018) highlighting the need for teacher education to explicitly challenge these frames to support the development of professional vision for ambitious and equitable teaching. Poster 7: Teacher-designed cases as a tool to support pre-service teacher noticing Tracy E. Dobie, Liza Escobar Aquino, Bailey N. Ondricek, Raven Burton, Angela Warnock Extensive research illustrates the value of supporting teachers’ noticing of student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010). We respond to the call for more research that investigates learning to notice from an equity frame (van Es et al., 2017) by examining cases (Shulman, 1992) as a tool to support pre-service teachers’ noticing for equity. Teacher noticing is commonly described as having three components – attending, interpreting, and responding (Jacobs et al., 2010). Research on noticing for equity explores various facets of this construct including noticing of individual student histories, anti-deficit discourses, and status and positioning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2017). Challenges include supporting pre -service teachers (PSTs) to attend to individual students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and notice more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Cases are written narratives describing authentic and complex teaching situations (Shulman, 1992) that can be intentionally designed to investigate certain themes (Dobie et al., 2024). We use cases to help PSTs grapple with the challenges of enacting equitable mathematics and science instruction —or leveraging students’ multiple strengths, honoring students’ diverse lived experiences, dismantling classroom power and status hierarchies, and challenging dominant perspectives (e.g., Aguirre et al., 2013). We partnered with local U.S. teachers, who designed cases exploring themes such as assumptions about multilingual students, inequitable group dynamics, and school structures that disadvantage minoritized students (Dobie et al., 2024). Data include PSTs’ written responses (N=1,036; 224 PSTs) to prompts for six cases that were implemented 2 -4 times each in an elementary math or science methods course. Our team deductively and inductively developed a coding scheme (Miles et al., 2014) capturing a) case details (what PSTs attended to), b) equity-oriented interpretations (PSTs’ reasoning), and c) solutions (ideas about how to respond). Two coders coded every response, and discrepancies were resolved. We highlight three findings: 1) Cases support PSTs to attend to details about students and their actions, 2) Cases and prompts can be designed to support PSTs to make wide-ranging equity-oriented interpretations, and 3) Case prompts elicit solutions that include in-the-moment actions, changes for future instruction, and advocacy- based actions including gathering data and research. We offer frequency counts across the dataset, PST quotes, and case comparisons. As an example, we explore how a subtle difference in prompts influenced PSTs’ breadth of interpretations in two similar cases focused on group dynamics: In one case, 83% of responses offering equity- oriented interpretations focused on a general imbalance in group dynamics; in the other, PSTs reasoned about a general imbalance in group dynamics (39%), as well as the roles of friendship (46%), language (43%), prior school experiences (24%), and gender (15%). Cases have significant potential for supporting PSTs’ noticing for equity including details of specific students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Questions remain about trajectories of noticing over time and the impact of noticing in cases on noticing in classrooms. 2324 Poster 8: Accounting for teacher learning in a video club: Learning a noticing discourse Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Melissa Luna Video-based professional development has been shown to support mathematics and science teachers’ learning to notice for responsive and equitable instruction (Santagata et al., 2021). This vision of teaching calls on teachers to attend to the substantive contributions students make toward the learning goals and adopt an inquiry stance to validate and interpret student thinking to position students’ ideas as resources for their own and others’ learning. What is less understood is how and why these settings support teacher learning. Thus, we ask what might be mechanisms of teacher learning to notice in the context of video- based professional development centered on noticing student thinking? We conceptualize video-based professional development as complex activity systems in which the video clips, the norms for participation, and the cultural and historical practices of professional development all coordinate to influence teachers’ opportunities to learn in these settings (Barnhart, 2021). Our research is informed by an often overlooked feature of complex activity systems of professional development that may be supporting teachers’ learning to notice: the nature of talk that takes place in video- based professional learning contexts. Professional discourse plays a central role in teacher learning (Lefstein et al., 2020), yet less is known about the character of talk that results in teachers’ learning to notice. Data include video recordings and transcripts from two video clubs to support teachers to learn to notice the complexity of teacher -student learning interactions. Video club facilitators prompted teachers to explore the details of student thinking, potential interpretations of their ideas, in relation to teaching. One video club included nine 4th and 5th grade mathematics teachers that met ten times for about one hour over the academic year, approximately once a month. The second video club focused on supporting six middle school science teachers’ learning to notice student thinking and teaching in seven hour -long sessions throughout an academic year. We analyzed an early and late video club meeting for both groups to identify features of a noticing discourse that were present in each meeting (van Es et al., 2024; Table 1). To account for teachers’ learning a noticing discourse, we coded the video club data and wrote analytic memos for evidence and disconfirming evidence of the noticing discourse features, also noting who enacted the talk moves that represented the noticing discourse features. Findings show that both groups shifted in their enactment of a noticing discourse over time. Both groups shifting their talk to highlight more ideas represented in the clips as worthwhile for noticing (i.e., negotiating noteworthy phenomena), pursue these ideas as objects of inquiry for the group to analyze (i.e., creating moments for further inquiry), anchor their analyses of student thinking in classroom evidence (i.e., being accountable to evidence), and demonstrate an openness to explore students’ ideas as resources for learning. Moreover, teachers demonstrated an accountability to the learning community by enacting talk that balanced respecting and honoring teachers' practice represented in the video, while also pressing on what was going on to further understand student thinking and teaching. This finding offers additional insights into features of talk that are enacted to support teachers’ learning to notice, which we argue represents the importance of collective sensemaking as a critical component of noticing discourse in professional learning. Looking across both video-clubs, this study provides evidence for a noticing discourse as key to teachers’ learning to notice, and has implications for design features, such as creating moments for further inquiry, to make video club discourse generative for teacher learning. Poster 9: Science teachers’ learning to notice expansively Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Jennifer Richards There is growing agreement in the field that teacher noticing is critical in ambitious forms of teaching that center students (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023). Joining other scholars in exploring the complexities of noticing (e.g., van Es et al., 2022), our ongoing work considers the multidimensionality of teachers' noticing for facilitating students’ sensemaking in science classrooms (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). However, there is much to learn about what supports teachers to develop multidimensional noticing practices. In this study, we explored whether a group of science teachers shifted their noticing through engaging in a specific video- based professional learning (PL) design. Briefly, with multidimensional noticing, we bring together key threads from prior work on noticing, such as the importance of noticing student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010) as well as pedagogy connected to student thinking (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa & Stein, 2015), and working toward anti -deficit ways of noticing disciplines and 2325 students (e.g., Louie et al., 2021). Taking a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000), which emphasizes learning through interaction in activity systems, we sought to embody these noticing practices in PL tools and routines (Greeno, 2006; Sandoval, 2014). This study was conducted within the context of an NSF -funded project, Implementing Practices of Ambitious Teaching for Complex Assessment Tasks (IMPACT). IMPACT PL is centered around the implementation of science performance assessments, providing a laboratory for teachers to work with students’ ideas. Five 8th -grade science teachers from different schools in a large urban district in the United States participated. Teachers engaged in collaborative analysis of performance assessment video clips intentional ly selected to highlight relations between student thinking and ambitious teaching principles (Windschitl et al., 2018) and were consistently asked to focus first on student thinking, then aspects of teaching that seemed to support student thinking. To explore changes in teachers’ noticing, we analyzed teachers’ baseline and exit interviews during which they were asked to share what they noticed and how they might respond to events in a ~7- minute video clip. We separated teachers’ interview transcripts into idea units and coded each idea unit with respect to teachers’ noticing, using the multidimensional noticing framework as an analytical lens (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). At the end of the IMPACT PL, there was growing attention to student thinking among all five teachers. When they noticed student thinking, they began to see what students were saying or appeared to be thinking as valuable, taking an asset-based frame. Moreover, in the exit interviews, teachers focused more on ways to work with students' ideas as opposed to only correcting those ideas. In short, the video- based PL tools and routines seemed to hold promise for supporting shifts in multiple dimensions of teache rs’ noticing in concert with each other. Future research can elaborate on the dynamics of teachers’ noticing practices throughout the PL, particularly how teachers iterated among noticing student thinking and pedagogy. Poster 10: A learning to notice for equity framework Jose Mendez, Elizabeth A. van Es Descriptive accounts of teachers’ noticing for equity contribute to theorizing the complexity of teachers’ in the moment attention and sensemaking to advance responsive and equitable instruction (e.g. Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). What is less understood is how teachers learn to notice for equity. Teacher noticing for equity is characterized by teachers ’ attention to multiple dimensions of the classroom environment including linguistic resources, power dynamics, relational interactions, social i dentities, and sociopolitical narratives (van Es et al., 2022). We theorize that learning to attend to equity involves the ability to name these classroom dynamics and see them as interconnected (e.g., Rubin & van Es, 2025). The second dimension involves the development of an interpretive practice , which entails continuously engaging with evidence to better understand and support students’ needs (Sherin & Russ, 2017). The third dimension involves embodied engagement , drawing on recent noticing-as-embodied c onceptualizations that highlight the nuanced and multi -sensory aspects of noticing (Mason, 2002; Scheiner, 2021). Embodied engagement of one’s noticing includes both actions, such as shaping, to position oneself to notice more expansively, and choosing to ignore particular aspects of classroom interactions that are less generative for student learning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). Embodied engagement that disrupts inequities is a reflection of developing one’s noticing for equity (Scheiner, 2021). We qualitatively analyzed data from a research practice partnership that explored whether and how co - designing and analyzing practical measurement data could provoke a mathematics teacher’s learning to notice for equity (Mendez & van Es, 2025). We adopt sociopolitical perspectives to theorize teachers’ learning to notice as tied to their personal histories and the power -laden environments they teach in (Louie et al., 2021). We also theorize learning as a progression that can support teachers and teacher educators formatively documenting changes in teachers’ noticing over time (e.g., van Es, 2011). Data included transcripts of co- design meetings to develop a survey as a form of practical measurement data and data discussions of iterative cycles of survey implementation. This poster will present a framework for learning to notice for equity that consists of four levels. Each level is characterized by shifts in noticing along the dimensions of attending to equity, interpretive practice, and embodied engagement. As the case study teacher shifted in his noticing for equity, he came to see noticing as multidimensional and integrated, shifting frames to interpret events from an asset- and evidence-based stance. He also made connections to his practice and considered how to disrupt persistent inequities to create a responsive classroom through shaping noticing interactions focused on students’ ideas and patterns of participation. This framework moves from descriptive accounts of teacher noticing for equity to characterize the prog ression of learning to noticing from an equity lens over time. In doing so, this tool offers a framework to study teachers’ 2326 learning to notice for equity, while also providing guidance for designing experiences to support teachers’ expansive noticing. papers.title: Co-Designing Hybrid Intelligent Learning Environments: One Educator’s Journey Navigating Relationships with AI
papers.authors: Lili Yan, Jina Kang
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have resulted in a “replacement framing” in education. Hybrid intelligence (HI) has been proposed to reframe the relationship between educators and AI as collaborative, positioning humans and AI as partners in learning. Empirically, however, little is known about the impact of the HI system on the complex ecologies of learning in K -12 classrooms. To foreground educators’ agency in shaping HI systems for learning, we partner with a group of secondary science teachers exploring the role of hybrid intelligent systems in science learning contexts. We present a case of one educator’s experience to illustrate how teachers navigated their relationship with AI during the process to co-design a hybrid learning environment based on the existing science learning simulation, HoloOrbits. Findings highlight teachers’ evolving trajectories and leadership in co- designing AI-augmented systems, which reveals how teachers negotiate forms of AI-teaming aligned with their pedagogical visions.

papers.title: Designing the Next Generation of Computational Modeling and Learning with AI
papers.authors: Tamar Fuhrmann, Line Have Musaeus, Ole Sejer Iversen, Paulo Blikstein
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: As generative AI rapidly transforms how humans interact with computation, it challenges the foundations of many educational technologies designed to teach coding, modeling, and computational thinking. Systems that were once built around writing or arranging code—whether block-based or text-based—now coexist with tools that generate programs through natural language. This workshop invites the learning sciences and design research community to collectively explore how educational technologies that include coding must be re-envisioned in light of these shifts. What will it mean to “code,” “debug,” or “model” when AI becomes a co-author? How might our existing environments—like MoDa, a block-based modeling platform, or text-based NetLogo simulations—need to be rethought for an era where learners reason through prompts, outputs, and model interpretation rather than syntax and structure? Our goal is to identify key design principles, challenges, and opportunities to guide the next generation of AI-powered computational learning environments. Theoretical background and significance Integrating computational thinking (CT) into science education equips students with powerful tools to explore scientific phenomena, foster deeper conceptual understanding, and engage in authentic scientific practices. The interdisciplinary potential of this work empowers students and practitioners to engage meaningfully with emerging local and global challenges (Barr et al., 2011; Weintrop et al., 2016). Existing literature identifies several core CT practices: abstraction, generalization, decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debugging (Caeli & Yadav, 2020). Computational modeling, including agent-based modeling (ABM), has long been recognized as a valuable tool that can simultaneously support students' science learning and CT (e.g., Wilkerson et al., 2015; Musaeus et al., 2023; Musaeus et al., 2022). Recently, however, developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced new possibilities for how learners and educators may interact with computational models (Chen et al., 2023). In the future, it may no longer be necessary to write code to create scientific computer models, putting learners in the role of collaborators with generative AI. For decades, coding has served as both a tool for learning and a language for thinking (Papert, 1980; diSessa, 2000). Block-based and text-based environments embody constructionist ideals, empowering learners to express, test, and refine ideas through computation. Yet today, this paradigm is shifting. AI’s ability to generate executable code from natural language redefines what it means to “speak computation.” As we transition from programming languages to prompting, foundational concepts—such as loops, conditions, and agents—risk becoming invisible. At the same time, new epistemic practices emerge: prompt engineering, iterative interpretation of AI outputs, and ethical reasoning about algorithmic agency. This timely workshop for the field of learning sciences demands that we rethink not only curricula, but also what fundamental concepts in programming that we still need to teach and how to design the tools themselves; how they mediate learning, distribute agency, and scaffold understanding when code is no longer the learner’s sole artifact of construction. Organizing team Line Have Musaeus leads research at the Center for Computational Thinking & Design, focusing on computing education, computational modeling, and STEM learning. Her work explores how integrating computational thinking into school subjects supports both student learning and teacher development. She co-designed CoTinker and has extensive experience organizing workshops on computing and AI in education. Tamar Fuhrmann leads research at the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab at Teachers College, Columbia University. She is a founding leader of the MoDa project, focusing on computational modeling in science education. Her work integrates STEM, AI, and constructionist approaches, and she regularly leads professional development and international collaborations. Paulo Blikstein is an Associate Professor at Columbia University and director of the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab. His research focuses on using technology to t ransform learning in STEM and AI. He founded the FabLearn program and has received major awards, including the NSF CAREER and AERA Early Career Award. Ole Sejer Iversen is a professor at Aarhus University and director of the Center for Computational Thinking & Design. His research focuses on computational empowerment, helping young people become active creators of technology. He works at the intersection of participatory design, computing education, and policy, leading large-scale international projects. Workshop goals and intended audience This workshop is designed for researchers, designers, and educators in the learning sciences, computing education, and educational technology who are exploring the future of computational learning in the age of AI. It will particularly interest those developing or studying coding-based environments—such as block-based, text-based, or modeling tools—and those investigating how generative AI transforms students’ epistemic, creative, and design practices. Participants with backgrounds in design-based research, computational modeling, or AI in education will find opportunities to share perspectives, contribute to collaborative redesign activities, and help shape a research agenda for rethinking the role of coding and modeling in AI-mediated learning environments. Outline of planned activities and facility requirements The four-hour workshop (plus one hour for lunch and coffee) will begin with an opening and framing session (20 minutes) introducing key tensions in AI-integrated coding environments. This will be followed by case study provocations (40 minutes), during which participants engage with two computational modeling environments: MoDa, a block-based agent-based modeling tool, and CoTinker, a collaborative modeling environment. Participants will explore and design models while considering how these tools might evolve as learners use AI to generate, modify, and explain models. In the collaborative design challenge (60 minutes), small groups will reimagine an educational technology that includes coding, redesigning it to integrate AI while preserving learners’ epistemic and creative engagement. This will lead into a group synthesis and discussion (40 minutes), during which participants share insights, identify emerging principles, and surface tensions, producing a poster as the group outcome. The workshop will conclude with a closing reflection (20 minutes), focusing on articulating open research questions and opportunities for future collaboration. Participation requirements Participation is open to researchers, designers, educators, and graduate students interested in computational modeling, coding education, or AI-supported learning environments. No specific technical expertise or prior experience with educational learning environments is required. We would like to support a dynamic, collaborative environment in which multiple perspectives on the redesign of coding-based educational technologies can emerge. Relationship to similar events conducted in the past Over the past several years, ISLS conferences have hosted numerous workshops and symposia exploring computational modeling, data science education, and AI-supported learning, for example, Kafai et al., 2025; Wagh et al., 2024; Fuhrmann et al., 2022; Fuhrmann et al., 2024; and McElhaney et al., 2020. These events advanced theoretical and design frameworks for integrating computational practices into science and engineering education. However, few have directly addressed the implications of generative AI for redesigning the educational technologies that include coding, particularly how block-based and text-based modeling environments must evolve when learners can construct programs through natural language. This workshop builds on that lineage but reframes the central question: not how to teach coding, but how coding itself—and the tools built around it—should be reimagined for an AI-mediated future. By convening researchers working at the intersection of computational modeling, design-based research, and AI in education, the session extends ongoing ISLS dialogues toward a new design agenda: understanding how AI reshapes the epistemic and pedagogical foundations of computational learning tools. Expected outcome and outputs The workshop will strengthen a community of practice focused on designing tools that preserve human sense- making and agency alongside AI assistance. It will generate open-ended questions that help rethink computational educational technologies in an AI-mediated context, and build a shared vocabulary around emerging hybrid practices where coding, prompting, and modeling intersect. Rather than defining what the future of coding should be, the session aims to open a dialogue on how our tools—and our field—must evolve to meet it. papers.authors: Trang C. Tran, Raesheena Kennedy
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Kennedy co-designed and facilitated lessons on the forced incarceration of Japanese American during World War II, organizing curriculum materials that encouraged affective, embodied, and justice -focused learning. Employing the emotional configurations (Vea, 2020) and data feminism (D'Ignazio & Klein, 2020) frameworks, our analysis illustrates how one student, Mhina, traversed across interdisciplinary practices and intertwin ed emotional dimensions to craft a data story. Incorporating narrative and storytelling approaches, we depict emotional, moral, and political considerations that were embedded in and mediating student investigations and sense-making with and through data.

papers.title: Lowering Barriers for Designing AI-Embodied Robots for Learning
papers.authors: Amy Eguchi, Emile Kroeger
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper presents RoboHearts AI, a web-based platform that enables educators, students, and researchers to easily design and deploy large-language-model (LLM)–powered characters on embodied robots such as Pepper, NAO, and LEGO-based extensions. By combining LLM-driven conversational capabilities with robots’ multimodal features, including gesture, animated movement, gaze, and visual display, RoboHearts AI supports naturalistic, adaptive, and contextualized interactions that extend beyond traditional screen-based chatbots. The paper introduces practical applications across educational and non-educational settings, and proposes two pedagogical scenarios: learning with AI, where robots act as tutors or learning companions, and learning about AI, where students gain AI literacy and deepen their understanding of AI by designing and iteratively refining robot characters. This hands-on demonstration guides participants in character creation and multimodal behavior design. This work lowers barriers to embodied AI adoption and highlights new opportunities for research, instructional innovation, and human-centered learning with AI-embodied robots.

papers.title: How Educational Practitioners Envision Employment-Focused Transition Services for Students with Disabilities: Insights from a Game-Based Activity
papers.authors: Indu Garg, LuEttaMae Lawrence, Stephen Kwiatek
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This paper explores how educational practitioners conceptualize employment‑focused transition services for students with disabilities through a collaborative, game‑based planning activity. Drawing on a fictional case study of a high school student, practitioners worked in cross‑role teams to design a four‑year plan to document how they can support the student’s transition from high school into adulthood. Analysis of 217 practitioner contributions, coded using Lee and Carter’s (2012) framework of high‑qualit y employment transition services, revealed that career development experiences and customized transition supports were most frequently emphasized, while family support, job‑related supports, and self‑determination appeared less consistently and often only in response to roadblocks. These findings align with established predictors of post‑school success but also highlight gaps in proactive family engagement, and employer and interagency collaboration. The study demonstrates how designed, game‑based environme nts can surface practitioner reasoning, mediate professional learning, and inform the design of more inclusive, employment‑focused transition services.
