papers.title: Reconceptualizing Imagination as Social Practice in Science Education
papers.authors: Hannah H. Ziegler
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In science education, imagination has largely been framed as a cognitive process, with comparatively less attention to its social, political, and ecological dimensions. This conceptual paper reconceptualizes imagination as a social practice that reshapes how we imagine and design possible futures. At the micro- level, I reframe imagination as a subjective and situated practice, shaped by individual histories and sociopolitical contexts. At the meso- level, it is explored as a relational act, co -produced through intergenerational collaboration, care, and the navigation of structural constraints. At the macro-level, an ecological imagination extends this practice to include socioecological relations with more -than-human partners, drawing on Indigenous and pluriversal ontologies. By analyzing imagination across these interacting levels, this paper offers a pathway for designing more just and thriving futures. Purpose: Why imagination matters in science education We often give the most attention to children's imaginative engagement in early childhood or elementary classrooms, usually linked to children's play. However, imagination as a pedagogical practice tends to lose legitimacy as kids grow older, especially in science education contexts. Building on existing cognitive and sociocultural scholarship, I propose theorizing imagination as a social practice that foregrounds its relational and sociopolitical dimensions. Recent work in the learning sciences has advanced speculative approaches to justice- oriented futures (e.g., Arada et al., 2023; Garcia & Mirra, 2023). My argument complements this work by focusing more specifically on imagination as the social and relational practice that undergirds such efforts. My work presents imaginative engagement not as naive dreaming, but as a powerful tool for re -worlding that involves complex ideological struggles against frameworks like neoliberalism. Here, I define imagination as a sociohistorically situated practice of world -making through which certain futures become thinkable, legitimate, and actionable. This practice is best pursued in community, including youth and more -than-human partners. Drawing inspiration from marginalized worldviews, imagination as social practice dis rupts tradition by asking new questions: What are the sources of our imagination, what values does it reflect, and whose imaginations are legitimized? Revisiting existing frames of imagination While important work has examined imagination from cognitive and sociocultural perspectives, imagination in science education remains underdeveloped from an explicitly socioecological and political perspective. Early sociocultural traditions help us understand that imagination is not created from nothing, but uses real -world experiences as building blocks. However, theorizing imagination solely within cognitivist or sociocultural traditions leaves certain political and structural dimensions underexplored. F irst, imagination is not a neutral cognitive skill but is situated in our historical, cultural, and political contexts. Second, these renderings fail to recognize the consequential potential of imagination in both micro- and macro -level systems. Theorizing imagination solely at the level of the individual risks overlooking the relational and structural dimensions that shape what becomes imaginable. In defining imagination as a social practice, I draw from Holland & Lave’s (2019) theory of social practice, which considers how participation shapes a person’s daily lives in relation to power and politics. Imagination as social practice does not seek to understand people’s actions as isolated individual acts, but always in relation to other people, practices, and systems. The remainder of this paper is organized into three sections in which I illustrate how imagination -as-social-practice can open up new o nto-epistemologies at the micro - (intrapersonal), meso- (relational), and macro- (ecological) levels. These analytic levels are not mutually exclusive but offer a framing to discuss key facets of imagination as we contend with political systems, cultural histories, and ideological frameworks. Micro level: The individual imagination From cognition to situated subjectivity 1917 The most prevalent theories around imagination largely establish it as a cognitive function contained within an individual’s mind, with some recognition of cultural contexts. Experiential perspectives acknowledge how children blend existing experiences to create new ways of thinking: Vygotsky (2004) discusses imagination as a cultural activity of dissociating and recombining elements of reality in creative ways. This individualistic framing is evident in Egan’s (2005) articulation of imagination as a set of cognitive toolkits divided by developmental stages. This cognitivist tradition has shaped how imagination is researched and implemented in education—in terms of an individual’s cognitive performance. Numerous psychological studies have since examined how imagination mediates learning, viewing it as a mental technique to enhance comprehension and retention. Nonetheless, these studies bypass explanations around how the individual imagination is shaped by our own histories, cultures, emotions, and relations. Cognitive views have also dominated how the field has conceived of disciplinary practices in science education. Kuhn’s (1977) concept of thought experiments, for instance, describes a decontextualized view of the individual imagination in scientific thinking. While both Kuhn and Vygotsky (2004) imply that the individual imagination consists of subjective renderings of a person’s experiences, a chief focus on the tangible, sensory, and cognitive elements could conceal the value -laden subjectivities that driv e our scientific sensemaking. Thus, an inquiry into the role of aesthetics and wonder in science education enables us to see both the personal and deeply social dimensions of our imagination. While aesthetic experiences are seemingly experienced in private and subjective ways (Wickman et al., 2022), science education is seldom theorized as a subjective experience, despite being full of such moments. What we find interesting, wonderful, or strange depends on the observer, whose experiences are deeply situated. After all, Egan (2005) reckons anything has the potential to be seen as wonderful if “seen in the right light” (p. 92). Then, I argue that changing the so- called “light,” or the subjective lens with which we view the world, can alter what we perceive as wonderful, beautiful, or worth imagining. Science as socially constructed Framing the individual imagination as a social practice also makes visible the sociopolitical conditions which have driven our collective inquiry. Disciplinary knowledge is produced through socially organized processes, rather than existing outside historical and cultural contexts. Latour (1987) frames scientific facts as a set of ideas that are socially constructed, contested, and settled through a community of scientists. In other words, what counts as science is socially and interactionally constructed a mong members of the science community. Thus, disciplinary knowledge consists of a fluid, socially-constructed body of knowledge rather than a permanent, rigid set of concepts. Similarly, Medin & Bang (2014) argue that scientific ideas are often “settled” t hrough a social process. They also speak to how science education reflects the values of its adherents, most often dominated by Western scientists. Establishing the disciplinary canon involves a collective process dominated by those who yield social power. Similarly, I view imagination as a dynamic process subject to power relations; whose imaginations get taken up and pursued are deeply shaped by our subjective judgments and the social positions of those making them. Recognizing the subjectivities of the individual imagination offers an entry point to examine how our politically-shaped values permeate our “scientific” imagination. Imagination is constituted through people’s histories, values, identities, emotions, and relations to place. Afrofuturist practices exemplify how individual imaginations can contest social norms to create new forms of culture. As a form of political worlding, afrofuturism demonstrates how the individual imagination can simultaneously engage in cultural critique, resistance, and counter-stories. Speculative storytelling can also prompt resistance by blurring boundaries of present -future and real-imagined (Tomin & Collis, 2024). An exploration of the subjectivities of our imagination at the intrapersonal level mandates that we challenge dominant onto- epistemologies that shape “current and possible meaning, meaning-making, positioning, and relations in cultural ecologies” (Bang et al., 2016, p. 29). Then, it becomes necessary to critically question how our imagination can marginalize perspectives we often need the most. While this section foregrounds subjectivity, imagination does not remain within individuals; it becomes consequential in relation with others and broader systems. Meso level: The relational imagination Relationality as ethical matters I now examine imagination as a social practice that is not only subjective, but relational. By “relational imagination,” I mean more than collaboration; it references to the co -production of worlds mediated by social norms and roles. I stress the importance of questioning how social hierarchies and dominant narratives shape how we imagine at the interpersonal level. Relational imagination is driven by care, agency, and affect. With whom we imagine is just as important as what we imagine. In line with social practice theory (Holland & Lave, 2019), 1918 social hierarchies are central to imagination. Bang and colleagues (2016) suggest that normative relations in learning environments can reproduce power and inequity. They employ the term “withness designing” to underscore a relational approach, proposing intergenerational engagement with elders and youth to constitute community-based change. The relational imagination emphasizes learning across generations and requires role remediation through re-negotiations of power. Therefore, with whom we work, design, and imagine becomes an ethical matter. Reframing children as co-visionaries Children have been historically positioned as naive and questionable sources of knowledge. Silin (2014) emphasizes the need not only to listen to children but also to dissolve the boundaries between adult-child relations. If we were to view people’s experiences and emotions from a collective perspective regardless of age, then science education should focus on empowering and healing young people. This ideological liberation of age segregation is best pursued through collaboration where adults and children inspire and fuel each other’s imaginations. While both adults’ and children’s ideas may reflect and reproduce problematic social norms, I argue that we are more likely to create radical visions in community. In this sense, relational imagination explicitly centers the co - production of ideas —how people imagine with and for one another. Chang & Philip (2025) illustrate such orientation as they cultivated a co -design space that disrupted normative roles in adult -youth partnerships. They critique co -design work that centers adult stakeholders’ needs; instead, they argue the valued outcome is the negotiation of existing social relationships as newly figured worlds. These relational shifts surface how affect, agency, and imagination are jointly situated in practice. Relational imagination amid institutional constraints These relational practices contend with institutional logics that privatize youths’ emotions. Formal schooling is seldom sufficient in meeting youths’ emotional needs (Vamvalis, 2023). Hence, youths’ abilities to navigate the present and shape their futures are constrained by social structures. This is unsurprising given that American schools were primarily established for socializing students to reward passivity and compliance. As such, schools enculturate students into neoliberal systems rather than prepare them to critique and resist the status quo of science education. Hence, this raises a central tension: How can we design science teaching and learning to help us overcome structural limitations and foster imagination as a path to collective wellbeing? Macro level: The ecological imagination Ecologizing multiple worldviews Macro-level ecological imagination asks not only who imagines what, but with whom and to what ends. The macro level pushes us beyond our human partnerships, toward living well with the natural world, recognizing agency as distributed across human and more-than-human communities. However, these orientations must be accompanied by ontological shifts at the macro level, where multiple worldviews co -shape science education alongside more - than-human partners. I argue that diversity and heterogeneity alone cannot dismantle systems of power and privilege. Thus, the ecological imagination draws from Escobar’s (2018) pluriversal design calls for designing new ways of being in the world—ontologies —centered on culture and community. In particular, pluriversality challenges us to abandon Western assumptions of viewing the world that have jeopardized the fundamental human experience, such as frameworks of modernity (Escobar, 2018; Latour, 2013). Specifically, Latour (2013) calls for ecologization in place of modernization. Such aims necessitate that we interrogate the Western “scientific worldview” that is responsible for establishing subject-object relations. In fact, Latour (2013) contends that nature plays the role of the active subject, sharing agency with other subjec ts. This critique sets the stage for rethinking settled expectations in sciece as part of our ecological imagination. Extending agency to more-than-humans The relational imagination discussed ways to achieve more equitable relations between youth and science. Here, I shift to the absence of ecological onto- epistemologies in science education. Historically, the natural world has been objectified by and differentiated from human culture. This objectification captures the dominant narrative of humans’ exploitation of nature, rooted in science’s dominance over more -than-human beings. It has promoted inequitable extraction of Earth’s resources, and this cost is shared disproportionately among Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) groups (Monarrez et al., 2022). The troubling history of science has also made its way into classrooms—where the valuing of Western scientific practices denies Indigenous ways of understanding and caring for the natural world (Bang & Medin, 2010). In engineering education, technocratic discourses emphasize the design of anthropocentric solutions at the cost of natural resources (Gunckel & Tolbert, 2018). To 1919 explore the roots of our domineering relations with the natural world, I turn to Latour (2013), who challenges the myth of a nature -culture binary, or “bifurcation.” He calls us naive for deanimating natural entities, which calls for a re-distribution of agency across human and more -than-human actors. This work calls for a reconsideration of dominant Western ontological assumptions about nature and culture to take up relational and Indigenous perspectives on inhabiting an animate world. The work of Lees & Bang (2022) embodies such orientations by centering the Indigenous framing of humans as “a part of,” rather than “apart from,” the natural world. In their STEM summer program, youth explored biodiversity in tide pools while learning about their “beach relat ives.” By referring to the starfish as “he” rather than “it,” more-than-humans were imbued with a sense of personhood. Through this experience, children developed socioecological reasoning while acknowledging the agency of these creatures. In Warren & Rose bery’s (2011) study, Jonathan, a Black boy, challenges the Western classification system for living and non- living things. Jonathan constitutes the sun as a living organism based on its essential role in the ecosystem. His challenge of the canon’s binary classification allowed the teacher to reframe Jonathan as a competent science learner, illustrating the potential for the ecological imagination to disrupt dominant onto - epistemologies that pervade science education. Conclusion: Designing for pluriversality Across the micro, meso, and macro levels, we have reframed imagination as subjective, relational, and socioecological world-making processes. I use these levels as analytic lenses, informed by social practice theory, to trace how imagination operates across subjectivity, relational interaction, and broader socioecological systems. Imagination emerges through our lived histories and social relations, shaping how we interpret and imagine possible futures. Imagination- as-social-practice refutes individualistic notions of thriving, foregrounding collectivity instead.

papers.title: Trend Trackers: Building Data Literacy Through Problem-Based Learning
papers.authors: Anna Amato Shao, Jessica Ochoa Hendrix, Mandë Holford, Noelle Posadas Shang, Christopher Pollati
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Middle School Students; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: In this demo, we discuss the co-design of an interactive, problem-based science supplement called Trend Trackers. Trend Trackers aims to engage middle school students with socioscientific issues that impact cities and communities all over the world. Students take up the role of a data scientist to address public health problems within the fictional city of Springfield. In this demo, we will explore a challenge in which students are asked to design a vaccination plan to reduce the rates of flu in Springfield. Students engage in interactive and immersive activities to collect wastewater samples, measure rates of flu in the community, and generate evidence through a series of wrangling, visualization, and analysis activities. Students then share their findings and collaborate with their team to co-construct a vaccination plan for Springfield.

papers.title: Designing for Affective Equity in Partnerships
papers.authors: Blanca Gamez-Djokic
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) have become central to the learning sciences as infrastructures for addressing educational challenges. While much scholarship emphasizes their design principles and effectiveness, less attention has been paid to the affective life of partnerships. This paper advances a conceptual argument that RPPs function as pedagogical sites of affectivity. They not only rely on dispositions such as trust, humility, or perseverance but also cultivate, normalize, and organize which affective orientations become legitimate forms of participation. I call this the ontological goodness of RPPs – the assumption that collaboration is inherently moral and transformative which imbues partnerships with affective demands that shape who can participate fully and on what terms. Reframing purpose as an affective terrain highlights a hidden curriculum of partnership and raises new learning and design questions: what would it mean to design RPPs for affective equity where multiple orientations are legible and recognized as legitimate forms of participation?

papers.title: Programming Self-Efficacy and Outcomes, and Programming-oriented Prompting: A Comparison of Two Human–AI Collaboration Configurations
papers.authors: Ying-Tien Wu, Yi-Hong Zeng, Ching-Hui Kuan
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effects of GenAI -assisted programming learning on fifth graders’ computational thinking, programming self-efficacy and outcomes, and programming - oriented prompting. A total of 99 fifth graders from four classes participated and were randomly assigned to two GenAI -assisted programming instruction groups with different human– AI collaboration configurations: single student -AI collaboration (SSAC), in which each student worked individually with a computer with ChatGPT, and dyad student -AI collaboration (DSAC), in which two students worked in pairs, collaboratively using a shared computer with ChatGPT. The instruction was implemented over 6 weeks (1 class per week). This study revealed no significant difference in computational thinking between the two groups of students after GenAI-assisted programming instruction ( p>0.05). In contrast, the students in the DSAC group showed significantly higher programming self -efficacy and better programming outcomes ( p<0.05). Moreover, significant differences in the distribution of programming- oriented prompting between these two groups of students were also found ( p<0.05).

papers.title: A “Co-Design Intervention” with AI analytics to Support the Academically Productive Talk of Title 1 School Math Tutors and their Students: A Comparative Interrupted Time Series Analysis
papers.authors: Amirpasha Zandieh, Jeffrey Bush Tayne, Chelsea Brown, Jennifer Jacobs, Sandra Sawaya
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines whether a co- design-based professional learning intervention for tutors, supported by an AI feedback tool, influenced students’ Academically Productive Talk (APT) within a high-dosage algebra tutoring program in Title 1 schools in an urban U.S. school district. Using a comparative interrupted time series (CITS) design, we analyzed 9,037 tutoring sessions over the 42 weeks of one academic year, comparing tutors who participated in a nine - week co-design process with those who did not. Tuto rs in the intervention co -designed an AI interface called the “Talk Trees”, visualizing student talk patterns to guide student reflection on collaborative discourse. Results show short -term, positive shifts in students’ relating to academic ideas of their peers following the intervention, with modest, non- significant gains in instances of students making claims and providing reasoning. These findings highlight co- design’s potential to foster dialogic pedagogy in the context of boundary-crossing professional learning. They also demonstrate how CITS methods can evaluate AI-mediated interventions in authentic educational contexts.

papers.title: From Solo to Collaborative: Design Affordances in Multi-User Immersive VR Simulations for Transforming Science Learning
papers.authors: Michelle Lui, Sunnie Gong, Chloe Lok
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) shows promise for science learning by enabling visualization of microscopic phenomena and dynamic processes. However, research has focused predominantly on individual learning experiences, overlooking the social nature of learning. This study investigates the collaborative affordances of multi -user IVR for science education through participatory design, involving six teams of undergraduate students and educators who co- created IVR learning simulations. Findings revealed seven science learning affordances: microscopic visualization, spatial relationships, scale traversal, representational connections, perspective-taking, temporal phenomena, and procedural skills—which multi-user IVR amplified through embodied communication, role -taking that grounds collaborative discourse, and distributed perspectives that require coordination. Analysis of designs highlights how narrative structures establish group- worthy joint tasks, fostering six collaborative activity types. Variations in structuring collaborative processes emerged from play- level scripts with undifferentiated roles, and scene -level scripts with defined roles enhanc ing interdependence. Results provide design insights for leveraging IVR ’s spatial and embodied features in collaborative science learning.

papers.title: Co-designing and Implementing Reflective Tools and Routines with Children in Cooperative Inquiry
papers.authors: Elana Blinder
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Reflection is a valuable component of learning and design processes, yet motivating children to reflect in informal learning contexts can be challenging. My dissertation examines this issue in a university-based Cooperative Inquiry co-design team where children and adults collaborate as equal design partners. Leveraging a DBR approach, I conduct two studies. The first investigates how children co-design reflection tools and processes that align with their values and mental models. The second explores how they use these systems over time and how this shapes their developing self-concept as designers. Through this research, I will contribute an adaptable infrastructure for authentically integrating reflection into child co-design, insights into how DBR can meaningfully include children as co-design stakeholders, and a deeper understanding of how children think, learn, and develop their identities through co-design. Motivation and background The learning sciences have long documented the importance of reflection for a range of learning processes (Dewey, 1986; Moon, 2004; Schön, 2017), with classrooms traditionally serving as important spaces for developing children’s reflective learning. Though less structured and systematic, informal learning contexts can also offer rich environments for reflection and identity development, but it can be challenging to motivate children to pause and reflect in the absence of standard classroom norms and enforcing structures (Gardner et al., 2006). As a doctoral student at the University of Maryland with an interest in how children learn and develop their identities through co-design, I have experienced some of these challenges firsthand through my participation in UMD KidsTeam—an intergenerational co-design team where university faculty and students collaborate with children between the ages of 7 and 12 to design new child-facing technologies. Guided by the Cooperative Inquiry (CI) co-design framework (Druin, 1999; Guha et al., 2013), which aims to involve children as equal collaborators with adults across the entire design cycle, our team employs a variety of established CI ‘design techniques’ aimed at making co-design accessible, engaging, equitable, and empowering for children. One such technique that has been mentioned in the literature, but which has received considerably less attention, is ‘journaling’, which has been described as a tool for “design partners to reflect on their experiences by writing or drawing” (Guha et al., 2013). Despite this directive, CI scholars and practitioners have observed child design partners’ lack of intrinsic motivation to engage in reflective journaling and have reported challenges in communicating the goals and value of this technique in a manner that resonates with children’s personal interests and values (Blinder et al., 2025). Issues with implementing reflective journaling in CI are further complicated by logistical challenges (e.g., time constraints, the need for adult writing support), ideological challenges (e.g., adult discomfort with the solitary school-like nature of written reflection) and adult and child design partners’ conflicting conceptualizations of journaling (with children prioritizing documenting and remembering design ideas and adults prioritizing process- and identity-oriented reflection) (Blinder et al., 2025). These challenges indicate an opportunity to explore additional approaches toward fostering purposeful sustained reflection within CI and other child co-design contexts. In my dissertation, I capitalize on this opportunity by engaging UMD KidsTeam children in contemplating the role reflection can play in their lives and identities as designers through co-designing new developmentally accessible and personally meaningful reflection tools and routines to be used in our co-design context. I then examine how children’s engagement with these reflection approaches and their self-perceptions as designers evolve over time.

papers.title: Stories, Futures and Histories: Co-design Routines to Center Community Knowledge for Environmental Education in India
papers.authors: Gautam Bisht, Vishesh Kumar, Pankaj Dev, Jyoti Tiwari, Ankit Bhatt, Lata Upreti, Kiran Pant
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Centering co-design as a site of social justice, we analyze a collaboration between learning scientists and local teachers from a non-profit organization in the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, India. We ask, what design routines support the emergence of c ommunity-driven ideas for ecological education, and how do they build on each other to deepen cultural, imaginative, and historical engagement? Data for this paper comes from the initial phase of collaboration, which consisted of six online meetings, each two hour long. We conducted thematic analysis along to identify three interconnected routines: (i) autecology narratives surfaced ecological connections grounded in community and personal rituals, (ii) speculative futuring opened imaginative engagement with communication, technology, and markets; and (iii) interactions with community elders supported the development of critical historicity. Together, these routines illustrate a co -design approach which fosters collective sense -making integrating cultural, imaginative, and historical dimensions of community life .

papers.title: Playful Learning in the Community: An interactive tour of community based early learning installations
papers.authors: Andres S. Bustamante, Maria J. Anderson-Coto, Karlena D. Ochoa, Annelise Pesch, Julie Salazar
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Playful Learning Landscapes (PLL) transforms everyday community spaces like parks, bus-stops, and grocery stores into conduits for caregiver-child interactions and early learning. During this workshop, attendees will visit a series of PLL installations in Santa Ana, CA, which were co-designed by researchers from UC Irvine and Temple University, and families from the Santa Ana Early Learning Initiative, a local grassroots non-profit community organization. Attendees will engage with the PLL installations and learn about the design process and impact of the installations on community members and caregiver child interactions at PLL sites. The session will also demonstrate how this project was conducted in partnership with the City of Santa Ana’s Parks and Recreation and Public Works departments who own and maintain the installations and have begun to replicate them using public funds in other community spaces. Challenges, lessons learned, plans for sustainability, and practical and theoretical insights will be discussed. Playful learning in the community: An interactive tour of community based early learning installations Informal learning environments like children’s museums, zoos, and maker spaces are powerful contexts for supporting young children’s science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) learning and identity. Unfortunately, children from low-income families have less access to these spaces due to a variety of barriers like admission prices, transportation challenges, or even an awareness of their existence. In addition to these barriers, linguistically and ethnically minoritized families can feel alienated in these spaces which rarely center their languages, cultural values, and practices. Playful Learning Landscapes is an international initiative that brings informal learning installations to everyday spaces like parks, bus-stops, grocery stores, laundry mats, medical clinic waiting rooms, sidewalks, and walls (Hassinger-Das, 2018; Bustamante et al., 2019). Playful Learning Landscapes promote the caregiver-child conversations and interactions that decades of developmental and learning sciences research suggest lead to learning, such as conversational turns, STEM language, and hands-on engagement (Bustamante et al., 2020; Hassinger-Das et al., 2021; Pesch et al., 2025). In addition to designing PLLs based on the latest research in developmental and learning sciences, they are also designed in partnership with local families, so the installations build from families’ values, routines, and cultural practices (Bermudez et al., 2023). Understanding learning as a cultural process situates family’s participation in learning environments and design as dictated by values, routines, and cultural practices (Bang & Medin, 2010; Rogoff et al, 2007). Leveraging cultural assets, practices, and values can therefore increase relevance and significance for families, in turn increasing inclusivity, sustainability, and engagement. Partners The PLL work in Santa Ana, CA, is conducted in the context of a long-term research practice partnership between the Santa Ana Early Learning Initiative (SAELI), the University of California Irvine, and the City of Santa Ana. SAELI is a grassroots non-profit community organization bringing together local families, non-profit organizations, and leadership from the Santa Ana Unified School district to support families with children between 0-9 years of age. SAELI is led by director Wendy Gomez and uses a multigenerational approach through which promotoras (e.g., Chen et al., 2023) promote wellness through initiatives on child development, connecting families with resources, and local advocacy projects. On the university side, these projects are led by UC Irvine S chool of Education Professors Andres Bustamante and June Ahn and Temple University Psychology Professor Kathy Hirsh-Pasek. This research team brings expertise in child development, early education, participatory design, and research practice partnerships. The City of Santa Ana supported the project through their Parks and Recreation Department and Public Works Department, with support from the City Manager’s Office, Mayor's Office, and City Council. Other organizations and businesses included in this work were Northgate Gonzalez Market grocery chain, the Santa Ana Unified School District, First Five Orange County, and Orange County Health Care Agency. In this RPP, we endeavored to center families’ voices in all phases of the process from designing the installations, to deciding their locations, to the evaluation research, and dissemination of the findings. Importantly, trust and relationship-building with families were central to the design sessions. Personal stories and family values were shared through informal conversations over meals. These informal opportunities to connect allowed trust to be built over time, which uniquely positioned researchers and families as equals. We believe this allowed families to share openly and addressed traditional power dynamics between researchers and families. Decisions were taken jointly through parallel conversations with partners and interested parties, requiring transparency, trust-building, multiple channels of communication, rapid problem-solving, adaptation, and other forms of invisible relational labor. However, tensions emerged throughout the process particularly when navigating the intersection of large bureaucracies including federal funding, university systems, and city government. The project faced multiple challenges, including changing project timelines and material constraints, changes in organizational leadership, physical limitations of the public spaces designated for installations, and the complex social and political contexts of the community. Given existing power differentials between governmental partners and community stakeholders, our university team played a critical intermediary role, advocating on behalf of the community in certain cases. Whereas in other cases, our community partners stepped up and advocated for the project using their influence as voting constituents and activists in their community. Ultimately, the political capital of all stake- holders was necessary to bring this project to fruition. Research design in the community The Santa Ana PLLs were supported by an Advancing Informal STEM Learning (AISL) award from the National Science Foundation. The project began in 2020, and due to the pandemic, all design sessions in the first year of the project were held on Zoom. We held seven 90-minute co-design sessions where we learned about families histories and experiences with their community spaces, and used participatory design activities such as bags-of- stuff, photo-elicitation, story boarding, and storytelling to encourage families to share their goals and routines in their community spaces (for a detailed description of design process see Bermudez et al., 2023; Garcia et al., 2022; Chew et al., 2022). Through an inductive thematic analysis of these co-design sessions, we surfaced community values, practices, and aspirations such as promoting intergenerational learning, and increasing family time. As part of these themes, we also surfaced ways in which families' own routines and practices already involved STEM concepts and practices. We iteratively combined these themes and existing practices with the science practices and crosscutting concepts from the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and principles from developmental science for creating high-quality early learning environments that are active, engaging, iterative, social, meaningful, and joyful (Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2015). While a single design could not meet all the criteria, we sought balance across community values, developmental principles, and science learning goals (see Bermudez et al., 2023 for more detail). Further, we were intentional to align these practices with SAELI’s three step design model that included engaging parents in discovery & dreaming, designing, and creating a sustainability plan. Using these design goals and guiding frameworks, we conducted prototype ideation sessions with SAELI families and then subsequent sessions where we created low-fidelity mock-ups of the prototypes for play testing and iteration during the second and third years of the project. Children and parents were interviewed to hear their feedback on the designs and learn about their experiences playing with the physical prototypes. These sessions were key to evaluate factors from usability to how and if families’ interactions aligned with their values and practices. These sessions were held in person at their local Community Center, started with a shared meal, followed by a design activity, reflections and share outs. Through these sessions we iterated and refined the prototypes until they were ready to be shared with our fabrication partners. Fabrication and launch For fabrication, we contracted a Los Angeles based museum installation design shop. We worked closely with their engineers to adapt the co-designed prototypes for durability, usability, safety, cost efficiency, and regulation compliance. All designs were reviewed by City of Santa Ana Parks and Recreation or Public Works departments and UC Irvine’s Facilities Management department. We worked collaboratively with the City of Santa Ana and S AELI to decide where the installations would go, taking advantage of existing city renovation efforts to save costs and create efficiencies when possible. We also worked with legal representation from UCI and the City of Santa Ana to execute a Memorandum of Understanding that the PLL installations were being donated to the city by UCI and the City of Santa Ana would own and maintain them. This process took approximately two years from the beginning of the fabrication process to installation in public spaces. The installations were implemented between Fall 2024 and Spring 2025 with a grand opening ribbon cutting ceremony held on May 10th, 2025, as part of the NSF’s 75th anniversary celebration and Mother’s Day in many Latin American countries. The ceremony was hosted at Madison Park in Santa Ana and attended by the Mayor, Director of Parks and Recreation, several city council members, and the Dean of the UCI School of Education. Data collection Our data collection protocol included baseline observations of STEM language and caregiver child interactions at each of the five installation sites pre-installation as well as a matched comparison site (e.g., for a bus-stop installation we observed a comparison bus stop in the same neighborhood). We also trained SAELI parents to collect surveys at all PLL and control sites of caregiver’s self-efficacy in teaching STEM to their children, perceptions of safety and learning opportunities in their community spaces, and attitudes around the connection between play and learning. We then performed the observational and survey data collection protocol post- installation to examine the impacts of the PLL’s on caregiver child interactions and experiences in community spaces. While post-installation data collection is on-going we expect to present findings from these analyses at the ISLS workshop in June 2026. For a more detailed description of our analytical plans please refer to our project pre-registration on the Open Science Framework. Workshop details The tour will be hosted by UCI Associate Professor and project PI Andres Bustamante, UCI Professor and project Co-PI June Ahn, SAELI Director Wendy Gomez, and several SAELI parents who participated in the design and data collection processes. The hosts will offer insights into the project’s co-design approach, the partnership with the city (challenges and opportunities), parents’ roles as designers, data collectors, and project advocates, impact results, and future plans for policy agenda towards sustainability and scaling. The timetable of activities and sites to be visited are shown below (Table 1). We will also discuss several cross-site design considerations, including Playful Learning Principles, culturally responsive design, the use of public spaces as learning environments, multigenerational engagement, attention to accessibility, and low-burden participation that aligns with families’ everyday routines. Table 1 Timetable of Activities Hour Activity 8:00 am Meet at the conference hotel at 8am PST on June 15th, 2026. We will depart on a charter bus to tour the five PLL sites in Santa Ana. 8:30 am Arrive at Santa Ana, touring the 5 different sites (see text below). 11:30 am End of the tour. The charter bus will be taking people back to the conference hotel. Site 1: Madison Park. Madison Park features the largest of the Santa Ana PLL installation, Parkopolis, the life-sized board game for math and science learning. Parkopolis is a giant board game where children spin life sized dice and advance around the board completing math and science games like playing patterns on musical pipes, and measuring how far you can jump on a giant ruler. Through the co-design process, we learned about games like Basta, a category game that many SAELI families play, and integrated them into Parkopolis games. During the co-design sessions, many families expressed concerns about visiting their neighborhood parks and cited the bathroom facility in the back of Madison Park as a hotspot for illicit activities like drug use and prostitution. In response, the city demolished those bathrooms replacing them with new bathroom facilities in another part of the park, and we constructed Parkopolis where the old bathrooms were transforming a hot spot for criminal activity into a hub for early learning, a powerful example of community voice leading to impact in public infrastructure. Site 2: Abacus bus stop. T he giant abacus at the bus stop on the corner of Main Street and McFadden Avenue in Santa Ana invites families to engage in conversations around numeracy and arithmetic. Many families in our design session reference using an abacus to learn math when they were children in Mexico and other countries in Latin America and wondered why their children’s schools didn’t use an abacus. This installation is a powerful symbol of scalability because it was not funded by our NSF grant. The city of Santa Ana was renovating bus stops in this area and due to the awareness of our projects, leveraged existing funds to execute the design. Site 3: Northgate Gonzalez market. Northgate is a family owned local grocery chain that many of the SAELI families shop at. During our co-design sessions, we used families stories about grocery shopping with their parents growing up or with their children now to develop signage that promote math and science interactions. Examples include a conversion chart between pounds and kilos at the deli and using your senses to pick out the best fruits and vegetables in the produce section. This installation is unique because it demonstrates how local business and the private sector can engage and support this work. Site 4: Angels Park. Angels Park features two PLL installations, La Lotería which is a giant version of the bingo style game that is very popular with local families, and How Tall Am I? which is a statue where children can measure their height in comparison to California animals. Both of these installations are a great example of intuitive design and leveraging existing knowledge to create engaging STEM learning experiences. How Tall Am I? invites immediate engagement through its visual design and integrated measurement markers, requiring only minimal instruction in the form of a single guiding question. Similarly, Lotería is among the most popular family games in this community, lengthy instructions are not necessary. Instead, we simply embed short STEM activities into the playing cards for families to integrate into the game play. In addition to supporting informal STEM learning, both of these installations were co-designed with the intention of supporting intergenerational learning which is a core value of Latine families. Site 5: Washington elementary school. The last stop on the tour will visit the Yo Veo (I See) Mural, an interactive art exhibit where children look for hidden objects that reflect local cultural and community activities. This is another example of a local institution adopting a project design. This mural was funded by the Santa Ana Unified School District, who were renovating this school and directed funds for murals. This school also features a different project, Fraction Ball, a redesigned basketball court for math learning. Future directions During the May 10th ribbon cutting event, the City of Santa Ana made an official proclamation that May will be Early Childhood Education month in the city in recognition of this innovative work. Building on this momentum, we are working with city officials on a resolution to integrate PLLs into the city’s on-going process for new public amenities leveraging existing budget from local institutions. We plan to position SAELI as drivers of future PLL efforts where they engage local community members in a design process of new public amenities that center early learning and build from local families’ funds of knowledge. This work represents a scalable and community centered vision for designing public infrastructure to promote child development and civic engagement. Invitation to ICLS participants This session examines the evolution of a project and partnership from initial creation through implementation, using this project as a live case study to surface challenges, lessons learned, and future directions from different points of view. In doing so, we demonstrate how partnering with purpose can generate meaningful community impact and offer useful insights for other scholars and initiatives seeking to engage in collaborative, community- centered work. papers.title: Co-design as a Catalyst for Becoming: Identity, Practice, and Learning Trajectories in Undergraduate Science
papers.authors: Sunnie Gong, Michelle Lui, Aidyn Intykbekov
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Co-design is a collaborative methodology for creating educational innovations involving researchers, educators, and developers. While research -practice partnerships in the Learning Sciences have historically co-designed with teachers, recent developments have begun involving students. However, research on students’ experiences of co- design remains limited. This study explores what students learn from engaging in co-design through a situated learning framework linking learning to identity formation. Using a multiple case study methodology, the relationships between the identities, learning, and participation of six undergraduate science students were examined in a co -design project for creating educational virtual reality simulations. Findings reveal that identity, practice, and learning exist in dynamic and reciprocal relationships within co -design contexts. Students’ existing identities informed their co- design engagement. Through practice, students developed collaboration skills and learned about themselves which led to diverse identity development trajectories. These findings suggest engaging students as co-design partners creates unique opportunities for integrated learning and identity development.

papers.title: Designing an AI-Powered Reflective Partner: Translating Self-Regulated Learning Theory into Generative Chatbot Scaffolds
papers.authors: Na Liu, John Nietfeld
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students
papers.abstract: This interactive tool paper presents the design and development of an AI-powered chatbot that scaffolds college students’ self-regulated learning (SRL). Grounded in Pintrich’s SRL framework and informed by meta-analytic evidence on effective SRL interventions, the chatbot is designed as a reflective learning partner that supports metacognitive monitoring, strategic deployment, and affective regulation. Using a design-based research (DBR) approach, this study explores how SRL theory can guide the development of generative AI–mediated interactions. We describe the theoretical rationale underlying the tool, articulate key design principles, present the prototype’s architecture, and discuss implications for improving evidence-based, equitable AI scaffolds to enhance undergraduate learning outcomes.

papers.title: Teacher Agency in Learning Sciences Co-design: Dubious or Undocumented?
papers.authors: Abigail A. Williams, Sam H. Ross, R. Benjamin Shapiro
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Frequent mentions of co- design in the learning sciences (LS) reflect an increasing effort to create resources through partnerships where researchers and educators share agency. Whether these partnerships meaningfully lead to new, teacher -shaped innovations depends on the dynamics of cross-role collaborations, including who gets to make design choices. We use Bratteteig and Wagner’s (2016) conceptual framework for the types of decision- making in co- design to evaluate LS research that involves co -designing with teachers. Our review reveals substantial gaps in descriptions of teacher decision- making, indicating either insufficiently described or insufficiently empowering co-design practices. We advocate for more transparent and egalitarian approaches to co- design at all phases of the design process, to increase the equity, robustness, research contributions, and potential real-world impact of co-design.

papers.abstract: This practice -oriented paper describes the design of a partnership between StreetCode Academy and the Stanford Institute for Diversity in the Arts, created to connect community learners in a technology education program with university students and resources through a co llaborative learning model. In this endeavor, social capital was emphasized as a lever for engagement to create opportunities for relationship- building across community and institutional networks. These relationships functioned as pathways for reciprocal learning and network expansion, which supported students’ and instructors’ engagement with technical skills and their development as innovators. Preliminary findings indicate increased student interest in continued participation in technology education. Instructors and mentors also reported an increase in confidence, skill development, and sense of purpose. This paper presents design considerations for operationalizing social capital and it shows how community- university partnerships can serve as a two -way bridge for reciprocal learning and network-building to expand pathways into technology education. Objectives and theoretical grounding Despite the growth of opportunities in the innovation economy, participation in computing and technology education continues to be marked by inequity, particularly for students from communities historically excluded from access to institutional networks. While several factors influence engagement and persistence in this area, including inequitable access to digital resources and high -quality STEM learning experiences, another critical factor is how learning environments are designed to recognize and extend existing relationships and forms of support that enable participants to navigate and persist in technology pathways. S ocial capital refers to the relational supports people access and share through family, friends, teachers, and communities (Bourdieu, 1980; Coleman, 1988), and as a potential factor contributing to ongoing marginalization, should be examined more thoughtfully. In STEM research, social capital is often used as an explainer of disparities in tech participation. In this paper, however, social capital is discussed as an existing asset that can be leveraged and designed to activate new, mutually beneficial relationships across institutional networks that expand access and support participation in technology pathways. This paper presents an ongoing partnership between StreetCode Academy, a community- based technology education nonprofit, and Stanford University, a world-renowned institution of higher learning known for its culture of innovation. Founded in 2014, StreetCode Academy is committed to bridging the technology education gap by offering free coding, entrepreneurship, and design classes to youth and their families in communities with longstanding histories of creativity and technological ingenuity, where access to technology learning opportunities is not always equitably available . The Stanford Institute for Diversity in the Arts is a “student-facing and serving organization" committed to offering opportunities to practice leadership, creative expression, and social responsibility through the arts. This partnership extended StreetCode ’s community-based learning model for communities historically underrepresented in formal technology institutions onto Stanford’s campus, a university with a strong institutional emphasis on technology and innovation, intentionally repositioning who participates in and belongs within these spaces. This created opportunities for students and their families to build new connections and engage with university spaces that are not often available or accessible to the public. For many participants, this included taking classes on a university campus for the first time, which positively influenced their sense of belonging and possibility within technology and higher education pathways. It also created meaningful opportunities for 2171 university students pursuing fields adjacent to technology, education, design, and the arts to contribute as mentors and instructors while developing their own perspectives and skills. Through this initiative, they were able to apply their disciplinary knowledge in authentic, culturally grounded contexts, which helped them experience affirmation and support that reinforced their sense of belonging in fields where they may have otherwise experienced marginalization (McGee, 2020). Positioning the role of social capital in tech education is significant because it can serve as an existing and malleable design resource within educational systems. Students bring with them unique social and cultural resources that serve as valuable assets in supporting their learning trajectories (Yosso, 2005). V aluing and leveraging students' existing networks and intentionally curating expanded connections, educators can engage relational dimensions that can be critical to fostering greater participation in technology-related learning pathways and academic settings, particularly among historically underrepresented groups. These relations can positively impact learners’ feelings of inclusion and their self -esteem as they navigate technology-related fields , which positively influence learning and identity development. In this context, social capital was treated as a catalyst as well as an outcome, cultivated to foster social and academic growth among the students and educators participating in the program. In this process, relationships were mutually constituted through ongoing interaction, as participants both drew on and contributed to shared relational networks. These dynamics created opportunities for co -development, where learners and instructors built confidence and capacity through shared engagement. This has the potential to extend existing research on social networks and opportunity (Chetty et al., 2024) , demonstrating how social capital can be intentionally designed within learning environments to encourage reciprocal relationships that help shape participants’ engagement and aspirational trajectories. These theoretical perspectives informed the program’s design, guiding its intention to respect and position all participants as active contributors to the learning culture, and structure community engagement in a way that centered reciprocal identity development, where students, mentors, and instructors developed in distinct but interconnected ways through their engagement in teaching, learning, and collaboration. Design The StreetCode Academy and Stanford University Institute for Diversity in the Arts (IDA) partnership shared three intersecting goals: the first was to increase accessibility to top -tier learning opportunities. StreetCode Academy is committed to providing learning experiences that help participants gain foundational skills in a variety of coding, design, and media platforms. Stanford University is a global research institution of higher education, known for its contributions to the innovation economy. The Institute for Diversity in the Arts, founded 25 years ago, was established to educate, activate, and transform students at Stanford and extend that mission to the local community. The second goal was to advance the conversation around culture, arts, and technology, exploring how these intersect to inspire creativity, expression, and innovation. The third was to bridge perceived and actual divides across communities by fostering belonging and community across institutional boundaries between the university and the local community. Designing for access, belonging, and shared participation To support these goals, the partnership was designed for both entities to contribute in complementary ways. Regarding accessibility, the Institute for Diversity in the Arts provided financial resources so StreetCode could coordinate free transportation, provide free laptop rentals and usage for students, and even offer free meals for participants, removing many of the logistical barriers that can often prevent engagement. Framing access as a design principle helped to promote more equitable participation and expand participants’ connections to social networks through the structural organization of the learning environment. The program design prioritized a family- centered learning environment. This partnership offered intergenerational learning spaces where youth, elders, children, and parents could learn together. This is atypical for many K12 or university classrooms, which are traditionally designed for a specific age range. One participant, a 76-year-old Spanish-speaking StreetCode student, spoke at the final-quarter Demo Day, sharing that it had been her dream to take a course at Stanford, and that, through this program, it was finally achieved. This example illustrates how designing for intergenerational participation supported a spirit of lifelong learning and expanded who could belong in the space while also creating opportunities for individuals across generations to l earn alongside one another and reimagine themselves as technology innovators. 2172 Building on these design choices, this program aimed to operationalize social capital so that learners and instructors could interact as mutual recipients and co-producers of value. This was an intentional move away from traditional one-directional service-oriented models of technology education, toward a more connected and empowering model of shared learning. Grounded in the principle of “learning through participation,” the project centered an epistemology of development that recognized access to diverse people, experiences, and environments as integral to how participants form affirming mindsets and identities as technologists and innovators. Across the program, three design considerations for operationalizing social capital were prioritized: reducing barriers to participation, centering shared participation and belonging, and expanding opportunities for purposeful network- building to support sustained engagement. Implementation A fourteen-week program was developed, encompassing a variety of courses. Courses were thematically designed around the topic of “culture and tech” and introduced participants to cutting-edge and emerging technology. Each course included opportunities to engage in practical, technical use of technology and in theoretical and philosophical discussions about how each person could use these tools to preserve and positively advance their cultural traditions and personal goals. This approach reaffirmed education as a force of personal liberation and advancement for each student as well as their local and global communities. Courses were offered in two seven -week rotations, with sessions held once a week for 2.5 hours each. Offerings included courses like “Storytelling & Tech,” “Music & Tech,” “Design & Tech,” “Jr. Design & Tech,” “Intro to Code,” and “STEMLabs Mechanical Engi neering.” Classes were hosted on Stanford’s campus at the IDA “house” and the Black Community Services Center, where the community room and lobby became classrooms that “felt like home” for students, filled with art, music, and warmth that reflected the students’ community aesthetics and values. Enacting bonding through shared rituals Classes began with a 30-minute ritual called “Huddle-up,” intended to inspire students for the upcoming courses and connect them with one another over food, engaging activities, and presentations by featured students or special guests. Huddle -ups began wit h a shared dinner, during which announcements highlighted past student accomplishments and upcoming events. Activities were designed to have students interact with one another so they could learn about each other. Discussing a topic around a table or acting out a scenario would bring people together. Huddle-ups also featured guest speakers or showcased the work and talents of community members, which often led students to follow up with each other or with a guest speaker about an opportunity they might not otherwise have known about. Following Huddle-Up, students would break into their courses, which were facilitated by several lead instructors and taught by StreetCode alumni, industry experts, and Stanford students. Each class had one or two lead instructors and was supported by three to four mentors. While 66% of classes were taught by Stanford students, every course had a lead teacher or mentor who represented the geographical or cultural background of the StreetCode students. StreetCode community members, industry representatives, a nd the Stanford affiliates were all treated as co -designers who collaborated on curriculum design, logistics, and pedagogy throughout the quarters. Enacting network expansion across community, university, and industry To deepen the connection to industry, each quarter had a day committed to exploring the field. Experiences included a trip to the Stanford innovation program, hosted by the director of publications and co- director of the K-12 Lab, and a visit to OpenAI, where a workshop was led by a former StreetCode instructor and Stanford alumnus and colleague. These trips were designed to strengthen the relationship between these organizations and the StreetCode community, empowering the social capital participants could access through more formal network development. Quarterly courses ended with a Demo Day, a community- wide public celebration that invited members of the broader community to experience a showcase of what students had learned and accomplished. Nearly 20 employees from Amazon and 15 members of Links, a professional organization of African American women, attended one of the Demo Days, along with numerous Stanford students, StreetCode community members, family, and friends. Students presented their work and exchanged information with visiting guests. One student who 2173 created a movie using an AI platform even raised $250 from attendees who wanted to support his continued subscription to the platform beyond the course. Through outside speaking engagements, field trips, and Demo Days, these relationships were nurtured beyond what was gained in the classroom, with enrolled participants expanding their personal and professional networks of opportunities and support. The implementation of each activity and the program overall was thoughtfully curated to expand the realization and potential of social capital across residential, academic, and industry communities, connecting StreetCode students with professors and students at S tanford University; also connecting Stanford University and industry partners and affiliates with genuine opportunities to engage with local community members around relevant and resonant partnerships. In doing so, the program strengthened individual trajectories and cultivated an ecosystem of shared learning and mutual investment. Practice-based learnings There are many context -specific factors that may have affected the efficacy of these efforts. However, early findings are encouraging. Participant feedback collected through post-class surveys indicated that 94% of students expressed a desire to continue learning about technology; and 70% reported an increase in their sense of identity as innovators. These data suggest positive implications for this approach, providing a generative introduction to technology for community participants. In addition, instructor feedback indicated that assuming the role of mentor or teacher supported the development of confidence and skills as they, too, navigated exploratory conversations and reflected on their growth as emerging professionals in computing and education. They also gained valuable first -hand experience designing learning environments aligned with principles they apply in their STEM courses (e.g., design thinking, Universal Design for Learning, Understanding by Design), reinforcing their technical skill development. Teachers also discussed how this experience acted as a space for personal mindset renewal. It provided opportunities to reflect on their relationships with technology and to reconnect with their motivating hopes and aims, empowering their journeys as developing professionals and technologists. In this way, teaching became a creative means of sustaining motivation and recharging their sense of purpose. Meaning- making is recognized as a dimension of well-being (Seligman, 2011). Connecting their academic work to an authentic teaching experience, student - teachers were able to deepen the connection between their learning and real -world practice. This contributed to their positive identity development and overall personal wellness. Outcomes experienced by all participants, students and instructors, point to a reinforcing developmental experience which was supported by shared participation, strengthened relationships, and expanded network connections. Instructors’ growing confidence in their skills and renewed sense of purpose were nurtured by their experiences teaching and supporting students, who affirmed their developing expert ise. Similarly, students’ increased confidence and emerging innovator identities developed through their engagement with near-peer instructors, whose mentorship and presence as accessible role models helped shape their identities as technologists. Relevance Preliminary learnings from this project implicate the need for more research to better understand the degree to which social capital, and in what forms, influences levels of student engagement and sustained participation in computing pathways. Future research might also inquire how a model like this could help to address gaps between student needs and available school offerings, particularly in expanding opportunities to develop technical skills and strengthen psychological supports. Implications for future practice-based initiatives include identifying community assets and opportunities to triangulate practice, bringing together resources that connect community organizations and academic institutions, with opportunities to connect to industry to spur individual and communal development through designed pathways across locally situated learning ecologies. This partnership’s preliminary outcomes suggest the potential for more strategic programming to expand equitable participation , positioning social capital as a designable mechanism for reciprocal learning and network-building across community and university contexts. papers.title: Productive Entanglements: Patterns of Partnership for Learning Technology Innovation
papers.authors: Alyssa Friend Wise
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Impactful learning technology innovation doesn’t happen in isolation; it grows through relationships, among researchers, educators, students, technologists, designers, and institutional leaders. While some collaborations are carefully structured, others take root more organically, evolving to meet shifting needs and opportunities. In this keynote, Dr. Alyssa Wise explores how purposeful partnerships drive innovation across the technological, social, conceptual, and practical dimensions of learning, tracing three kinds of partnerships that have unfolded over the past decade in her work. Flexible Coupling articulates how institutional partnerships can leverage complementary strengths without becoming over-structured. In a longstanding collaboration with a university learning analytics service unit, in vivo studies of instructors’ analytics use informed both theoretical models of sense-making and applied tool design. Constructive Responsiveness describes how partnerships with educators can evolve around a shared object of inquiry when goals are not yet fully defined. In work with dental educators implementing an online reflection tool, the collaboration advanced from examinations of reflection quality to generate domain-specific insights into failure attribution and professional identity formation. Finally, Generative Pluralism characterizes interdisciplinary partnerships among researchers or co-designers where the goal is not convergence but conceptual creation. These collaborations embraced multiplicity, surfacing productive tensions, methodological bridges, and new vocabularies for imagining learning technologies. Together, these patterns illustrate partnerships as adaptable forms of collaboration, each suited to different problems, people, and purposes. This talk highlights how designing, studying, and sustaining learning with the support of technology can be supported by purposeful partnerships that bridge disciplines, organizations, and stakeholder perspectives. Bio: Dr. Alyssa Wise is Professor of Technology and Education at Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College, with a courtesy appointment in Computer Science in the College of Connected Computing. She also serves as Director of the LIVE Learning Innovation Incubator, Vanderbilt’s interdisciplinary hub for impactful learning technology innovation. Her research productively integrates tools of computational data science, theories of learning sciences and collaborative learning, and practices of human-centered design to build and study analytic and artificial intelligence systems that promote powerful learning for individuals situated in social context. She also conducts mixed-method investigations into how educational practices are being reshaped by new sources of data and the growing availability of new generative artificial intelligence capabilities. Dr. Wise holds a Ph.D. in Learning Sciences and M.S. in Instructional Systems Technology from Indiana University, as well as a B.S. in Chemistry from Yale University, was previously a Professor of Learning Sciences and Educational Technology and Director of the Learning Analytics Research Network (LEARN) at New York University and has worked in industry, with non-profits, and in classrooms across the Americas. https://tinyurl.com/alyssawisescholar https://peabody.vanderbilt.edu/bio/?pid=alyssa-wise https://lab.vanderbilt.edu/live https://www.linkedin.com/in/alyssawise

papers.title: Towards Teachers-AI Collaboration for Professional Development in Learning Design
papers.authors: Shatha N. Alkhasawneh, Davinia Hernández-Leo
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can enhance learning design (LD) by exploring stakeholders’ preferences for five conceptual GenAI -based conversational agent functions —Authoring Assistant, Inspiration Hub, Design Feedback, Possibility Engine, and Ethics Guardian—adapted from the GenAI Speculative Functions Framework for LD. Proposed for the TRAILS teacher professional development platform, these functions target underexplored early phases of LD. Using a convergent mixed-methods design, 56 participants evaluated these functions, their support needs across design phases, and related opportunities and concerns. Findings reveal a two- pillar demand: creative inspiration, prioritized in the Investigation phase through the Inspiration Hub, and drafting efficiency, prioritized in the Authoring phase through the Authoring Assistant. The analysis revealed role- dependent value: experienced practitioners favored generative and creativity -oriented functions, while prospective teachers emp hasized diagnostic and feedback support. The Ethics Guardian emerged as an essential ambient safeguard. The study offers practical guidance for integrating human- centered GenAI into teacher professional development platforms and human-AI collaboration in LD.
