papers.title: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity : Designing STEM Futures Through Play, Media, and Imagination
papers.authors: Kareem Edouard
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Prolepsis ’Till Infinity calls for an education that recognizes imagination as infrastructure. Dr. Kareem Edouard invites us to rethink how we build STEM spaces that honor culture, creativity, and care as the foundation of learning. His research at the ILLEST Lab challenges systems that reward compliance over curiosity, asking what becomes possible when play, storytelling, and design are treated as serious forms of knowledge, particularly for those most marginalized in STEAM, Black boys. Drawing from his design practices across learning, children’s media, and informal STEAM environments, Dr. Edouard examines how learners develop identity, agency, and understanding through participatory, culturally responsive experiences, highlighting key insights from the learning sciences. For example, in co-design projects with educators and youth, students engage in creative problem-solving and media production, positioning them as knowledge-makers whose ideas actively shape the learning environment. These collaborative partnerships demonstrate how purposeful engagement between educators, researchers, and communities fosters equitable and imaginative learning outcomes. Dr. Edouard envisions an educational future where play, imagination, and community are essential for liberation. This keynote invites us to build toward proleptic, possible, and connected futures already in motion, where creativity and meaning-making shape how we learn, teach, and thrive together. By treating play, imagination, and community as foundational, Dr. Edouard shows how learning and partnership are inseparable in designing educational spaces that cultivate curiosity, empowerment, and cultural relevance. Bio: Dr. Kareem Edouard is an Assistant Professor of Learning Technologies at Drexel University’s School of Education and Co-Director of the Informal Learning Linking Engineering, Science and Technology (ILLEST) Lab. His work explores how design, as a cultural, creative, and communal practice, intersects informal STEM education and children’s media to promote meaningful knowledge transfer across learning spaces. He examines how storytelling and co-creation cultivate belonging, purpose, and imagination in environments shaped by inequity. Through initiatives like the Black Male Animation Lab, Dr. Edouard redefines STEM as a space for cultural creation and collective care, empowering Black boys as designers, storytellers, and innovators. He focuses on Black boys because their experiences sharpen the stakes of equity work in STEM: to support those most marginalized by systemic exclusion is to test whether design can truly be liberatory. His liberatory co-design framework examines how collaborative creation transforms educational systems and expands equity and representation. In the Sneaker Lab, design, material science, and cultural expression are explored for their impact on identity and innovation. The GRIND initiative further investigates how sports, data, and technology can foster community-driven STEM engagement. Dr. Edouard integrates his co-liberty design framing vision into children’s STEM media. This approach combines his experience as a former music video and commercial director with his academic research. As Executive Producer of MayNERD’s Wild World of Science (YouTube Kids), Built From Scratch, and Creative Producer of Work It Out Wombats! (PBS KIDS), he uses media as a conduit to share STEM learning and engagement, which remains at the heart of his work with children’s media. https://drexel.edu/soe/faculty-and-staff/faculty/Edouard-Kareem https://www.linkedin.com/in/kareemedouard https://www.olegreensgroup.com/home Special Session

papers.title: Examining Youth Authority in Community Member Interviews during the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
papers.authors: Yuxi Huang, Symone Gyles, Aakriti Bisht, Rossella Santagata, Hosun Kang, Sara Ludovise
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines youth authority in interviews with community members during a series of environmental engineering curriculum co -design sessions. Seven high school students, together with teachers, university researchers and informal environmental educators, participated in this multi- session task. The study aimed to understand how youth articulate, realize, and negotiate authority throughout the process. The qualitative analysis of audio recordings from co -design group discussions, formal interviews, reflections, and end- of-year interviews yielded three themes. First, youth authority drew from different sources across different activities. Second, facilitated activities scaffolded youth to realize epistemic and deontic authority. Third, youth authority emerged through adapting and challenging tasks. These findings extend the previous macro-level analyses of power dynamics and suggest that a balance between scaffolding and autonomy is critical to allow youth to exercise authority. This work also contributes to broader literature on power, authority, and equitable youth engagement in curriculum design.

papers.title: Entities Detonating Potentials: Interuniversity Design Workshop TiUD as an Exploratory Lab for Actants of the Futures
papers.authors: Inés Alvarez-Icaza, Claudia Garduño-García, Edrei Ibarra-Martínez, Reneé Harari Masri
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The Interuniversity Design Workshop is an exploratory laboratory that promotes the study of design activism, sustainable design, and transition design. The seventh edition of the workshop aimed to visualize the organizations, institutions, or companies that must be created to enable Mexico City to reach its potential for social well-being. The object of this educational experience is to enable design students to discover new ways to promote social activation through design as a professional activity. A group of 60 undergraduate design students from five high education institutions (HEI,’s) analyzed their own contexts, emphasi zing the identification of potential sources of wellbeing; later, they were given the task to design interactions, including giving shape to the agents that would make them possible. Their projects revealed three key findings: (a) that students are able to identify potentials through contextual observation; (b) that the creation of new actors can potentially activate new realities; and (c) the proposed entities hint potential future roles of designers in Latin American contexts. This study contributes to the field of design, looking towards a fairer, more pluralistic and diverse future .

papers.title: A Tale of Two Rivers: Pedagogical Implications Learned Through the Co- Design of an Environmental Engineering Curriculum
papers.authors: Taryn Williams, Symone Gyles, Hosun Kang, Rossella Santagata, Yuxi Huang, Aakriti Bisht, Teresa Hachey, Jennifer Long, Erick Valdez, Sara Ludovise
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As the impacts of climate change intensify, it is critical to support high school students in developing Critical Science Agency (CSA) and Systems Thinking (ST) to leverage science learning to address environmental concerns in their local communities and beyond. This study is part of a project involving a collaboration between university researchers, informal science educators, and high school students and teachers to codesign a place - and community- based environmental engineering curriculum. We explore pedagogical implications surfaced through the analysis of teacher and student codesign experiences and reflections that focus on community- embedded and relational environmental learning. Findings highlight the importance of physical presence to support critical and informed socio-ecological understanding of place.

papers.title: Design-Based Approaches to Co-Analysis in Collaborative Research
papers.authors: Kylie Peppler, June Ahn, Maggie Dahn
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) and design- based implementation research (DBIR) emphasize co-design with stakeholders, yet approaches for collaborative data analysis remain underdeveloped. This paper examines how design approaches can scaffold quali tative and quantitative inquiry for diverse partners in co-analysis processes. We present two working examples: the TRACE Project, which developed a community -driven taxonomy of arts program outcomes through collaborative classification with 26 community arts organizations, and the Whole Child Analytics Project (WCAP), which employed AI -assisted reflection tools to measure college and career readiness competencies through teacher and student co-design in a large, urban school district. Through these cases, we illustrate methods for creating spaces that afford meaningful engagement from all partners while honoring multiple perspectives, voices, and worldviews in the analysis process.

papers.authors: Madison Allen Kuyenga
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: My research examines how cultural practices (e.g., barbering, cosmetology, fashion design) and epistemologies (i.e., ways of knowing) can be learned and sustained while acquiring computer science (CS) skills. I draw on ethnocomputing and leverage heritage algorithms— hybrids of computing and culture—to create simulations of cultural practices using algorithms. These simulations can be used to teach cultural ways of knowing and making as well as CS skills. Overall, my research focuses on sustaining cultural making practices and cultivating the creative aspects of CS education through community-based participatory design research. In this statement, I share my previous work in CS education and ethnocomputing and situate future strands of my work in STEAM and the learning sciences.

papers.title: Multimodal Interactions with AI: Human–AI Partnerships in Learning, Teaching, and Research
papers.authors: Hanall Sung
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: My research program examines how multimodal interactions with AI shape learning, teaching, and research. I investigate how learners build and express knowledge across verbal, embodied, and digital modalities, and how AI can meaningfully participate in these processes. My work spans three interconnected strands. First, I design AI-based systems that personalize learning by assessing cognitive processes through multimodal data triangulation. Second, I develop human–AI hybrid intelligence approaches for modeling complex, temporally layered learning processes, leveraging methods such as the interleaving approach, epistemic network analysis, and computer vision. Third, I design immersive XR learning environments in which AI agents scaffold embodied STEM learning through interactive multimodal guidance. Across these strands, my goal is to advance theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous frameworks for understanding and designing human–AI partnerships that enhance multimodal sense-making and meaning-making in learning sciences and CSCL contexts.

papers.abstract: This paper examines how curriculum routines can mediate tensions between the convergent tendencies of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and the divergent, equity- oriented affordances of collaborative learning. Drawing on a multi -year partnership with te achers, we analyze the co -design and classroom enactment of a collaborative AI partner, CoBi , and associated “revisiting community agreement” routines. Using video data and thematic analysis, we show how these routines functioned as boundary objects linking design intent with classroom practice. Teachers enacted the routines with high integrity and creatively adapted them to local contexts, leveraging AI errors to foster AI literacy and critical reflection. papers.title: Telling the Spiders’ Stories: Relationship Building as Essential Infrastructuring for Climate Justice Learning
papers.authors: Helen L. Fitzmaurice, Emily V. Reigh, Chris Jadallah, Michelle Hernandez Romero, Lauren Daus
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: There is growing attention to the need to design climate and environmental learning opportunities that support collective action towards more just futures. In this symposium, we explore the many kinds of connections required for collective work: connecting diverse knowledge traditions and cultural paradigms, connecting histories to futures, and connecting youth and teachers with community-based actors who are advancing environmental justice. We use the metaphor of spiderwebs to describe the networks of knowledges, worldviews, and stakeholders that foster visions of more just futures. Moreover, we draw attention to the work of spiders, referring to the human actors who build and sustain these webs. Our studies explore the complexity of maintaining spiderwebs across disciplinary and institutional boundaries and underscore the relational work needed to address the associated power differentials. We argue that this web-weaving constitutes critical infrastructuring for climate justice teaching, learning, and action, and advocate for recognition and support of this indispensable form of labor. Symposium theme and overview Although climate change has typically been treated as a technical problem in science (e.g., Clark, 2024), there is growing recognition that it is a sociopolitical issue that has been driven by capitalism (Oreskes & Conway, 2010), colonialism ( Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2022), and other forms of environmental racism (Bullard, 1993). As a result, climate change exacerbates inequities that already exist for marginalized communities around the world, who face substantial barriers to protection and recovery. Young people today understand the severity of this issue; more than 85% of young people in the US experience climate anxiety (e.g. , Lewandowski et al., 2024). While there is a need to address climate change and the attendant inequities, teaching that is focused solely on histories of oppression can be disheartening and deepen students’ sense of despair about the future. Recent studies have pointed to the power of collective action to help youth develop a sense of critical hope for the future (Schwartz et al., 2023), an approach to “partnering with purpose” that warrants increased attention in science learning spaces. Through engaging in collective action, students develop their own identities as knowers, visionaries, organizers, and builders who can affect social and environmental change. Rather than framing climate action narrowly in terms of mitigation and adaptation, we echo the stance of Isha Clarke, a youth activist from Oakland who explained, “Climate justice is about completely reimagining the way that we live on the planet ... It is about collective liberation and dismantling systems of oppression in every way that they exist” (Milagro Henriquez, 2021). For models of this kind of work, we look to the “lifeworlds 2387 of Black, Indigenous, and Third World peoples” who have repeatedly survived world -ending events and bring long histories of collective struggle against injustice to “[build] the world anew” (Jadallah et al., 2025, pp. 9–11). By learning from and acting in solidarity with these communities who are again on the frontlines of injustice, we can work together to imagine new social systems. We aim to create opportunities for climate learning that are consequential (Hall & Jurow, 2015; Jurow et al., 2016), meaning that they move beyond the acquisition of knowledge and skills by considering the implications for students' lives. Climate and environmental learning are made consequential through spiderwebs, or constellations of people, institutions , and geographies. These spiderwebs bridge sites of formal learning and spaces of community -based action, fostering collaboration across different worldviews, knowledge -building practices, and timescales in ways that promote social transformation. We also shine a light on the importance of spiders, or the individuals who build and sustain relationships across learning ecologies to foster collective action. Sometimes the spiders are the youth themselves. Other times, the spiders are community organizers, parents, teachers, or school district administrators. Spiders do the complex work of navigating institutional norms, constraints, and power dynamics within and across learning environments, working both within and outside of existing institutional structures. The webs that they construct are dynamic and precarious; they are constantly torn, reattached, mended, and reformed , requiring substantial time, skill, and emotional labor to maintain. We position the spiderwebs describe d across our work as critical infrastructure for climate justice teaching, learning, and research. “Infrastructuring” reflects the activity required to “redesign components, relations, and routines of schools” in order to sustain learning innovations (Penuel, 2019, p. 1). Much of the current work on infrastructuring focuses on aspects of the schooling system, such as national standards, district policies, and instructional practices, as well as the people who enact them, such as teachers and administrators. In contrast, we build on the work of scholars who have suggested that infrastructuring for justice -focused innovation in schools requires the inclusion of a wider range of stakeholders, including those whose voices are not typically heard in formal schooling spaces (e.g., Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2022). Similarly, our papers argue that infrastructuring for climate justice requires designing for the inclusion of the experiences and worldviews of communities on the frontlines of climate change. In this symposium, we explore how climate justice learning can be made consequential by creating spiderwebs that bring diverse stakeholders together to work towards social change. Each paper offers a perspective on building these relational webs. Across papers, we present theoretical tools (paper 2), design principles (paper 3), instructional activities and practices (papers 1 and 4), and relational practices (paper 5). We demonstrate how these approaches support learners in building connections across timescales (papers 1 and 2), knowledge systems (papers 1, 2, 3), and school- and community-based learning sites (papers 3, 4, and 5). In this symposium, we position infrastructuring for climate and environmental justice as an essential aspect of “partnering with purpose.” Collectively, we will consider the extent to which the learning sciences community—as individuals, within institutions, and as a field —contributes to the work of web- building and how we can and should deepen that work. The presentation portion of the symposium will be arranged in three sections: (1) The chairs (Drs. Fitzmaurice and Reigh) will introduce the theme of the symposium, provide an overview of the sessions, and ask audience members to briefly reflect on their own involvement in web building [~7 min]. (2) Each presenter will present their work [~10 min each, 50 min total]. (3) Our discussant Heather Clark, a former high school scie nce teacher and expert in justice- focused climate change education who collaborates deeply with teachers, will synthesize and reflect on findings [10 min]. The remainder of the symposium will be devoted to discussion. Audience members will first discuss a series of questions in small groups and share their responses [~18 min]. Questions include: How should teacher educators and researchers engage in building or supporting networks of relationships across institutions, geographies, and positionalities through their work in the context of climate change or environmental justice? What barriers or supports exist within our own institutions for this work? What p ractices have we developed in our individual work contexts that build just and equitable partnerships? How do we negotiate the tensions related to time scales (the urgency of climate change and the long timescales of justice-focused learning surfaced in our studies) or length scales (the global nature of climate change and the importance of engaging learners in critical pedagogies of place and forming local connections)? Finally, the session chairs will facilitate audience questions for the presenters [~10 min]. 2388 Paper 1: Weaving relational webs across generations and geographies Chris Jadallah, Michelle Hernandez Romero, Lauren Daus Theoretical framework Building climate justice necessitates “looking back to look forward” (Winn & Tottenham, 2025, p. 70), where we weave relational webs that connect past, present, and future and that bring together human beings and the rest of the natural world in ways that recognize our mutually connected destinies (Simpson, 2017). Looking back provides an opportunity to re-member the ancestral knowledge and practices from which we have been dis - membered via colonial histories (wa Thiong’o, 2009), which provide a compass for living in better relation with lands and waters (Takeuchi et al., 2024). We theorize learning as a process of re -membering and weaving relational webs (Jurow et al., 2025; Meixi, 2022). In doing so, we draw on conceptualizations of learning as movement across home, school, and other community settings through which learners weave across these spaces, and across time, to “become conscious historical actors who begin to understand their present and future selves in relation to broader historical forces and spatial architectures” (Gutiérrez, 2020, p. 2). These perspectives support our work to design and study new forms of participation, learning, and relational becoming (Meixi, 2022) that are culturally sustaining and revitalizing (McCarty & Lee, 2014).

papers.title: Mapping Mathematical Intent: Investigating Conceptual Conflicts in Integrated Math and Computational Thinking Lessons
papers.authors: Asmaa Yazidi Alaoui, Jessi Lajos, Jody Clarke-Midura, Jessica Shumway, Deborah Silvis
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study investigates how second- grade students build connections between abstract mathematical concepts and concrete actions through the use of robot coding toys to support multiplicative reasoning. Drawing on the Onto-Semiotic Approach, we analyzed video data from three integrated mathematics and computational thinking lessons to identify semiotic conflicts, with a focus on conceptual conflicts. Our findings reveal that these conflicts emerged from four distinct variations: chunking, two loops in a row, usefulness of the last loop, and not locked in loop. These results underscore the critical role of the design of coding toys and offer practical implications for educators. Specifically, the study provides insights into how teachers can anticipate and mitigate these conflicts by being aware of their nature. This awareness can help facilitate students’ ability to connect abstract mathematical ideas, computational code, and concrete actions more effectively.

papers.abstract: Minority small businesses operating in resource -constrained areas are actively building their digital capacity while facing significant barriers that existing digital services fail to address. We designed and implemented the Community Tech Consultants (CTC s) program to address this gap by offering accessible and effective digital support grounded in a deep understanding of these businesses’ realities, challenges, and needs. To deepen community partnerships and meaningfully engage university students, this study aims to develop a community-engaged curriculum that prepares students for culturally responsive tech consulting with these businesses, and that can be adapted across diverse cultural and community contexts. Through design -based research and co -design with community partners, we propose a community-engaged curriculum design model with five interrelated elements: co -design and co-instruction, authentic learning, adaptive scaffolding, iteration, and adaptability. We extend the discourse on cultural responsiveness in community- engaged learning and underscore the value of co-design between the community and the university.

papers.title: Strategies for Self-Regulated Learning with AI in an Undergraduate Research Methods Course
papers.authors: Anna A. Shao, Sai Siddartha Maram, Camillia Matuk, Shayan Shirshekar, Elin Carstendottir, Edward Melcer, Steven Sutherland, Magy Seif El-Nasr, Casper Harteveld
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Undergraduate research methods education faces numerous challenges with respect to student affect, interest, and conceptual understanding. We incorporated a set of artificial intelligence chatbots into an introductory psychology research methods course, designed to promote students’ self-regulation while learning to design their own research studies. Analyses of student-AI interactions and student focus group interviews revealed instances in which students used AI to exercise agency over their learning, deepening their understanding of a topic, and engaging in self-regulation. Findings also revealed instances of students’ overreliance on AI. This study has implications for the design of AI chatbots to support research methods education, and self-regulated learning more broadly.

papers.authors: Benjamin Farmer Lacombe, Megan Stevens
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Open-source software development is a longstanding form of collaboration in the technology sector. As high school teachers, we explore the open-source model as a pedagogical framework, building on our work in a graduate-level Knowledge Building course at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education. We suggest that framing computer science education around the open-source model can support pervasive and authentic knowledge building discourses, by producing explicit artifacts made accessible to the local community and beyond to support continual idea improvement.

papers.abstract: This paper explores the design of two types of pedagogical agents—teaching and peer—in a collaborative STEM+C learning environment, C2STEM, where high school students learn physics (kinematics) and computing by building computational models that simulate the motion of objects. Through in-depth case study interviews with teachers and students, we identify role-based features for these agents to support collaborative learning in open-ended STEM+C learning environments. We propose twelve design principles—four for teaching agents, four for peer agents, and four shared by both—contributing to foundational guidelines for developing agents that enhance collaborative learning through computational modeling.

papers.title: The Role of Teacher Framing in Shaping Student Agency in Human-AI Partnered Science Classrooms
papers.authors: ChanMin Kim, Jung Eun Ha, Dana Gnesdilow, Rebecca J. Passonneau, Sadhana Puntambekar
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study is part of a larger research project aimed at developing and implementing an NLP-enabled AI feedback tool called PyrEval to support middle school students’ science explanation writing. We explored how human-AI integrated classrooms can invite students to harness AI tools while still being agentic learners. Building on theory of new materialism with posthumanist perspectives, we examined teacher framing to see how the nature of PyrEval was communicated, thereby orienting students to partner with or rely on PyrEval. We analyzed one teacher’s talk in multiple classrooms as well as that of students in small groups. We found student agency was fostered through teacher framing of (a) PyrEval as a non-neutral actor and a co-investigator and (b) students’ participation as an author and their understanding of the nature of PyrEval as core task and purpose. Findings and implications are discussed.

papers.authors: Susan Harrington, Sonja Klein, Alice Catherine Fratoni, Charlott Sellberg, Oskar Lindwall
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Simulators have become central in professional training, in this case maritime education, where they support the development and assessment of skills and competencies required of competent seafarers. This study aims to inform the design of a learning analytics dashboard utilizing multimodal learning analytics to deliver automated, adaptive feedback to maritime students. Feedback is critical in simulator-based training, yet the characteristics of meaningful automated feedback in professional training remain underexplored. Drawing on a participatory design workshop with maritime students, the study examines tensions arising from the conceptualization of automated feedback. Using cultural historical activity theory, we frame tensions as opportunities for innovation, highlighting the dynamic interplay between students, instructors, and technology. In doing so, we offer insights into designing meaningful automated feedback for simulation training, and the need to balance students’ dual roles as learners and future professionals, reconciling collaborative learning with personalized feedback, and prioritizing educational goals over technological innovation.

papers.abstract: Educators’ self-perception as individuals who could engineer influences their motivation and support they provide during engineering learning. This study examines ways to support engineering identity development of library professionals and position them as educators for children’s engineering learning. Drawing from the theory of identities-in-practice and the concept of boundary crossing, this study conducts a case study to investigate how rural library professionals developed traces of emerging engineering identity. By examining nine library professionals’ engagement over two years in a three-year project to co-design and facilitate an online engineering program for children and their parents, this study contributes to the understanding of how public library professionals perform boundary crossing practices to position themselves as engineering learners and educators. The study further illuminates the potential of public libraries to serve as transformative spaces for engineering engagement and encourages public libraries to redefine library professionals’ roles.

papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, driven by large language models (LLMs), are increasingly explored for their potential in educational contexts. However, significant concerns remain regarding their efficacy, cognitive impacts, and ethical implications. The Computer Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) community faces critical questions regarding the broader implications of this technology for the field. While GenAI offers advanced opportunities for collaborative learning through conversational interactions and other functions, research in this area is still in its early stages. This symposium presents five contributions that explore the opportunities, challenges, and initial findings of integrating GenAI into educational settings. The goal is to provide evidence-based recommendations for practice and identify key research directions and challenges for the future of CSCL in the context of GenAI.

papers.abstract: This exploratory study investigated the use of magic performance to promote empathy and perspective-taking skills of design students. The results suggest that magic not only increased students’ awareness of their bias but also encouraged them to form a user-centered mindset. This study highlights the potential of using magic as an innovative pedagogy to facilitate critical thinking, empathy, and perspective-taking.

papers.authors: Sarah Lilly, Eric Bredder, Anne M. McAlister, Jennifer L. Chiu
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: As computer science (CS) is integrated in elementary science curricula, it is important to consider teachers’ perceptions in how they access CS and support students to engage in CS skills and standards through NGSS-aligned activities. This single case study utilizes the Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) to examine teacher change and explore the perspectives of a teacher, through semi-structured interviews, as he implements an NGSS-aligned, project-based CS unit over the course of four years. Findings indicate that the teacher perceived that changes in his practice helped inform changes in student outcomes and the curriculum and, in turn, these changes in outcomes further informed his teaching practice in the next iteration of the unit. Results highlight the importance of reflection and feedback as a way to impact the teaching practice of integrating CS in elementary science education.

papers.title: Space and Time as Elements to Design With in Engineering for Sustainability
papers.authors: Max K. Sherard, Jessie Zarazaga, Anthony J. Petrosino
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Engineering co-design projects have great potential for developing sustainable solutions to global environmental and social crises. Rooted in sociocultural and sociomaterial theories of learning and activity, we examined a group of engineers, architects, and community members who gathered in rural Tanzania to co-design a sustainable roof tile. Using tools from microethnography and interaction analysis, we demonstrate how the successful co-design of the roof tile required collaboration between individuals (from different disciplinary, linguistic, and cultural backgrounds) and materials. This collaboration illuminated how the spatial and temporal trajectories of one material, rice husks, was critical for the design of the roof tile. This research highlights the central importance of local knowledge, systems thinking, and spatiotemporal reasoning for sustainability-focused engineering co-design.

papers.title: Amplifying Teacher Voice in Collaborative Research
papers.authors: April Luehmann, Elizabeth A. van Es, Adma Gama-Krummel, Alison Munzer, Elizabeth Wilson
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Research practice partnerships (RPPs) are a promising approach to transforming educational practice by amplifying the voices of teachers. This approach is especially powerful for disrupting educational inequities by positioning local actors as experts to generate solutions and take action. This cross-case study examines how engaging mathematics and science teachers in collaborative inquiry gave voice to teachers’ experiences as they sought to transform their instruction for equity and justice. Informed by process and practice theory perspectives, we describe how the social arrangement of cowriting supported teacher researchers in generating new concepts and practices for equitable and just instruction. We identify four specific practices - gaining clarity and consensus on equity for STEM instruction, generating representations, thinking through example cases, and cycles of feedback and accountability. Together, these practices enabled teachers to contribute to knowledge generation by advancing theory on instructional practice for justice-oriented practice through experimentation and analysis of teaching practice.

papers.title: Design Considerations for Evaluating Middle School AI Knowledge
papers.authors: Xueru Yu, William Gelder, David Touretzky, Christina Gardner-McCune, Judith Uchidiuno
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: K-12 students need to understand technical and ethical knowledge about Artificial Intelligence to utilize ubiquitous AI-powered technologies responsibly. Recent studies have explored ways to teach AI to K-12 students effectively, but little is known about ways to assess their learning. In this study, we describe how five computer science teachers from urban and rural Georgia school districts designed, adapted, and implemented assessments in their classrooms while teaching a middle school elective course aligned with the Five Big Ideas of AI. Analyzing artifacts from 201 students, we explore the efficacy of different assessment instruments co-designed with teachers, measuring students’ understanding of sensors and the societal impacts of autonomous vehicles. We suggest design considerations for AI knowledge assessments to meet the needs and challenges in diverse classroom contexts.

papers.abstract: Here we introduce a “Disciplinary Analytics” approach to helping learning scientists see and understand research communities and themes in the field. papers.title: Learning to Serve: Building a Research-Practice Partnership Informed by Ethnic Studies to Improve Higher Education for Asian American and Pacific Islander Students
papers.authors: Ung-Sang Lee, Odorico San Nicolas, Xinghua Wu, Mike Hoa Nguyen, Federick Ngo, Caroline Hong, Amy Wan, Annabelle Park, Soniya Munshi
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Federal Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander Serving Institutions (AANAPISI) funding is intended to serve the racialized needs of Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) students in higher education (HE) in the United States. This requires institutions, and practitioners within them, to learn to move beyond colorblind norms in HE and offer race-conscious programming. We report on how a research-practice partnership (RPP) between an AANAPISI program and a research team organized learning to ensure the AANAPISI program responds to the racialized contexts and needs of AAPI students. We share three core practices in the partnership that organizes learning: building on Asian American and Ethnic Studies, leveraging interdisciplinary expertise, and engaging in multi-level sensemaking.

papers.abstract: This paper explores justice-centered sensemaking and practice among future educators within the context of a redesigned future educator technology course at a Primarily White Institution (PWI) that brings together sociocultural theories of learning with Afrofuturist principles of learning and design. Specifically, this paper highlights justice-centered educator reflection and practice or Afrofuturist pedagogical prototypes within course final projects. These prototypes embody learning around four main Afrofuturist principles: justice-centered, future-oriented, tech-mediated, and collective. Findings from this study point to the importance of tech-mediated co-design with youth for the imagination and enactment of more just learning futures and technologies.

papers.title: Orientations to Material Agency in Science Learning
papers.authors: Anastasia Y. Goodwin, Jessica Watkins, Yeung Tang
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In the absence of adequate conceptual and methodological frameworks to notice how materials contribute to ontological shifts in science learning, it becomes difficult to set up conditions for these shifts to occur. We present our framework of orientations to material agency in order to recognize when materials become more than mediational tools of learning and instead gain a social presence as agentic participants that help build scientific knowledge. We illustrate this framework through examples of interactional experiences of secondary school science teachers, showing how orienting to material agency can begin to move them toward shifts in how they view and value the non-human in science. This in turn demonstrates ways in which working with materials has the potential to become central to culturally rich engagements in science learning.

papers.title: Curriculum Routines and a Community Builder AI Agent: Synergy to Mediate the Convergent Tendencies of AI
papers.authors: Jeffrey B. Bush, Quentin Biddy, Michael Alan Chang, Greg Benedis Grab, Thomas Breideband, Tamara Sumner, William R. Penuel, John Weatherley, Tilak Singh, Sidney D’Mello
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: AI technologies, while powerful and the subject of much innovation, have inherent bias towards convergent thinking: reproducing and mimicking patterns already seen in its training data. Learning sciences and CSCL research focus on studying tools, including AI, in authentic spaces where diversity of thought and contributions are highly valued. Focusing on an AI agent designed for supporting socio-collaborative learning in classroom spaces, we explore how these design tensions can be mediated through boundary-spanning curriculum routines. This analysis provides a roadmap from theory to practice for AI powered tools in classroom spaces that aim to leverage diversity in collaborative learning while mitigating the harms of over-attending to convergent thinking.

papers.title: Charting the Learning Sciences Neuroverse: Theorizing and Building Neurodiversity-Affirming STEM Education
papers.authors: Sofia Tancredi, Crystal Menzies, Rachel Bonnettte, Rachel Lambert, Edmund Harriss, Zeynep Akdemir-Beveridge, Arash Esmaeili Zaghi, Connie Syharat, Katherine Lewis
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: The neurodiversity paradigm, originating from the autistic community, is reshaping the scope and approach to research on human cognition and sociality across fields, from psychology to medicine. Neurodiversity calls for a valuing of neurological diversity, critiquing deficit-oriented framings of minoritized neurotypes such as autism and dyslexia. This symposium challenges the learning sciences to reckon with this emerging paradigm’s implications for the core theory, approaches, and aims of the field, focusing on possibilities within STEM education research.

papers.title: Enhancing Student Metacognitive Thinking and Content Learning in Chinese and Science Classrooms with Generative AI Chatbots
papers.authors: Siyun Chen, Guangji Yuan, Chew Lee Teo, Raymond Kangshun Chan, Xinyi Soh, Zhijin Han, Xin Pang, Yaling Wang, Tsui Lan Yap
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study explores the practical application of a chatbot driven in Chinese and Science classes, focusing on cultivating students' metacognitive thinking and guiding students' subject learning. The chatbot embedded prompts are designed to stimulate students' inquiry skills, guide subjective learning, and metacognitive thinking. At the same time, teachers have designed supplementary prompts to provide scaffolding support for students' interactions. This two-tiered design approach ensures that Fairbot can both serve as an effective learning assistant and align with subject-specific teaching frameworks. The study involved 94 fifth-grade primary school students and two teachers, and the data sources included classroom observations, teacher reflections and student feedback. The findings show that Fairbot demonstrates its potential in supporting reflective thinking, teaching guidance, and text comprehension. This study highlights the potential of AI tools in classroom while pointing out the importance of integrating AI capabilities with instructional strategies through collaborative instructional design.

papers.title: Teaching Machine Learning as Adaptive Design Work
papers.authors: Victoria Delaney, Megan Selbach-Allen
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: To broaden and improve machine learning (ML) education, researchers must partner with teachers and study the affordances and challenges of ML instruction. Yet, most teachers are not ML experts and may need curricula that align ML concepts with their disciplinary expertise. This study explores three cases of classroom enactments of Mathematics of Facial Recognition (FaceID): five co-designed ML lessons aligned to high school statistics standards. Each teacher was encouraged to adapt FaceID to meet their instructional goals. Drawing from Brown’s Design Capacity for Enactment framework, we examine the frequency and substance of teachers’ adaptations of FaceID, and the design resources that enabled their adaptations. We found that teachers’ prior knowledge of ML, their statistics pedagogical content knowledge, and their knowledge of students supported their adaptations. From these findings, we illustrate triumphs and challenges that teachers who are new to ML may face when enacting ML lessons.

papers.title: Interdisciplinary Curricular Co-Design: An Interaction Analysis of Teacher-Researcher Collaboration
papers.authors: Emily Oswald, Crina Damşa
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Drawing on a prominent theorization of collaboration, this paper analyzes interaction between a teacher and a researcher engaged in curricular co-design. The episode occurred during a process to develop a new interdisciplinary teaching sequence for secondary students on the sustainable use of electric vehicle batteries. The analysis illustrates the dynamics of collaboration in curricular co-design, highlighting joint work on the problem of what topics to teach. The participants’ work on this problem proceeded by co-elaborating candidate topics; evaluating the suitability of topics for the teaching at hand; and reformulating one topic in light of participants’ knowledge and expertise. This activity involved the teacher and researcher orienting to different knowledge resources, only some of which had been introduced in the task. This empirical illustration demonstrates how collaboration in the domain of curricular co-design may proceed, and contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how teachers and researchers learn in co-design processes.

papers.title: Teacher Co-Design for Student-Driven Authentic Research with Community Partners
papers.authors: Dongni Guo, Jianwei Zhang, Thomas Underwood, Ding Lei, Alae Sherafat, Ge Song, Lana Hower, Jennifer Muirhead, Jean Kerr
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Using an interactional ethnography approach, this study traced the two-year co-design process of three teachers to support student-driven authentic research at an innovative high school, collaborating with community partners. Grounded theory analysis of teacher interviews, lesson documents, and teacher meeting observations revealed six learning design areas, including ill-defined goals, supportive materials and student-driven learning processes. These elements initialized and evolved over time through co-design by complex partnerships involving interdisciplinary teachers, researchers, and business partners.

papers.authors: Aditi Wagh, Jennifer Elisabeth Mesiner, Daniel Wendel
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: There is a need to examine how to support teacher uptake of computational modeling in science classrooms. This poster presents code-the-familiar modeling to foster teacher uptake of computational modeling using code. Drawing on a case study of two high school teachers from a research-practice partnership, we examine data from professional development and interviews to illustrate how teachers shift in their uptake, and share two lessons learned: Supporting bite-sized changes and leaning into teachers’ conceptual expertise.

papers.title: Centering the Lived Experiences of Youth Who Have Been Marginalized to Co-Design Social Justice Campaigns
papers.authors: Jaleesa Trapp
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This paper examines the design of the Youth Activism and Advocacy program within the Clubhouse Network. Young people at ten of the Clubhouse sites around the world used their creativity, lived experiences, and civic imagination to develop and sustain social justice campaigns in their communities. This paper focuses on the design elements that allow young people who have been marginalized to leverage their lived experiences in their research, development, and implementation of their campaigns. Qualitative results indicate that providing participatory design training to the adults supporting the campaigns allowed the youth participants to take relevant civic action that led to positive impacts within their communities.

papers.title: Data Reels: An Analytic Approach to Creating Data Stories in Video Analysis
papers.authors: Amy Stornaiuolo, Rabani Garg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the data reel as an analytic approach to working with video data. Like social media reels in which users curate and layer together multimodal content, data reels are short, annotated texts that stitch together video and other multimodal clips to ‘story’ the data. This paper describes how data reels emerged as an analytic approach in a design-research study about youth writing with generative AI. In illustrating how youth writers developed strategies to ensure their writerly voices were not overpowered by AI, we sought to use the methods of the medium to create data stories with screen capture video and other multimodal data collected at different points in time. We found that data reels served as a form of multimodal analysis that made researchers' interpretive work visible and opened space for sense-making with significant (often overwhelming) amounts of video data.

papers.title: Long and Winding Road to Coconstructing Knowledge in Design-Based Research Practice Partnerships
papers.authors: Matan Barak
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Design-based research-practice partnerships (RPPs) bridge research and practice through shared design and knowledge co-construction. This paper examines two frameworks – design cycles and boundary crossing – while arguing they often understate inherent conflicts. Analysis of RPP data reveals how conflicts are minimized, sometimes marginalizing perspectives. Two additional frameworks – the narrative fiction act and the crossroad – are introduced as metaphors to understand discord's transformative potential in strengthening collaboration and promoting inclusive knowledge co-construction in design-based RPPs.

papers.title: The Evolution of Shared Artifacts in CSCL: A Knowledge Synthesis Intervention for Productive Collaborative Discourse
papers.authors: Xinran Zhu, Bodong Chen
papers.design_stakeholders: Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: In CSCL, productive collaborative discourse requires continual advancement of student ideas, often through the creation and modification of digital artifacts. To support this process, this study proposes a knowledge synthesis intervention, supported by technological and pedagogical designs, to facilitate the continual development of digital artifacts in a graduate class. To examine the enactment of this intervention, we asked: How did the knowledge synthesis artifacts facilitate the progression of collaborative discourse? How did they facilitate the development of shared group artifacts? Findings revealed diverse ways in which synthesis artifacts facilitated discourse navigation, fostered various knowledge practices, and facilitated the evolution of group artifacts. This study contributes to CSCL and online learning research by facilitating knowledge synthesis and examining its role in deepening collaborative discourse, generating technological and pedagogical designs applicable in broader contexts.

papers.title: Visualizing Local Data: Facilitator as Technology Conduit when using ArcGIS StoryMaps for Collaborative Map Building
papers.authors: Heather Killen
papers.design_stakeholders: Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Within a collaborative map-building experience, the six participants, all women between the ages of 45 and 85, chose a hands-off approach to ArcGIS StoryMap technology, instead insisting the facilitator act as a technology conduit. This choice, which contradicts commonly held ideas about the importance of hands-on technology design, produced no discernable negative impact in participant’s sense of agency or engagement. Rather, participants report that avoiding direct engagement with technology enhanced their design experience.

papers.title: Constructions of Feasibility within Expansive Designs for Justice with Communities
papers.authors: Michael Alan Chang, Antti Rajala, Thomas M. Philip, Arturo Cortez, Mia Shaw, Jarmo Lehtinen, Ilona Taimela, Jorge Eduardo Garcia, Aditya Vishwanath, Roy Pea, Nicole Mirra
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Design-based research (DBR) has served as an important methodological building block for researchers interested in working with communities to envision equitable possibilities for learning, particularly ones that differ from the status quo. Especially within these expansive design contexts, feasibility is a thorny issue precisely because it has historically been leveraged as a rigid, objective means to delimit what is possible in the world as it is, as opposed to what it could be. At the same time, we cannot ignore issues of feasibility if our goal is to realize expansive designs in real learning environments. This symposium brings together five papers across different phases of DBR and collectively illustrate a conception of feasibility that is dynamic, contextual, and contested. We design this symposium specifically to engage the learning sciences community about how such conceptions of feasibility can open up expansive possibilities for design.

papers.title: Learning from Failure Through Game Testing Feedback in Virtual Collaborative Design
papers.authors: Shulong Yan, Yu Xia
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study investigates how learning from failure can be supported through game design feedback activities in a virtual collaborative environment. Through analyzing video recordings of three checkpoint sessions in a two-week virtual game design camp with nine youth participants (ages 8-13), we identified six feedback styles and examined how designers responded to feedback. Our findings reveal that game design feedback in virtual environments transcends traditional linear relationships, forming a complex discursive relationship among testers, designers, and game artifacts. Screen sharing emerged as a crucial boundary object, facilitating communication and transforming traditional critique sessions into collaborative learning experiences. Facilitators played vital roles by modeling playfulness, vulnerability, and productive failure responses. The study demonstrates that successful virtual design feedback requires thoughtfully curated environments that balance structured facilitation with playful engagement. These findings have implications for design education in virtual settings and suggest new approaches for supporting learning from failure in collaborative contexts.

papers.title: Collaborative Inquiry into Climate Change Information Literacy: A Participatory Approach with Young Learners
papers.authors: Matthew Li, Aimee Chen, Qingna Jin
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This study explores how participatory research and mentorship enhance critical information literacy (CIL) regarding climate change information. Grounded in socio-constructivist theory, the research involved a Grade 11 student mentor working with Grade 6 students. Findings indicate that through collaborative activities, students developed their knowledge about climate change-related topics and strategies for critically evaluating digital information, demonstrating increased empowerment and engagement.

papers.title: Designing for Expansive Forms of STEAM Disciplinary Engagement
papers.authors: Carrie Tzou, Elizabeth Starks, Veronica Cassone McGowan, Bryan White, Jordan Sherry-Wagner, Symone Gyles, Forrest Bruce, Christa Haverly, Mario Guerra, Megan Bang, Angela Booker
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Increasingly, calls from within the natural and computational sciences are recognizing the need for more expansive forms of disciplinary theory building and practice to connect social theories in the study of natural systems. Within science education and science teacher education, there is an increasing recognition of the need for expansive forms science teaching that connect sociopolitical contexts of science with both the professional learning of teachers and the science taught in K12 classrooms. In this symposium, we explore designs for expansive STEAM disciplinary engagement across classroom, professional learning, and informal Indigenous STEAM settings to understand the ways in which work at the edges of disciplines can transform STEAM teaching and learning for educators and students.

papers.title: Curation As Design: Co-designing Learning Experiences for Public School Education System
papers.authors: Sadaqat Mulla, Anil Mammen
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This practice-oriented paper shares insights from a research-practice partnership for designing learning experiences through curation of open educational resources (OERs). The collaboration aimed to improve classroom interactions, inclusivity, and learning outcomes in secondary schools by maximizing the pedagogical affordances of Interactive Flat Panels (IFP). This paper identifies the curation process as a complex exercise entailing design iterations while negotiating stakeholder expectations and outlines the intricacies and challenges faced during this process. It highlights how the curation team navigated these challenges to co-design learning experiences, emphasizing that pedagogically informed curation is not just about identifying relevant educational resources and mapping to curricular requirements – it is very much a design process. Exploring the practice of curation as design, the paper reveals emergence of negotiated space in a research-practice partnership and shares insights about the considerations involved in OER curation for large-scale implementation in a state education system.

papers.title: Authenticity and Entomology Knowledge in Science Classrooms
papers.authors: David Stroupe, Megan Walser, Peter White
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: A long-standing goal of science education has been for students to engage in “authentic” science. This goal of authentic science has appeared in many policy documents, and most recently, in the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS, Achieve, 2013) in the United States. Thirteen years after the release of NGSS, we still wonder about how to support students to engage in “authentic” science in classrooms. Our presentation will examine relationships between authenticity, epistemic agency, and uncertainty, and equity. The presentations will approach the topic in two ways: expectations and norms for students, and the role of teachers. Students may be engaging in “authentic” science when they are exercising epistemic agency. We will conclude with questions for the field to consider.

papers.title: Design Future(s) Collective: New Directions for Educational Design Research
papers.authors: Anna Keune, Eve Manz, Christina Siry, Jasmine Y., Jennifer Rowsell, Kathrin Dörfler, Kristiina Kumpulainen, Kylie Peppler, Meike Schalk, Naomi Thompson, Pierluigi D’Acunto, Sara Wilmes, Susan Jurow
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Advancing new directions in design research is crucial, especially as our understanding of learning is confronted by novel semi-autonomous and AI technologies, social phenomena, and global environmental crises. This symposium seeks to advance a vision for the future(s) of educational design research and consider questions that rupture core assumptions about design in the learning sciences. These include who and what design agents are, how sustainability can become core to educational design, and how design processes and responsibilities can shift considering new design purposes and partners. The papers present four contributions to design research, allowing us to explore: (1) Commitments and groundings for design, (2) lifecycle approaches made visible when materials are treated as contributors, (3) the importance of new co-analysis approaches, and (4) the unfinished and unexpected nature of educational design.

papers.title: Attending to Teacher Perspective on the Role of Network Visualizations in the Humanities
papers.authors: Kyle M. Dunbar, Jerika Miller, Jess Alanís, Merijke Coenraad, Kalani Craig, Joshua Danish, Mengxi Zhou
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: To provide students with opportunities to develop data and network literacy in K-12 learning, we aim to understand how to support teachers in their design and implementation of network visualization lessons. This study examines teacher reflections on the enactment of network visualization lessons in middle school humanities classrooms, a relatively nascent field. Teacher adoption of new practices like network visualization requires changes in knowledge and attitudes that are influenced by and have influence on teachers’ implementation of these new strategies. We used Clarke and Hollingsworth’s Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (2002) to identify shifts in teachers’ knowledge and attitudes when implementing these lessons. We found student social and cognitive engagement salient for teachers, impacting their changes in beliefs about network visualizations in the humanities. Findings indicate professional development for network visualization in the humanities should be designed with a focus on student connections and interests as well as curricular alignment.

papers.title: Centering Community-Rooted Actions of Hope: Beyond Knowledge Monoculture
papers.authors: Miwa A. Takeuchi, Deborah Dutta, Fernanda Coelho Liberali, Tyrell Anderson, Racquel Banazsak, Michael Bakal, Michael Cole, Moises Esteban-Guitart, Lisa Ghost, Kris D. Gutiérrez, Shakhnoza Kayumova, Meixi, Erma Mujic, Samira Mukherjee, Preeti Patil, Antti Rajala, George Spears, Darci Ann Sigana
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Our symposium is a confluence of researchers/pedagogues/designers/practitioners who embrace porousness of these identity categories, toward collectively questioning and challenging knowledge and environmental monoculture (Shiva, 1993). We recognize the resurgence of endangered ways of knowing and ways of living as a necessary intervention to environmental destruction and coloniality. While facing the overwhelming devastation of environmental degradation and repercussions from globalization and colonialism, we refuse to cede with ontological negation (Bang, 2020). Instead, we together seek to ground ourselves in community-rooted praxis and pedagogy of hope (Freire, 1992; Gutiérrez, 2016). We collectively present locally and globally relevant socio-environmental issues that arose from communities beyond academic siloes. Together, we highlight community-based actions of hope representing diverse geographical localities and histories. Collectively, we gesture toward knowledge polyculture that is life affirming and orients us toward plural alternative visions of multi-species flourishing.

papers.title: Generative AI in Project-Based Learning for Sustainable Development
papers.authors: Davinia Hernández-Leo, Emily Theophilou, Shatha N. Alkhasawneh
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) offers potential to enhance learning scenarios. However, research on specific use-cases and roles within educational frameworks is limited. This paper focuses on UNESCO’s Education for Sustainable Development framework and its recommendation to use Project-Based Learning (PBL) to develop key-competences for addressing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The research investigates expert teachers' views on the potential for human-AI collaboration, focusing on the role of genAI in use-cases designed to enhance individual and collaborative learning within PBLxSDG. A workshop involving 33 participants yielded 11 use-cases. Along with 10 use-cases derived from the literature and evaluations from participants, forming the foundation of our analysis. Insights from our analysis saw genAI assuming diverse roles for human-AI collaboration within PBLxSDG. However, concerns were raised about overreliance on AI, learning outcomes, and the need for teacher guidance. This work provides insights for educators and researchers exploring genAI implementation in collaborative, active learning scenarios.

papers.title: High School Teachers’ Approaches for Integrating AI Literacy into Planned Instruction: Uniformity or Heterogeneity?
papers.authors: Ibrahim Oluwajoba Adisa, Christopher Mah, Victor R. Lee
papers.design_stakeholders: High School Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: While various frameworks exist to promote K-12 AI education, little is known about how teachers bring AI literacy into their classrooms. In this study, we examined how two teachers designed and implemented AI literacy in their individual classes. Using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to analyze co-design records and interviews, we found that both teachers shared a common goal of enhancing student learning with AI but diverged in how they emphasized foundational and technical understanding of AI versus responsible and practical use. These varied approaches highlight the complexity of AI literacy and illustrate that a one-size-fits-all model does not apply. By examining these multiple pathways, we offer insight into how educators can tailor AI literacy instruction to meet diverse student needs and instructional contexts.

papers.title: Developing a Counter-Space for Learning, Belonging, and Becoming in and Through Calculus
papers.authors: Siqi Huang
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a counter-space that integrates disciplinary rigor with identity-empowering practices to support historically marginalized STEM students at the University of California, Berkeley. Situated within a social design experiment, the counter-space fostered a collaborative community where students engaged deeply with core calculus ideas while cultivating positive mathematical identities and a stronger sense of belonging. The paper elaborates on the key design principles of the counter-space as well as its structure and curriculum. Analysis of students’ weekly reflection journals revealed significant gains in students’ mathematical understanding, performance, confidence, sense of belonging, and self-perceptions as capable mathematical thinkers. This study offers a model for disciplinary-rigorous and identity-empowering counter-spaces that institutions can adapt to address systemic barriers and promote sustainable STEM pathways for historically marginalized students.

papers.title: Examining Mentoring in a Professional Society: Early Insights from a New Design Case in the Geosciences
papers.authors: Adam Papendieck, Megan Tucker, Samira Rosario Martinez, Stephen K. Boss, Elizabeth Long, Katherine K. Ellins, Julia A. Clarke
papers.design_stakeholders: Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Mentoring is increasingly recognized as an important developmental process in STEM; however, most research and programming has focused on academic research contexts. Here we examine a pilot mentoring program in a geosciences professional society, investigating situated perspectives on mentoring in this distinct setting. Early findings from surveys and participant observations highlight unique affordances of professional society mentorship for identity development and culture change, emphasizing the importance of this context for design and research.

papers.title: Spirituality and Linguistic Plurality in Learning: Centering Wholeness on the Land with Refugee Learners
papers.authors: Sophia Thraya, Miwa A. Takeuchi, Jrène Rahm
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Children’s wholeness, particularly for racialized, multilingual refugee learners, is often fragmented in institutionalized educational spaces. This work highlights spirituality as a vital, yet often silenced, dimension of learning. Within a co-designed land-based program, educators and children collaboratively created a multilingual poster that honored diverse spiritual and ecological connections to soil. This pedagogical moment illuminates the transformative potential of centering children’s languages, spiritual knowledges, and relational ties to land in educational spaces.

papers.authors: Linette Victor, Jerika Miller, Jessica McClain, Judi Fusco, Joshua Danish, Wendy Walter, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Dalila Dragnić-Cindrić, Krista Glazewski, Haesol Bae

It explores a two-day workshop focused on practitioner-identified challenges. The research highlighted the need to shift from researcher-centric approaches to balanced, collaborative methods. This study provides insights for developing bidirectional learning models that center practitioners' perspectives, aiming to bridge the gap between research and educational practice through more equitable and transformative partnerships.

papers.abstract: The COALESCE framework extends DBIR principles to AI-powered educational technology development, positioning educators as active co-creators. This study evaluates COALESCE through its application in designing an AI-assisted lesson-planning tool. Our findings show how deep educator involvement supports trust, ownership, and domain-specific improvements in AI-generated content. We discuss implications for participatory AI design and offer a replicable model for context-aware, educator-aligned innovation.

papers.title: Cultivating Wellbeing in Learning Environments: Storywork, Kinship and Affect With Lands and Waters
papers.authors: Megan Bang, Miguel Angel Ovies-Bocanegra, Cece Hoffman, Forrest Bruce, Nikki Barry, Jordan Sherry-Wagner, Anna Lees, Kaleb Germinaro
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: There is a pressing need to reimagine education for social and ecological well-being. Persistent inequalities and underimagined forms of education not only prevent these developments, but continue to erode human well-being and creativity. Substantive changes require paradigm shifts in foundational conceptualizations of educational challenges and possibilities, including transformative understandings of students’ sense making and holistic cultural and intellectual lives. This symposium brings together scholarship focused on storywork, relationality or kinship and affect in the design of learning environments. Further the studies in this symposium are specifically focused on these dimensions of learning tied to field based or land and water based learning environments.

papers.title: The Making of Competent Outsiders: Using Epistemic Practices of Science to Enhance Student’s Critical Evaluation of Misleading Scientific Explanations in Classrooms
papers.authors: Noora F. Noushad, Susan A. Yoon, Clark A. Chinn, Zhitong Yang, Claire LeBodvidge, Huma Hussain-Abidi, Kyle Hunkar
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Eroding public trust in science has become a critical challenge due to the proliferation of misleading scientific explanations in the media. Scholars recommend integrating scientific epistemic practices into classrooms to help students become competent outsiders—citizens who can critically evaluate misleading scientific explanations without being subject matter experts. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how teaching these practices influences students’ evaluation of misleading scientific claims. This study examines the performance of four high school students during a two-week inquiry unit where they used scientific epistemic practices to construct explanations for containing an epidemic similar to COVID-19. Students then evaluated misleading scientific explanations on three newspaper articles. Analysis of their pre- and post-responses revealed that students improved in identifying and critiquing erroneous representation of science in these articles. We discuss the implications of using epistemic practices to develop competent outsiders in classrooms.

papers.title: Building Capacity for Educational Innovation: Strategies to Scale Computational Thinking Pathways in K-12 School Districts
papers.authors: Kelly Mills, Merijke Coenraad, Kyle M. Dunbar, Alessandra Rangel, Quinn Burke
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: There are many examples of innovation within education, but oftentimes innovation happens in a single classroom or school without being able to scale to an entire district or beyond. When scaling innovations, it is difficult to adapt to new contexts and student needs while promoting authenticity and sustainability. In this paper, we examine how three districts within a research-practice partnership scaled computational thinking (CT) pathways to provide CT learning opportunities across their district. We first detail case studies of how the three districts scaled their CT pathway implementation. Then, we present cross-district strategies promoting depth, spread, ownership, and sustainability: Clarity and Awareness, Alignment with Existing Priorities, Standards and Curricula Integration, School Based Leadership, Sustained Professional Learning, and Student Voice. These strategies support educational leaders to strategically design implementations that promote the scale of new initiatives.

papers.title: Advancing Ecological Conceptualizations of Learning through Studying World-Making Practices in Interdisciplinary Education
papers.authors: Lina Markauskaite, Baruch B. Schwarz, Nurit Novis-Deutsch, Adam Papendieck, Natasha Arthars, Hanni Muukkonen, Crina Damşa, Etan Cohen, Julia A. Clarke, Rachelle Esterhazy, Einat Heyd-Metzuyanim, Anu Kajamaa, Boris Koichu, Liv Mathiesen, Michal Tabach, Hilde Wøien, Anat Yarden, Yael Kali, Peter Reimann

papers.abstract: Learning for complex world-making practices cannot be understood without embracing theoretical perspectives that acknowledge the complexity and dynamics of the interconnected and distributed among people and their environments nature of such practices. This symposium aims to advance the conceptual foundations for studying learning as an ecological phenomenon. It builds upon the recent special issue of Journal of the Learning Sciences, “Beyond disciplinary engagement: Researching the ecologies of interdisciplinary learning” (Markauskaite et al., 2024). The papers in this special issue adopted diverse ecological perspectives to study interdisciplinary learning, offering unique insights into how personal resourcefulness, teamwork dynamics, institutional processes, and disciplinary cultures intertwine in this context. However, the underpinning conceptual issues of theorizing and empirically studying learning as an ecological phenomenon were not specifically examined. In this symposium, we extend this work to unpack different ecological conceptualizations of learning and discuss critical directions for further development.
