papers.title: Exploring Students’ Perceptions of Contextualized Computing in an Introductory Computing Science Course for Non-majors
papers.authors: Yinmiao Li, Melissa Chen, Ayse Hunt, Michael S. Horn, Eleanor O’Rourke

papers.abstract: Introductory computer science courses for non-majors (CS0) aim to increase diversity and highlight the relevance of computing across disciplines. To enhance the accessibility and engagement of CS0, researchers have explored contextualized computing, where computing is integrated with another subject, to teach course content. While research has explored various designs for contextualized courses, we know less about how contextualized computing tasks impact students’ learning experiences. Through the lens of metacognition and affect, we conducted a secondary qualitative analysis on daily diary and retrospective interview data from 20 students in a CS0 course that applied coding to different contexts. Our findings demonstrate that students’ feeling of knowing and their perception of the task are two central themes that shape their affect and interest in the course. We conclude with design suggestions for contextualized computing in CS0 to better support students.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the Learning Lab intervention to address systemic injustice in a predominantly White school district in the U.S. Specifically, we focus on how a diverse group of students, parents, educators, and administrators fostered students' transformative agency amidst contradictions and the diverse motives members brought to the Learning Lab to create district level policy named Protocol for Addressing Harassment and Discrimination. papers.authors: Brande M. Otis, Sepehr Vakil, Kihana Ross, Nichole Pinkard, Arikpo Dada, Shai Moore, Peri Green

papers.title: “It Goes Both Ways”: Envisioning Mutually Compassionate Relations between Teachers and Students
papers.authors: Michael Alan Chang, William R. Penuel, Thomas M. Philip
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Cultivating compassion has been shown to support teachers in caring for non-dominant youth in K-12 schools. While students often show compassion for other students, students’ skillful caring for teachers has remained relatively underexplored. Here, within an intergenerational co-design context with students and their teachers, we explore the pedagogical conditions that support students and teachers to surface and develop the conditions for mutual compassionate relations. Our findings demonstrate that, when used in tandem, a User Persona activity and Theater of the Oppressed Activity supported students and their teachers in adopting compassionate stances towards each others’ suffering, thereby creating the relatively unusual opportunity for teacher participants to vulnerably share their suffering incurred while trying to care for the students. We conclude by showing how cultivating mutual compassionate relations as a goal of co-design spaces can open up expansive objects, including systemic changes motivated by the interlinked suffering of intergenerational stakeholders.

papers.title: Intertwining Epistemic and Relational Work in Scientific Modeling
papers.authors: Eve Manz, Annabel Stoler
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: As youth and teachers engage in modeling conversations, they are simultaneously negotiating how knowledge is generated and how people are accountable to each other in a community. Typically, design and analysis have privileged the epistemic focus, including within a recent emphasis on sensemaking and collective knowledge development. In this paper, we examine epistemic and relational work during science classroom modeling conversations. We share a close analysis of a typical conversation structure, where individuals present models and other students evaluate and build from their ideas. We show how classroom members experienced relational challenges and opportunities in these conversations. We also examine how alternative structures taken up by teachers and students presented different opportunities and constraints. This work contributes to the field’s understanding of science practices and suggests implications for work on evaluation and care in science classrooms.

An experiment was conducted with one control and two experimental conditions: 1) producing ID outcomes with a generic GenAI bot (ChatGPT), and 2) producing ID outcomes with a Co-instructional designer bot customized with a single ID model (Systems approach). ID outcomes were blindly analyzed by experts in ID and evaluated using a pairwise comparison technique, where two ID outcomes are holistically compared to determine which one is better. papers.title: Building Shared Meanings: Large-Scale Constructionist Professional Development in the Global South
papers.authors: Mariana Lederman, Paola Ricci, Fabio Cerqueira Campos, Nathan Rabinovitch, Claudia Peria, Paulo Blikstein
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: Implementing and sustaining large-scale technology-focused educational programs in public systems requires robust professional development (PD) programs. In this paper, we share our experience of creating shared meanings for teachers during a 17-week PD program as part of introducing a large-scale public policy that implements digital fabrication and maker labs in Brazil’s largest municipal public school network. We illustrate how a well-structured PD program, featuring constructionist hands-on investigative, creative, and reflective workshops, is key to instigating mindset changes and building shared meanings among teachers, which are essential for the implementation and sustainability of a large-scale educational reform centered on systems thinking, investigation, making, and project-based learning.

papers.title: When Transgression Becomes Developmental – Ethical-Political Empowerment Through Expansive Learning and Transformative Agency
papers.authors: Heila Lotz-Sisitka, Maletje Mponwana, Rob O’Donoghue, John Bhurekeni, Ben de Sousa, Wilma van Staden, Arorise Sibanda, Experencia Jalasi, Laura Conder-Aller, Juan Carlos Sandoval Rivera
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Learning in times of climate change and ongoing inequality, requires ethical-political engagements that are transgressive of unsustainable norms, including those left in coloniality’s wake (Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2017; 2023). However, a question arises as to when such transgressions become developmental (cf. Williams et al., 2018). This symposium addresses this question through analysis of five formative interventions (cf. Engeström et al., 2014). The studies advance a decolonial dialectic of transformation, enacted as a process of expansive, transgressive learning and emancipatory agency from below, grounded and expanding from living heritage and place; reflexively returning to it. Here co-engagement in expansive learning actions strengthen African relationality (Ubuntu relations), and collective (emancipatory) transformative agency (cf. Engeström and Sannino, 2010; 2021; Lotz-Sisitka et al., 2023). Studies emphasise ethical-political expansion of the object of activity in expansive learning struggles to address environmental degradation, gender and racial discrimination, and exclusions of living heritage, youth, and indigenous cultures.

papers.title: Designing Scientific Practices Through Exploration, Collaboration, Creation, and Reflection: A Multi-Layered Model
papers.authors: Xueqi Feng, Yuqin Yang, Carol K. K. Chan, Jianhua Zhao
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examined a knowledge-building environment mediated by Knowledge Forum®, enhanced by a multi-layered scientific practices model designed to foster collective knowledge advancement. Forty-eight Grade 5 students participated in scientific practices centered on Lighting a Small Bulb, engaging in the model comprising four interconnected layers: exploration, collaboration, creation, and reflection. Quantitative analyses revealed significant improvements in students’ contributions to collective knowledge advancement across phases, with notable variations among high-, medium-, and low-contribution groups. Qualitative findings illustrated how students engaged in increasingly sophisticated scientific practices, transitioning from group exploration to scientific communication, extending scientific field knowledge, and incorporating epistemic reflection. This study highlights the role of the multi-layered model in scaffolding young learners to participate in authentic scientific practices, promoting collective epistemic agency and sustained knowledge advancement.

papers.title: “How Can We Lift Them Up and Make Them Feel That Their Voices are Valuable?”: A Case Study of One Teacher’s Pedagogical Responsibilities
papers.authors: Annabel Stoler
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Science teachers seeking to engage students in collective sensemaking must attend to not only students’ epistemic development, but also to their relationships with each other. This paper examines the intertwined epistemic and relational responsibilities of science teaching through a case study of Ms. Shaw, a fifth-grade teacher. The analysis reveals the responsibilities that Ms. Shaw felt in creating an equitable learning environment where all students felt valued, as well as emerging tensions between her epistemic and relational goals for classroom activity. Ms. Shaw’s reflections highlight the complexity of navigating these dual responsibilities as well as the difficulties in disrupting inequitable patterns of classroom participation.

papers.abstract: In response to research arguing for integrating culture into science education contexts, this analysis looks at how culture was an actor with agency in an elementary teacher professional development (PD) project. Drawing on actor network theory, we asked: How does culture as an actor exercise agency to shape an assemblage within elementary science PD activity? We focused on the Korean language and 도토리묵 (dotori-muk: Korean acorn jelly) as manifestations of Korean culture within our assemblage. Microgenetic analysis revealed three transitions where relationships between actors were re-assembled and translated into new learning trajectories. papers.abstract: Teachers play a crucial role in shaping learning opportunities within classrooms, and yet their voices are often missing from educational design efforts. Our work resists the normative roles ascribed to teachers in world-making efforts and partners with them to (re)design a justice-oriented high school computing program. We present findings from a collaborative video analysis of a co-design session (~40 minutes) where nine high school computing teachers, two researchers, and a senior designer engaged in a design activity uncovering what it means to center justice within computing classrooms and to support new teachers to teach justice-oriented computing. They emphasized ongoing professional and personal growth, relatable professional learning experiences, and opportunities for reflection as teachers become “co-conspirators” for social justice. We discuss findings in connection to STEM teacher preparation and solidarity.

papers.title: Fostering Inclusive Practices in Educational Policy Reform
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Elizabeth Schrader

papers.abstract: In this paper, we examine how a group of diverse stakeholders in a predominantly White school district expanded their practice of inclusion through an intentional co-design process. The Aleph School District (ASD) in New England, U.S., co-designed a protocol for addressing discrimination and harassment, a persistent concern affecting historically marginalized students with and without disabilities. The school district partnered with the local university and employed the Learning Lab intervention (Bal et al., 2016; 2018), an inclusive, process-oriented methodology to enable the local stakeholders most impacted the chance to better understand and address their concerns. papers.abstract: Schools are not neutral sites of learning, and (re)produce white supremacy through seemingly neutral teaching and learning interactions. Heeding the calls to incorporate the sociopolitical into science education, we developed a high school biology unit that critically engages genetics education. The unit highlights environments as not neutral and not benign, and that the inequities plaguing these environments were created through structures and forces of oppression. We analyzed post interviews to understand the extent to which students developed non-deterministic views of genes and sociopolitical awareness of the nature of the environments in gene-environment interactions. Our findings suggest that students understood trait variation as resulting from interactions between genes and the environment and were able to reason about the environment in these interactions as non-neutral and harmful for marginalized communities. However, they struggled to explain how gene-environment interactions work at the biological level and the intentionality of environmental inequities.

papers.authors: Angela Calabrese Barton, Edna Tan, Wisam Sedawi

papers.abstract: Minoritized parents have historically been sidelined in parent-school engagement opportunities. Research-practice-partnerships (RPP) have been one way to bring together stakeholders across communities in collective sense-making. papers.authors: Wisam Sedawi, Angela Calabrese Barton, Edna Tan

papers.abstract: Supporting parental/familial presence in STEM education requires forging new parent-teacher relationships and epistemologies to bridge home and school. Through the FamJam project, using participatory critical design ethnographic methods, we collaborated with an urban public-school teacher, immigrant students, and their mothers to foster familial rightful presence in a STEM unit focused on engineering for sustainable communities. Our study employs the “Identities-in-Practice” framework to investigate how relationships among mothers, teachers, and students cultivate emerging epistemologies and new social learning practices. papers.abstract: World-making has not been commonly considered in data science education. We are scholars working in diverse contexts united by a broad interpretation of what data is and can be. By entering a collaborative, sustained dialog, grounded within and across our research projects, we recognized that adopting a world-making lens supported us to envision the now and future more pluralistically and agentically by recognizing the multidimensional, multifaceted world(s) present in our research. High school students used The Hidden Village – Online, a motion capture video game that allows them to create new content through movements and perform these movements while evaluating the veracity of geometric conjectures. papers.abstract: Effective researcher-coach relationships need reciprocal learning, which allows practitioners to share valuable contextual knowledge while researchers share evidence-based ideas. Findings reveal that initial tensions foster deeper understanding through negotiated power exchanges. The study underscores that openness, mutual trust, and reflective dialogue are essential for sustainable partnerships, advancing the understanding of power dynamics in researcher-coach collaborations.

papers.title: Competing to See
papers.authors: Elizabeth Metts
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study explores how an experienced mathematics teacher organized and disciplined a student’s perception during a lesson that incorporated data science practices. As data science gains national attention, this research addresses the complexities teachers face in integrating data practices into mathematics curricula. Drawing from a multiyear design-based study, the analysis focuses on classroom interactions during a “Barbie Bungee” lesson, highlighting competing disciplinary goals of mathematics and data science. Using an interactionist perspective and the construct of disciplined perception, this paper illuminates the breakdowns and interactional work involved in aligning student understanding with mathematical concepts like slope while grappling with noisy, real-world data. This case underscores the need to address competing disciplinary practices in classroom contexts, offering insights into fostering interdisciplinary engagement and reshaping data science integration in mathematics education.

papers.abstract: This study examines how boundary infrastructures in Research-Practice Partnerships (RPPs) facilitate learning and collaboration between a rural school district and two universities. Using the Learning at the Boundaries framework, we analyze design team meetings, teacher feedback, and co-designed curricular materials. Our findings highlight the roles of boundary spanners, practices, and objects in bridging gaps among stakeholders and fostering sustainable collaboration. This research contributes to the learning sciences by documenting effective processes for organizational learning, emphasizing the importance of structured co-design in educational improvement.

papers.title: Designing Chatbots for Place-based Environmental Education
papers.authors: Ashley Hernandez, Jennifer Pei, Ha Nguyen, Sara Ludovise, Rossella Santagata

papers.abstract: Place-based education facilitates understanding of the links between human activities and ecosystems. We outline the design process to integrate local knowledge into Large Language Models (LLMs) chatbots to promote environmental education. We find that chatbot responses vary with chatbot profiles in discussing climate change’s root causes and economic impacts. Our chatbots ask more questions to connect to students, compared to a default LLM. We discuss how to design LLM-based technology to support learning about place.

papers.title: Leveling Up Inclusive and Collaborative Learning Through Experiential Game Design Model
papers.authors: Emre Dinç, Jose Sandoval-Llanos
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: We present the Experiential Game Design Model as a student-centered approach to fostering collaborative learning through game design. Rooted in experiential learning theory and Vygotsky’s emphasis on social interaction, this model addresses common challenges, such as conflict and disengagement, by focusing on four core components: knowledge, identity, culture, and values. Students collaboratively plan, design, and revise games. Teachers guide students through iterative development and reflective practices. Emphasizing culturally responsive pedagogy and shared goal-setting, the model offers a framework where students can express unique perspectives and engage in meaningful and collaborative learning.

papers.title: From Questions to Impact: Unveiling Teachers' Power to Support Actionable Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Nan Wang, Nancy Law
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: With the widespread adoption of e-learning and advances in educational data mining and AI, research publications in learning analytics (LA) have surged in recent years. However, LA has not significantly impacted learning and teaching in authentic educational contexts. As teachers’ uptake of LA depends on whether their pedagogical concerns are addressed, it is important to understand teachers’ LA needs in relation to their learning design contexts. We report on an investigation of the nature of teachers’ LA questions at different levels of design granularity—a learning task, a task sequence, or a course—identified through a systematic review of published empirical LA studies that engage teachers at some stage of the LA research process. The findings show that teachers seek actionable feedback on learning processes and progress. However, available LA often focus on course-level performance or task-level engagement, yet actionable insights need to consider relationships among a sequence of tasks.

papers.title: Co-Creation of Visual Stories: Representing Agency for Mathematics Learning with Forcibly Displaced Students
papers.authors: Shima Dadkhahfard, Miwa A. Takeuchi
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: This study examines the impact of visual stories co-created with forcibly displaced children to express their agentic possibilities within the school context, particularly in mathematics classrooms. Using participatory co-design processes, six arts-based workshops were designed and facilitated for families to collaboratively illustrate stories of agency, identity, and belonging. Findings, in the form of co-designed visual stories, demonstrate students' use of visual representations to reclaim agency after experiencing forced displacement. The visual stories also highlight educators' roles in facilitating in-school mathematics learning experiences. This research underscores the potential of arts-based co-creation as a tool for children experiencing intersectional oppression to voice their lived experiences.

Through this structured poster session, we expand theoretical underpinnings and attend to the ways that emerging scholars from different areas of the learning sciences are taking up the mantle.

papers.title: Mirroring What’s in the Shared Repertoires of Two Communities of Practice: A Cultural-Historical Perspective Using Generative AI
papers.authors: Thérèse Laferrière, Elizabeth S. Charles
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This paper explores the development of the shared repertoires (Wenger, 1998) of two web-supported Communities of Practice (CoPs). The co-authors of this paper were the initiators of these CoPs and continue to be involved in them. Using the shared repertoire of each of these communities as a lens, the evolution of their activity was explored. Referring to the CHAT’s change lab process of mirroring to participants their past activity (Engeström, 1987, 2015), two generative AI tools were prompted to focus on the websites of the two CoPs, especially collaborative activities and artefacts, and to ‘report on’ the evolution of their shared repertoires. Accounts underwent human validation. For ethical reasons, no transcript was analysed of the interactions between the participants that may have led, through meaning negotiation, to the production or use of artefacts as well as to problem setting, problem solving or knowledge building. Results show that 1) the generative AI tools were accurate in their ‘reports’; and 2) identified possible limitations in the shared repertoires; such observations providing topics for future negotiation of values among members and between these communities.

This study explores opportunities for co-designing inclusive makerspaces for broadening participation and fostering socio-emotional learning by combining AI-generated art and tangible tools.

papers.title: Future Trends in Digital Learning for Enabling Holistic Student Development: Review of Educational Policy
papers.authors: Chandan Dasgupta, Natasha Dmoshinskaia, Marie Xhauflair, Sara van der Linden
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; K-12 Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: There is a push to adopt educational practices fostering holistic student development in K-12 due to current uncertain times. To understand what these new practices entail, we take a global policy perspective and identify trends that will likely shape the future of education focused on holistic student development. We identified eight trends for future-focused education and discuss how these can be mapped to holistic student development. These trends represent three interconnected dimensions of education – Why (goals for education), How (the design and organization of education), and What (the content of education). We identified 20 sub-trends that reflect the multifaceted nature of the trends. Teacher capabilities required to facilitate the implementation of these trends were described as well. These provide a robust base for (re)imagining how to prepare K-12 students (and teachers) as change-agents instead of only a workforce.

Each project exemplifies how co-design not only creates more effective and responsive tools but also builds communities and promotes systemic change. Attendees will gain practical insights into recruiting and engaging co-designers, navigating challenges, and sustaining equitable collaborations, with a focus on scaling these practices for broader impact. Through these examples, the symposium illustrates how co-design can reimagine learning systems to better serve all learners and create more equitable educational experiences.

papers.title: Towards Decolonizing Agency in Addressing Racialization of Behaviors in Settler Colonial Schools
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Aydin Bal, Dosun Ko, Linda Orie, Elizabeth Schrader, Jahyun Yoo

Six dimensions of decolonizing agency emerged based on our research-practice partnership to address the racialization of behavioral problems in a school serving Indigenous students.

papers.title: Enhancing Elementary Teachers’ AI-TPACK through a Professional Development Workshop
papers.authors: Ying-Tien Wu, Li-Jen Wang, Tsun-Hui Shih
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary / Early Childhood Teachers; Students & Learners
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI presents new opportunities for personalized learning and adaptive instruction in elementary education. However, many teachers lack the necessary AI-TPACK competencies to integrate AI effectively. This study examines the impact of a two-day professional development workshop designed to enhance elementary educators' AI knowledge, pedagogical applications, and ethical awareness. Findings from pre- and post-workshop assessments indicate significant improvements in AI proficiency, instructional integration, and ethical considerations. Educators reported increased confidence in using AI for lesson planning and student engagement, yet highlighted the need for ongoing training in ethical AI use, privacy, and fairness. These results underscore the importance of structured, hands-on AI training to support responsible and effective AI integration in classrooms. Future research should explore long-term impacts on teacher engagement and student learning outcomes.

papers.title: Desiring Learning in a Hospital School Arts Education Program
papers.authors: Christian Ehret, Ji Yoon Chung
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study analyzes desire as a dynamic force driving learning in a children’s hospital school arts education program. Data come from an ongoing, three-year co-design project addressing a challenge for hospital schools in designing learning opportunities that move students to participate through ongoing social and emotional disruption, and that maintain continuity in students’ sense of themselves as learners. Analysis shows how students’ affective revelations while working collaboratively on a map-based art project are inseparable from the ongoing production of desiring learning that is essential to their elective participation. This conceptualization of affective revelations contributes to learning sciences research theorizing how affect relates to learning and learning ecology design. Drawing on critical design-based research in the learning sciences, the project challenges infirming narratives of children undergoing hospitalization, and it illustrates how coming to feel differently is an essential dimension of coming to know differently while learning in the arts.

papers.title: Exploring the Intersection of Emotions and Epistemic Engagement
papers.authors: Eleni A. Kyza, Christiana Varda, Susan A. Yoon, Jooeun Shim, Weiyi Zhang, Vivian Leung, Zoe Nguyen, Tiina Törmänen, Hanna Järvenoja, Chew Lee Teo, Carol Chan, Aloysius Ong, Trang C. Tran, Joseph L. Polman, Iris Tabak, Nirit Reznick, Josh Radinsky, David Hammer

papers.abstract: This symposium explores the complex relationship between emotions and epistemic engagement across diverse learning contexts. Emotions, integral to cognitive processes, can enhance epistemic engagement by triggering curiosity, focus, and critical evaluation, especially when knowledge-building is the goal. This session will present studies on the relationships between emotions and epistemic cognition, within different thematic areas, such as social media interactions, bioinformatics education, data-infused interdisciplinary learning, and knowledge-building collaborative online platforms. Each presentation aims to uncover the roles emotions play in fostering or inhibiting epistemic actions. The discussant will synthesize insights from these studies to shed light on the generative potential of emotions in supporting critical and reflective engagement. The outcomes of this symposium can deepen our understanding of the role emotions can play in fostering epistemic engagement in formal and informal settings.

papers.title: Co-Designing and Teaching Science in Students’ Heritage Language
papers.authors: Ana Bañuelos, April Valdez Garcia, Perla Ramos Carranza, Alejandra Yep, Jasmine Nation
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Through university-community partnerships (UCPs), educators and practitioners identify practices that leverage students’ assets to enhance science learning. We study Nuestra Ciencia, a UCP where undergraduates teach microbiology in Spanish to elementary students in bilingual schools in the United States. We describe how the program’s design transformations impacted elementary and undergraduate students’ perceptions of science, scientists, and their heritage language. Design-based framing enabled ongoing programmatic adjustments while identifying best practices for asset-based science learning. From analyzing 200 pre-post questionnaires, we found elementary students learned microbiology content and felt more like scientists after activities. We also analyzed focus groups with 34 Spanish-speaking undergraduates, revealing three themes related to science identity: using Spanish as a tool, reframing science as relevant, and healing their younger self. We describe how participants’ perceptions of science and science education helped us understand the impact of the program and ways to improve it.

papers.title: Culturally Revitalizing STEAM Learning as a Space for Ecologically Situated Identity Work
papers.authors: Kay E. Ramey, Alicia Velasquez, Kirk Cheyney, Margaret Beck, Marianna Cota, Bianca Schamberger, Zahra Baradaran Shoraka
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: This study examined the experiences of Indigenous American youth and adults participating in a culturally revitalizing science, technology, engineering, arts, and math (STEAM) learning workshop. Specifically, we examined how this workshop provided space for participants to explore, develop, and express their individual and collective identities through their creation of ribbon skirts and ribbon shirts, incorporating electronics and digital embroidery, and pottery beads painted with locally sourced, earth-based pigments. We analyzed video recordings, interviews, field notes, surveys, and participant-created artifacts, collected as part of a participatory design study. Drawing on situated, sociocultural, and ecological theories of learning, we identified five types of identities expressed and developed through design work during the workshop: individual identities, family identities, tribal identities, Indigenous community identities, and dual or hybrid identities. We also identified aspects of the workshop design, such as intergenerational, community based, and participant-driven learning that supported the exploration and expression of these identities.

papers.title: Decolonial and Postcolonial Possibilities for the Learning Sciences
papers.authors: Joe Curnow, Rishi Krishnamoorthy, Ali R. Blake, Gerardo Villagrán Becerra, Sophia Thraya, Arundhati Velamur, Ishita Pradhan, Tatiana Becerra, Mahati Kopparla

papers.abstract: This symposium brings together Learning Sciences scholarship rooted in diverse geopolitical contexts from different histories of coloniality. We engage with decolonial, anticolonial, and postcolonial theory within specific contexts to reconsider normative ideas about learning and knowing. Together the papers serve as an invitation and a provocation to unsettle normative colonial knowledge practices within the Learning Sciences. We ask, ‘how might the Learning Sciences rearticulate theories of learning that serve life rather than capital accumulation, and racialized and gendered hierarchy?’

Qualitative analysis of student-generated metaphors revealed their epistemic notions of research as an ever-deepening process with uncertainty. Students’ metaphorical embodiments of research make abstract epistemic notions tangible, shaping their ongoing engagement in research work.

papers.title: Teachers Grappling with Representing Historical and Political Contexts in Science Curriculum Materials
papers.authors: Katarzyna Pomian Bogdanov
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Science learning environments have been primarily shaped by Eurocentric ideologies that center science as a set of culturally neutral and color-blind systems which science teachers are often reluctant to acknowledge. However, current reforms in the U.S. ask science teachers to connect science to real world environmental and societal problems, which create opportunities to teach in more justice-oriented ways. This requires challenging shifts in teachers’ approaches. Co-design environments can be helpful learning spaces for teachers because they support deliberations around dilemmas through which teachers can deepen their content knowledge or practices. Dilemmas during design revolve around curricular values teachers bring into the design process. papers.title: Climate Education for Justice: Navigating Geographies, Data, and Agency
papers.authors: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Hosun Kang, Mary K. Stapleton, Kathryn Lanouette, Katie Headrick Taylor, Giulia Tasquier, Wonyong Park, Noemi Waight, Christopher St. Vil, Jennifer Tripp, Fatemeh Mozaffari, Helen L. Fitzmaurice, Jacob C. Barton, Michelle H. Wilkerson, Emily V. Reigh, Gita Dunhill

papers.abstract: This symposium brings together diverse research exploring the intersections of climate change education, social justice, and community empowerment. As climate change increasingly impacts vulnerable populations, the importance of integrating justice-oriented approaches in K-12 education becomes urgent. Studies featured in this symposium investigate how climate education can leverage community strengths, foster empathy through quantitative reasoning, and critique the racialized nature of data to promote environmental justice. Presentations will examine innovative uses of data in teaching, highlighting its role in addressing inequities and engaging students in climate justice advocacy. Key themes include fostering climate agency through cross-disciplinary approaches, rethinking the "natural disaster" narrative to highlight systemic inequalities, and designing professional learning programs to equip educators with tools to navigate climate-related injustices. Together, these studies underscore the need for inclusive, justice-focused climate education that empowers students to engage meaningfully with the climate crisis and advocate for systemic change.

papers.abstract: There is consensus that computational modeling can support integration of science with computing for student learning. However, it can be challenging for teachers to gain comfort with this relatively new practice, reconcile how it relates to science, and recognize its pedagogical value. Drawing on notes from co-design sessions, teacher interviews and student worksheets, we illustrate how a focal teacher shifted from initial reluctance to taking ownership of designing and teaching a computational modeling lesson sequence. We also briefly show how her students took up this work. Finally, we reflect on the importance of leveraging teachers’ existing domain and pedagogical expertise as we bring these new practices into their classrooms.

papers.authors: Chaeyeon Kim, Fangli Xia, Joel P. Beier, Michael I. Swart, Kelsey E. Schenck, Mitchell J. Nathan

papers.abstract: We explored how students interact with a computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) system for embodied learning in geometry. With The Hidden Village-Online (THV-O), fifteen high school students (six dyads, one triad) used movements to construct directed actions that depict geometry transformations collaboratively. THV-O is a web-based CSCL video game that uses a motion-capture to detect players’ movements, save movements they create, and play those created by their peers. papers.abstract: Gamebooks are non-linear narratives where reader choice determines what happens next in the story. papers.abstract: Centering students’ Funds of Identity (FOI) in the classroom is important for moving towards asset-based frameworks for learning. papers.abstract: The field of Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) is expanding, allowing researchers to capture rich, fine-grained data on learning processes in a variety of learning environments. Teacher candidates participated in immersive French and Korean science lessons where multilingualism and multiculturalism were centered as resources for learning. Analyzing post-course interviews with participants who referenced the experiences showed how the immersive experiences supported teacher candidates to recognize multilingual learners’ assets that support scientific sense-making. What participants recognized differed based on the language of instruction, facilitation style, and content of the activity, suggesting implications for equity-oriented research and course design.

The case analysis highlighted a teacher’s year-long professional development experience focused on integrating computational thinking. The evolving conjecture map provides a framework to trace and understand relationships between the learning designs, activities, and teacher outcomes. Using rich data from the teacher's experience, the study tests and refines the hypothesized connections laid out in the original conjecture map to build an understanding of effective computational thinking professional development design.

papers.title: Creating Thirdspace: Indigenous Learning Lab for Survivance
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Aydin Bal, Dosun Ko, Linda Orie, Morgan Mayer-Jochimsen
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Racialization of school discipline is an enduring systemic problem in the United States. This formative intervention study is based on a collaboration with 14 school stakeholders: American Indian students, parents, community members, and educators at a rural high school in a community-driven problem-solving process called Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL). Members analyzed the root causes of the racialized school discipline and created a new behavioral support system. Utilizing critical geography and decolonizing methodology, this formative intervention study aimed to unpack how ILL members formed Thirdspace—a space of resistance, possibilities, and hopes—to address enduring racial disproportionality in school discipline. Members challenged race-neutral representations of space, mapped out dystopia, revitalized American Indian epistemology, and mapped out a real utopian vision of schooling.

papers.title: Co-Designing an AI Tool to Support Discourse Based Math Instruction in a High-Dosage Tutoring Context
papers.authors: Chelsea Brown, Jeffrey B. Bush
papers.design_stakeholders: Math Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: TalkMoves is an AI assistive tool that provides automated feedback to educators to support their daily teaching practices. While originally designed for classroom math teachers, this tool can be useful in a broader context. The University of Colorado Boulder and Saga Education formed a co-design team tasked with re-contextualizing TalkMoves for coaches of novice math tutors to use in their ongoing professional development. To effectively adapt an existing technology to a new problem space, the co-design team iteratively exchanged ideas of what exactly TalkMoves could achieve, as well as the specific needs of the coaches. Facilitators used strategies such as communal orientation, expansive dreaming, backcasting, and revoicing to promote productive collaboration. Three main goals emerged: maximize opportunities for user agency, center design around goal setting, and integrate the tool into the existing workflow. Any adaptation of an AI tool would benefit from this approach.

papers.authors: Sarah C. Radke, Lisa Hardy, Jennifer B. Kahn
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: This paper examines youth storytelling during co-design of an identity-expressive educational game for learning data science. Using interaction analysis of co-design interviews with middle school students, we explore how storytelling allows participants to (a) use existing game elements to position themselves and (b) express their interests and identities through imagined game futures. We argue that analyzing youth's interactive storytelling and identity enactments during co-design can inform the development of game narratives that represent diverse youth. Our findings contribute to the design of inclusive virtual worlds for STEM learning that celebrate youth identities and experiences. We discuss implications for engaging youth voices in the co-design process and creating educational games that resonate with diverse learners.

papers.abstract: This article presents a qualitative experiment with instructional designers. It aimed at designing asymmetrical multiplayer role-playing scenarios using a digital visual modeling tool with two designers. We want to know if co-design with the tool RLG Maker can assist in developing scenarios and what the obstacles are. We assume that collaboration during the design phase encourages the construction and enrichment of the scenario. We have analyzed the speech acts of four groups of instructional designers and have confirmed that the tool, used collaboratively, encourages the scripting of these games. Some aspects need to be reworked, in particular navigation in the tool, to improve usability.

papers.title: Preparing Graduate Students to Enact Equity-Oriented Pedagogies for Science Outreach Programs
papers.authors: Erica Light, Enrique Suárez, Lynn Adler
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; Youth & Adolescents; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Informal Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) outreach programs have been promoted as a mechanism to redress under-representation of minoritized students in STEM fields. However, few studies have investigated how to support program leaders and implementers, who are often graduate students, to teach science for equity and justice. In this design-based research study, we explore how professional development (PD), grounded in situated teacher learning theories, facilitated life science graduate students’ development of a multilevel, equity-oriented pedagogy for a science outreach program with minoritized youth. Through qualitatively analyzing PD video recordings, interviews, and artifacts for evidence of graduate students’ attention to micro, meso, and macro levels of equitable science education, we found that situated PD challenged their baseline conceptions of equity work and aligned their multilevel pedagogical praxis. Our study contributes to scholarship on how to support informal science educators’ learning towards equity-oriented pedagogies.

papers.title: Expansive Ways of Knowing and Improving: Using Equity Tools and Approaches to Support Equity of Participation in Learning Activities
papers.authors: Ali Raza, William R. Penuel, June Ahn, Kara Jackson, Daniel L. Reinholz, Cathery Yeh, Hakeoung Hannah Lee, Frank Fischer, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: This symposium brings together projects that are developing and testing equity analytics in education. Equity analytics are a genre of learning analytics that attends to the distribution of and participation in opportunities to learn, with attention to inequities linked to students’ social identities and wider systems of marginalization and oppression that impact classrooms and schools. Each of the projects has engaged not only in developing tools for gathering data related to inequities of participation but also for helping educators take action to reduce inequities in their classrooms and schools. Findings generated from each project illustrate how, through working in close partnership with educators, equity analytics systems can be developed that are feasible to use and that can inform practice. These projects also underscore the challenges of implementing equity analytics within inequitable systems that emphasize goals of accountability and with educators with varied conceptions of what constitutes equitable participation and learning.

papers.title: Comparing In-person Vs. Online Professional Development for Brazilian Science and Technology Teacher Trainers
papers.authors: Paola Salmona Ricci, Tatiana F. Laganá, Claudia Godinho Peria, Cassia Fernandez, Paulo Blikstein, Martha Bevilacqua
papers.design_stakeholders: K-12 Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Pre-service and in-service teacher education in Brazil has increasingly moved online, with 6 out of 10 teachers graduating from exclusively online programs (Todos pela Educação, 2022). While there could be benefits to online learning in terms of access, evidence from the learning sciences and teacher accounts call for limitations of such approach, and more in-person learning experiences in the context of school systems in developing countries. Based on evidence from the design and implementation of a hybrid professional development constructionist learning program, we aim to shed light on the challenges and affordances of synchronous, asynchronous, and in-person modalities for professional development.

papers.authors: Yasmin B. Kafai, Chris Proctor, Shuang Cai, Francisco Castro, Victoria Delaney, Kayla DesPortes, Christopher Hoadley, Victor R. Lee, Duri Long, Brian Magerko, Jessica Roberts, Benjamin R. Shapiro, Tiffany Tseng, Vera Zhong, Carolyn P. Rosé

papers.abstract: The pervasiveness of Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning in the everyday lives of young people—impacting how they connect with friends, listen to music, play games, or attend school—coupled with the accessibility of applications powered by large language models and discussions about algorithmic justice has called for developing AI literacy in K-12 education. Panelists will (1) address questions about how deeply do we want students to engage with AI, (2) examine in which ways critical agency can be developed, and (3) discuss implications for research and designs how teachers and learners can develop and integrate conceptual and critical understandings about Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning that are increasingly important to participate in the world.

papers.title: Developing Relational Agency for Addressing Racialization of School Discipline in the U.S
papers.authors: Dian Mawene, Dosun Ko, Aydin Bal, Linda Orie, Elizabeth Schrader, Jahyun Yoo, Morgan Mayer-Jochimsen
papers.design_stakeholders: Educators & Practitioners; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: In this paper, we adapt Edwards's (2005; 2007) concept of relational agency, situating it within the context of racialized schooling in the U.S. We posit that the ability to recognize and leverage others' support in addressing a complex problem necessitates the ability to acknowledge the historical legacies of systemic racial violence ingrained in everyday school practices. To support our theoretical argument, we present a case from Indigenous Learning Lab (ILL), an inclusive task force established to design a culturally responsive behavioral support system addressing racial disproportionality in school discipline in a predominantly white high school serving American Indian students. Specifically, we emphasize the relational agency of Mr. Archer, the school principal, as he worked together with ILL members, particularly American Indian members.

papers.authors: Adiel Benjamin, Yotam Hod, Shiri Kashi, Liat Rahmian, Sahar Tueg
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: The digital age has drastically changed many aspects of human life, with significant implications on education. Transforming school structures so they can foster digital age competencies sustainably is a grand challenge for educational systems and research. Learning community pedagogies provide a potent way to approach this challenge. We present a large, multi-year study that is supported by the national department of education that attends to the learning processes, outcomes, and infrastructures necessary to do this.

papers.title: Playful Frameworks of Research: Play And Its Potential in Researching Learning Alongside Youth
papers.authors: Zachary Ryan
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Recent efforts to envision expansive frameworks of participatory research alongside communities, including youth, have produced particularly rich work in the learning sciences. In this paper, I frame the concept of play as a boundary practice while working alongside youth and unpack its potential role in the research process. I make a call for scholars to begin thinking deeply about how play can be integrated throughout the research process to better center the contributions of youth participants we research alongside. In doing so, I offer three primary dimensions of research that play is best suited for: 1) In the selection of methods, including research sites, topic of study, and methods of data collection; 2) In the capacity of participatory design research projects aimed at fostering material change in communities, and; 3) In the co-analysis of qualitative video data alongside youth to deepen our understanding of meaningful learning situated within playful interaction.

papers.title: Learning to See Beyond Anthropocentric Views on Bodies Through Transdisciplinary Soil-Centered Pedagogy
papers.authors: Miwa Aoki Takeuchi, Sophia Thraya, Tatenda Mambo
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: To examine how bodies were conceptualized by children and teachers who were co-learning, we analyzed videos, photos, and drawings that children, teachers, and researchers collectively created during a program that we designed with a soil-centered pedagogy. In our transdisciplinary program design, we centered intergenerational land-based wisdoms of communities with experiences of forced displacement in relation to soil, fungi, animals, and plants. Our findings depicted the ways in which the notion of bodies was expanded through the participants’ interactions on the land. As previously hidden connections became visible, children and teachers both came to see the interconnectedness between human bodies and the bodies of nonhumans, such as mushrooms and soil. This paper calls for our field to further amplify its learning to see the interconnectedness between more-than-human bodies and human bodies, thus moving beyond anthropocentrism.

papers.title: A Preliminary Model for Responsive Co-Design
papers.authors: Hillary Swanson, LuEttaMae Lawrence
papers.design_stakeholders: Science Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Education reform is pushing teachers to teach in ways that are unfamiliar and which present challenges. One approach to helping teachers build comfort and capacity for implementing new and innovative teaching strategies is co-design. In this paper, we build on prior research to concretely articulate how researchers can partner with teachers to foster mutual learning, build capacity, and cultivate comfort through responsive practices. Towards this, we present a theoretical model of a vision of co-design, which we call responsive co-design. Our model borrows concepts from responsive teaching, which is a family of pedagogical approaches that seek to elicit and build on student ideas. Our vision of responsive co-design expands how co-design has been theorized to include the generative, asset-based, and inclusive practices of responsive teaching.

papers.authors: G. R. Marvez, Greses Pérez

papers.abstract: STEM learning games can engage students across subjects at higher levels than lectures and provide avenues for students to “try on” STEM careers. However, many STEM learning games are not positioned around specific STEM concepts within a real-world community, a drawback for teaching highly contextualized topics in STEM. In this study, we investigate learning experiences of undergraduates who co-created game prototypes focused on a local engineering challenge in partnership with young students in local culturally and linguistically diverse communities. Preliminary findings indicate undergraduates understood and were critical towards the iterative co-design process while refining their games in collaboration with younger community members. This research suggests involving undergraduates in designing engineering learning games with and for local communities fosters an understanding of engineering practices and establishes a connection between undergraduate students and the communities they may eventually serve, offering a valuable educational approach for first-year undergraduates majoring in engineering.

papers.abstract: Integrated STEM education innovation cherishes the goal of preparing students for a rapidly changing world by developing their ability to generate knowledge and solve complex real-life problems. To achieve this, it is necessary to support teachers in curriculum innovation that aligns with the goals of the innovation. However, school-level constraints often hinder teachers’ innovation and learning. Fostering a conducive environment for innovation might necessitate school leaders’ learning. To investigate how teacher learning for STEM education innovation relates to school leaders’ learning, we used the MultiLevel MultiScale Model as a framework to examine the interdependency of learning at various levels for scalable innovation. This study was conducted within a design-based implementation research context and involved a multiple case study with four schools. The results showed that the engagement of school leaders can facilitate the establishment of school-level infrastructures that support teacher learning for curriculum innovation, leading to positive innovation outcomes.

This suggests how vital it is to invite collaborative partners to engage in the co-design process as part of design-based research.

papers.abstract: This research explores the integration of Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) with game-based learning (Garcia,2020; Aleman,2023; Zhou et al., 2023) to enhance student engagement and collaboration in addressing polarised societal attention. Using a co-design methodology, students transition from passive subjects to active researchers, creating and interacting in a game-based learning environment that reflects contemporary issues such as structural oppression, privacy infringements, and environmental unsustainability. In the "Fall of Artica: A Way Back Home" (FoA) game, in the University of Toronto Schools’ Grade 11 visual art and Grade 7 English classes, students work in groups to tackle wicked problems in a novel dystopian narrative. Through collective inquiry in diverse social contexts, students develop new narratives and visual assets, foster collective inquiry and critical reflections in visual and literary art creations, and form a culture of community and practice. Through several rounds of enhancement of this game-based curriculum, we have articulated a YPAR framework that could potentially advance FoA and other serious game-based research regarding student engagement beyond participation in gameplay, co-design, co-contribution, and content creation.

papers.abstract: In this study, we used Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to illustrate how nursing students’ behavioral patterns related to their practice of clinical judgment, person-centered care, and professionalism competencies in a virtual patient simulation, Elsevier’s Shadow Health Digital Clinical Experiences™ (DCE). We obtained transcripts (dialog and click data) from two undergraduate nursing students who completed one Contact Tracing assignment and two Focused Exam assignments using the DCE. We coded each learning event based on three behavioral interaction types and six cognitive and psychosocial competencies recommended by nursing regulatory bodies. Findings revealed that the two students made strong connections to clinical competencies through questioning the patient in the Contact Tracing assignment versus answering system prompts for patient assessment and care planning in the Focused Exam assignments. This study unpacks how simulation-based learning facilitates competency-based education for nursing students’ practice readiness, offering valuable insights for future analytics and design.

We define equitable participation as partners’ equal say in the decisions and balanced contributions to the co-design processes and outcomes. Accordingly, interviews with two teachers and three students who collaborated with researchers to revise the curriculum were analyzed to explore their perceived participation behaviors. The analysis revealed two primary themes: inclusive contributions through mediation and student-influenced teacher autonomy. Results showed that separate groups for students and teachers and mediation strategies facilitated inclusive contributions and influences on the design outcomes. In addition, strategies promoting psychological safety and balancing knowledge asymmetries were identified. The study contributes insights into achieving democratic and inclusive co-design practices, emphasizing the complexity of establishing equity in co-design partnerships.

papers.title: Newcomer Youths’ Ethical Stances in Representing War And Forced Migration
papers.authors: Santanu Dutta, Pratim Sengupta, Pallavi Banerjee
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: We illustrate how a group of newcomer (refugee) young women of color engaged in filmmaking using stop-motion animation to represent a story of a family becoming refugees in the face of war. We ask the following research question: How did the youth adopt, negotiate, and represent their ethical stances in telling stories of forced migration using stop-motion animation? Our analysis shows that through designing their narratives, and figural and gestural representations of marginal lives, bodies, and interactions, the youth centered axiological dimensions of representing violence, and amplified the ethical complexities experienced by families facing war and violent displacement. The youths’ work offers a necessary counter-imaginary for public education in which representational work through creating animations can become a context for making visible and centering ethical and affective dimensions of their experiences of forced migration that are otherwise silenced and invisibilized by the procedurality of refugee resettlement, and in their schools in Canada.

papers.abstract: This case study reveals how one teacher’s agency and leadership in a Research Practice Partnership (RPP) impacted the design of a justice-centered science unit. We analyze RPP documents and data, from design meetings, workshop transcripts, observations, and informal co-design conversations, to reveal the ways RPP activity structures helped to support the teachers’ leadership. Episode 3 reveals how conversations between the teacher and the learning scientist during unit implementation supported the refinement of the unit and reflection on teaching practice.

papers.authors: Jonan P. Donaldson, Ahreum Han, Shulong Yan, Seiyon Lee, Sean Kao

papers.abstract: This methodological paper interrogates the potential of network analysis within the design-based research (DBR) framework for improving the design of learning experiences. We present the learning experience network analysis (LENA) approach for analyzing learner-generated data about their experiences in learning activities. Utilizing a complex systems perspective, this study reveals how network analysis elucidates intricate patterns of interdependencies between experiences of struggles, aspects that worked well, and alignment of their experiences with principles from learning theories. Our findings underscore the capacity of this method to capture the dynamism and complexity inherent in learning environments, thereby informing more adaptive and responsive design strategies. This work extends the methodological toolkit available for DBR, advocating for a more complex, situated understanding of the ways in which the data-informed design can shape the learning experience from the learner’s perspective.

papers.title: Constraints and Boundaries for Collective Agency in Co-Design
papers.authors: Gavin Tierney, Kristina Stamatis
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Co-design in education has emerged as an avenue for including broader perspectives into the creation of curriculum and learning environments, while also positively impacting learning and identity development. This kind of co-design requires designers’ collective agentic participation. In this paper, we look across several sets of data to build understandings of the ways collective agency emerges and is constrained within co-design. While research has pointed to the ways that participation in co-design has potential to increase feelings of agency in practitioners and youth, there is still a need to understand the ways communities of designers build and use collective agency. Without theories that describe the ways that co-design teams leverage their collective identities toward common outcomes, we fear that the power of this kind of work can fall short of its potential.

papers.abstract: This structured poster session brings together eight presentations of research practice partnership (RPP) projects that have designed and deployed learning design (LD) tools to scaffold teachers’ learning and collaboration as designers. These tools are designed according to the design principles underpinning the respective RPP projects, playing an important role in their implementation. The LD tools presented have diverse features and functionalities, ranging from scaffolding peer review of LDs, visualization of the LD workflow, sharing of LDs for peer adoption, guidance in the design of specific learning activities, design of personalized feedback, fostering collaboration and learning of geographically distributed LD professionals, to the provision of an LD language for shared communication, layered LD decision-making and visualization of design analytics. The lessons derived provide an initial framework for designing PTLEs, highlighting three shared features: creating alternative forms of relationality, drawing on histories for transformation, and engaging in collective future-making for agentic teacher learning.

papers.authors: Annabel Stoler

papers.abstract: This study seeks to understand children’s experiences in a fifth-grade science classroom designed to incorporate the principles of collective activity, heterogeneity, and epistemic agency. Using a semi-structured interview approach, children were asked to describe their experiences within their class community. The findings reveal that the inequitable distribution of status in the classroom affected students’ engagement with science practice as well as the risks they perceived in participating in collective learning. This study provides student perspectives on what it means to engage in the practices of science and has implications for how educators and researchers attend to student experience when designing and analyzing learning environments.

papers.title: Identity, Power, and Imagination at a Children's Museum
papers.authors: Selena Steinberg, Joshua Quick, Chris Cruz-Gonzalez, Day Greenberg, Naomi G. Lau, Sarah Fox, Becky Wolfe
papers.design_stakeholders: Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: We share insights on co-design to support critical engagement with museum content towards identity development. We explore how a co-designed visitor activity can 1) support critical engagement with exhibit content; and 2) support youth to reflect on their identities and power to enact change in their communities. Data are generated in a participatory co-design process with museum leadership. We engage three themes that drove exhibit creation: identity, imagination, and power.

papers.title: Exploring the Potential of Design in Early Childhood Education for Sustainability
papers.authors: Yingqiao Du, Wanlin Zhang
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Elementary Students & Children; Educational Researchers & Designers; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Kindergarteners play a crucial role in driving sustainable changes, and there is a growing interest in combining design approaches with sustainable education. This paper presents empirical research on Early Childhood Education for Sustainability (ECEfS) conducted in China. It aims to examine the current situation of ECEfS implementation in Chinese kindergartens and investigate the role of design in promoting its objectives. Qualitative research techniques were adopted in this study, and data collected from a kindergarten were analyzed. Our findings reveal the integration of relevant practices into their nature-based learning curricula. In summary, their ECEfS-related practices fall into three design-oriented categories: a) project-based activities to foster sustainable awareness, b) environmental design to create sustainable learning spaces, and c) co-design approaches for exploring sustainable materials.

papers.title: Looking Back to See Myself: Analepsis as Tool to Deepen Proleptic Notions of Identity Development
papers.authors: Kristina Stamatis, Joseph L. Polman, Trang C. Tran, Jose Rogelio Manriquez Hernandez
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Educators & Practitioners; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners
papers.abstract: Studies of identity development have a long history in educational research; yet there remains a need to deepen understandings of ways communities who have been historically marginalized build identities across cultural contexts. Following scholars who have used the notion of prolepsis to explore youth identity development, we examine the potential for additional tools, such as analepsis, to understand the ways youth draw from family histories to inscribe themselves into the world. This study took place in a local history museum with Latine youth who co-designed a museum exhibit to represent their familial and cultural stories. Findings illustrate the potential for theoretical tools that expand upon studies of identity to unpack the ways youth draw upon the experiences of their ancestors, family members, and cultural figures to make sense of themselves in relation to their experiences as youth with cultural histories both within and outside of the U.S.

papers.title: Unpacking Paradox in Co-Design
papers.authors: Adam Papendieck, Gavin Tierney, Kevin Nguyen, Nikki James
papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Undergraduate / Graduate Students; Educational Researchers & Designers; Domain Experts & Technologists
papers.abstract: Here we examine “paradox,” a particular kind of contradiction inherent in participatory design and co-design. As with any perceived contradiction in human experience, paradoxes may urgently demand resolution, thereby motivating and orienting learning and changemaking through design. However, resolving a paradox involves grappling with an apparent antinomy between equally sound, justified or valued perspectives, processes or solutions. This may drive very rational, inclusive and well-structured co-design processes towards activities and outcomes that may seem irrational, ironically counterproductive and even absurd. We examine examples of paradox in participatory/co-design, showing how participants grapple with paradox in different ways, and how unpacking “paradox in practice” helps us understand (and potentially avoid) undesirable ends. We make the case that attention to paradox is critical for equitable design.

papers.title: Student Perspectives on Learning and Teaching Data Ethics Through Speculative Game Design
papers.authors: Nisha Devasia, Andrea Figueroa, Sarah Evans, Bernease Herman, Cecilia Aragon
papers.design_stakeholders: Higher Education Instructors / Faculty; High School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: From our smartphones to our social media, artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms are becoming ubiquitous in our everyday lives. However, the conveniences that they bring come alongside many potential social and political harms. It is imperative that members of the public develop data ethics literacy to interpret AI’s harms and benefits daily. The immersive and transformative nature of games may enable a wide range of people to explore complex ethical concepts in AI and data science through the lens of speculative design. In this project, we focus on the learning process of a diverse group of students from two universities as they embark upon a process of game design to teach ethical thinking in data science/AI. Through qualitative analysis of semi-structured interviews, we apply a speculative game design framework to identify aspects that aid student learning.

papers.design_stakeholders: Teachers; Students & Learners; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Existing research on teacher support for collaborative learning has focused on small groups in individual classrooms. The current study investigates how two teachers supported cross-classroom interaction between two Grade 5/6 classrooms. Students in the two classrooms studied human body systems for 10 weeks with the support of Knowledge Forum. While students in each classroom advanced their thinking in the discourse space of their home class, they had access to a shared meta-space for sharing knowledge advances across classrooms, presented in the format of “super notes.” Qualitative analyses of teacher interviews and classroom observations provided a detailed account of the teachers’ pedagogical approach to the meta-space and classroom support to guide students’ cross-classroom interaction.

papers.title: A Womanist Analysis of an Asset-Based Anti-Gun Violence Curriculum
papers.authors: Kayla DesPortes, Mia S. Shaw, Bella Afra Boateng, Dejarelle Gaines, Clarisa James
papers.design_stakeholders: Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers; Community Members & Partners; School Administrators & Leaders
papers.abstract: Researchers collaborated with a social justice organization to co-design a curriculum for elementary and middle school youth to create an interactive map highlighting community assets as an exploration towards how they might combat gun violence. The curriculum was designed around Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) to engage students in asset mapping for social action. However, the researchers noted a lack of guidance for addressing the systemic underpinnings of gun-violence. In response, the researchers applied a womanist lens—which reflects Black women and women of color’s everyday strategies for ending all forms of oppression—to examine how it might shape reflection and iteration on the curriculum. Analyzing curricular resources and codesign notes, the findings highlight the importance of fostering relationships to redistribute power, center dialogue for engaging in tensions, defining a collective communitarian approach with learners, supporting learners in storying their communities, and engaging in care and wellness as resistance.

papers.abstract: Mathematics and science teacher educators have worked to help current and pre-service teachers understand “computational thinking” (CT) and integrate it into their lessons. This structured poster session highlights an unexpected phenomenon we have observed across multiple contexts: teacher education efforts aimed at CT integration didn’t achieve their stated goals but somehow led teachers to rethink what counts as good mathematics/science inquiry and learning. The session aims to bring together scholars who study CT, CT integration, and STEM teacher education—the presenters and the session attendees—to explore the nature of this unexpected phenomena and brainstorm potential explanations to explore in future research.

papers.title: Reframing Design in Education: Proposing a Framework to Support Pre-Service Teachers in Adopting Designerly Stances
papers.authors: Douglas B. Clark, David Scott, Joshua P. DiPasquale, Sandra Becker
papers.design_stakeholders: Pre-service Teachers; Youth & Adolescents; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: Guided by contemporary theory and research from design fields and education, we propose a framework for conceptualizing K-12 pre-service teachers’ stances toward designerly thinking. We developed the framework following Crismond and Adams’ (2012) scholarship of integration approach combined with an inductive content analysis of 43 pre-service teachers’ conceptualizations of design across two versions of a design course. The resulting framework focuses on five dimensions including: (a) co-evolution of problem frames and possible solutions, (b) problem complexity and structure, (c) idea fluency and scope, (d) inquiry and stakeholder engagement, and (e) conceptualization of the design process. We elaborate each dimension, proposing anchor points based on the literature and an inductive content analysis of the data. Detailed examples will be presented in the conference session, and a full version of the paper is under review and is available by email from the first author.

papers.authors: Idris Solola, Hillary Swanson, LuEttaMae Lawrence
papers.design_stakeholders: Middle School Teachers; Middle School Students; Educational Researchers & Designers
papers.abstract: The Next Generation Science Standards promote students’ engagement in authentic science practices, including theory-building practices such as modeling and explanation. The role of teachers in NGSS-aligned classrooms includes devising strategies for identifying, understanding, and connecting students’ ideas. In other words, teachers are required to respond to student ideas. Yet, the demands of responsive teaching pose challenges for teachers. To address challenges and support teachers in implementing responsive teaching, we co-design classroom lessons and strategies with teachers. This paper presents our co-design approach to supporting teachers in developing responsive teaching strategies. We analyze classroom video of one teacher’s classroom from two consecutive implementations of co-designed lessons. Responsive teaching was made an explicit focus of co-design before the second implementation. We investigate the instructional moves of the teacher and present evidence that making responsive teaching the focus of teacher-researcher co-design causes a shift in the instructional moves of a teacher.

papers.abstract: Our research explored an in-service professional development (PD) program that was iteratively co-designed with educators at a rural school on the Big Island of Hawaii. Many Hawaiian schools are highly ruralized and demonstrate a dire need for meaningful PD in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Due to geographic and community considerations, in-service PD is an essential tool for improving education in low-income, rural communities. This confluence of considerations demands focus on supportive and effective training for rural and highly ruralized teachers. We situate this work in Ginsberg and Wlodkowski’s (2012) motivational framework for culturally responsive teaching which considers the conditions of attitude, meaning, competence, and inclusion. This paper examines the experiences of an Indigenous teacher with over 30 years of experience as she engages in PD that centers her Hawaiian community.
